ai-doctor-medical-students.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 18  Words: 1197/1267
================================================================================

SUMMARY

I’m confident in my mastery over what doctors do — history-taking, reasoning, communicating. I’m less confident about my continued mastery of an ever-evolving universe of facts. Training doctors in the A.I. age, then, means training them to think critically with a machine in the loop, for a speculative future of medicine that we can only glimpse.

ARTICLE

Being a Doctor Will Never Be the Same After A.I.
I’m confident in my mastery over what doctors do — and less confident about my continued mastery of an ever-evolving universe of facts.
By Rachael Bedard
Published 2026-09-25 09:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/25/opinion/ai-doctor-medical-students.html

I have a confession: A.I. is making me a better doctor. And I worry that it’s making doctors-in-training worse.

Amid our recent doom cycle about whether A.I. will lead to extreme societal harms, a parallel anxiety has taken hold in medicine about whether A.I. will one day replace physicians. In the context of that panic, I feel a little sheepish admitting that I already use the technology in my practice all the time — especially since I harbor anxieties about what its availability means for my students and residents, and therefore for the profession at large.

This summer, I used an A.I. tool — a platform called OpenEvidence, accessible only to health care providers — to help me choose antibiotics for one patient and to interpret unusual bloodwork for another. A.I. reminded me to consider migraines when a woman presented with dizziness. I chatted with the large language model about treatments for an older man with lung cancer. I have also consulted it about a rash on my father’s back, my son’s fever, a friend’s arm pain and my own difficulty sleeping.

I practice primary care, where every malady is my business. Almost every month, I’m confronted with a complaint or syndrome that I don’t recognize. I’m confident in my mastery over what doctors do — history-taking, reasoning, communicating. I’m less confident about my continued mastery of an ever-evolving universe of facts. Now, the chatbot in my pocket reassures me that I will always know enough, or have access to the cloud-based intelligence that generally does.

All of my students and residents also use OpenEvidence, however, and I worry about the consequences of introducing such a powerful decision aid so early in their careers. Not only have they memorized less than I’d like, but they can seem almost passive in their relationship to their machines.

It’s impractical and counterproductive to train physicians in 2026 without exposure to A.I. Doctoring — as opposed to writing, my other work — is not a creative act that needs to be protected from technological annexation. It’s a service that ought to embrace any resource that improves patient care. Training doctors in the A.I. age, then, means training them to think critically with a machine in the loop, for a speculative future of medicine that we can only glimpse.

I started medical school 20 years ago. Every day since, I have looked something up, skimmed a journal article or talked through a case with a colleague — medicine is a phone-a-friend profession. As a student, I walked around the hospital with “Pocket Medicine,” a standard-issue guide, tucked into my white coat pocket, and I consulted it all day long. I had to understand exactly what I was looking for when I flipped through its pages, and it could not tell me what to do with whatever knowledge I found there.

I haven’t carried “Pocket Medicine” for years. Instead, I am never without my phone. For years, I primarily took my questions to the widely used website UpToDate.com, an evidence-based medical encyclopedia. But now, several times a day, I use OpenEvidence.

OpenEvidence is trained exclusively on peer-reviewed evidence and guidelines, and includes citations for all its claims. Not every insight found there is useful or even accurate, because much of the medical literature it refers to falls short on both those counts. To use the app well, you must stay skeptical as you scroll. It does, however, allow me to trace a statement to a source so I can evaluate it for myself. OpenEvidence reports that over half of American doctors regularly use the app, and it recently announced a plan to expand free access to doctors in developing nations.

OpenEvidence and I can have an iterative conversation grounded in a case’s peculiarities, a difference in kind from when I used to look up general information and try to apply it to an individual situation. The app lets me input my patient’s labs, or upload an imaging report photo, and then offers suggestions about what it sees. Not infrequently, it suggests something I did not consider.

I’m surprised by how much I learn from, and enjoy, these interactions. More important, my patient care has improved as conversations with the agent push my thinking beyond its usual limits.

For the residents I supervise, however, the app’s speed and anticipatory helpfulness are a hindrance as much as an enhancement. When I skim a chatbot’s response to a question about back pain, I’m intuitively testing its suggestions against my hard-won mental model for how to approach back pain. Could I have developed that if I’d had a robot leading my thinking all along?

I asked Adam Rodman, a physician and A.I. researcher at Harvard Medical School, how to think about these risks. He said he shared my concern that trainees aren’t benefiting from “productive struggles” as much as their predecessors. “In experienced hands, decision support might cause a little de-skilling, but a little de-skilling probably doesn’t matter much to you,” Dr. Rodman told me. “But if you do that to somebody who has much less skill, the cognitive offloading can cause never-skilling.”

I don’t think it’s critical that my residents memorize every diagnostic protocol, just as it’s no longer critical that I recall my friends’ phone numbers. But I do want them to learn to hear problems the way a doctor is supposed to, as stories that contain clues that set off a cascade of cognitive associations. And I want them to develop the cardinal instincts that amount to good judgment in medicine: the ability to distinguish sick from not sick and to prioritize competing patient concerns, as well as the tact to effectively seek information beyond what a patient voluntarily reveals.

A.I. is only the latest tool to provoke a reckoning around which skills are truly essential to doctoring. As a student, I struggled valiantly to identify heart murmurs in my patients, even though I had access to imaging techniques that made my stethoscope somewhat redundant. Similarly, students today need opportunities to build cognitive muscles through study, even if they will seldom rely on their own memories over their machines.

Dr. Rodman shared ideas for how to help learners experience worthwhile friction despite the availability of A.I. — proposals like A.I.-free clinical reasoning sessions and A.I. literacy training. We don’t yet know, however, what caring for patients will even look like once artificial intelligence is fully integrated into medicine, nor what its capabilities will be.

Current doctors-to-be may be the most adversely affected generation when it comes to A.I. They’re training before we know enough about how to teach them well in this new paradigm. I want their patients to benefit, as I think mine are, from doctors supported by these tools. But I also want them to develop a talent for reasoning their way through complex problems full of distractions and ambiguities, and rich with emotional stakes.

The hardest parts of doctoring will stay hard, I think, even if some other tasks are made easier. Mastering those challenges will still be where the utility and the pleasure of medicine will be found. The profession has adapted to waves of paradigm-shifting technological change before, yet the privilege of taking care of people remains.

Rachael Bedard is a contributing Opinion writer, a geriatrician and a palliative care doctor.

donald-trump-administration-mean-girls.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 16  Words: 1131/1212
================================================================================

SUMMARY

I think about this a lot while watching how President Trump runs the White House and the world alongside a high school clique of dumb jocks (Pete Hegseth!) and hot cheerleaders (Natalie Harp!) and nerdy suck-ups (Mike Johnson!). My queen bee — my Regina George from “Mean Girls,” my Cher Horowitz from “Clueless” — wasn’t the president of the United States, but at the time she felt arbitrarily powerful, profoundly charismatic and definitely wealthier than I was. Mr. Trump’s favorite aide, Ms. Harp, passes the president positive news coverage and good polls like she’s the “Mean Girls” gossip Gretchen Wieners.

ARTICLE

The Mean Girls Presidency
Our government is being run by a clique of middle-aged guys.
By Molly Jong-Fast
Published 2026-09-27 10:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/27/opinion/donald-trump-administration-mean-girls.html

I was once a teenage girl, but not a very cool one. I never had the right vintage jeans. I never wore the right high-heeled Free Lance boots, the ones that all the cool girls had.

I think about this a lot while watching how President Trump runs the White House and the world alongside a high school clique of dumb jocks (Pete Hegseth!) and hot cheerleaders (Natalie Harp!) and nerdy suck-ups (Mike Johnson!). My queen bee — my Regina George from “Mean Girls,” my Cher Horowitz from “Clueless” — wasn’t the president of the United States, but at the time she felt arbitrarily powerful, profoundly charismatic and definitely wealthier than I was. She bullied me about my weight and lack of style. She had her friends shun me, too.

My peers were rewarded with the social relevance that comes from pleasing the top of the food chain. Now, looking at the White House, I almost feel sympathy for Marco Rubio, wearing uncomfortable shoes in the hopes of fitting in.

Mr. Trump’s cabinet of curiosities wears matching $145 Florsheim oxfords, gifted by the president himself. They’re reportedly eating the same “living diet,” which consists almost entirely of hunks of meat and globs of sauerkraut. (Adherents are said to include: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, Vice President JD Vance and Robert F. Kennedy Jr. himself.) Mr. Trump’s favorite aide, Ms. Harp, passes the president positive news coverage and good polls like she’s the “Mean Girls” gossip Gretchen Wieners. Other White House staffers and cabinet members have begun to emulate the president’s leggy blond echo chamber cultivator, so much so that the White House has been overtaken by a kind of sycophancy Olympics; members of Mr. Trump’s inner circle never miss the chance to praise him in televised cabinet meetings.

In short, our government is being run by a clique of middle-aged men. Mr. Rubio and Mr. Hegseth don’t drink identical iced banana bread matchas or wear pink on Wednesdays, but the social-emotional engine behind our government is the same as the one that runs the popular girls’ clique at Spence. This dynamic — more than another unnecessary war or even a cost of living crisis — will be the key to Mr. Trump’s undoing.

Historically, White Houses have been byzantine power structures with wildly elaborate interpersonal dynamics. Even George Washington’s cabinet was legendary for the fierce tension between Alexander Hamilton and Thomas Jefferson. Centuries later, Joe Biden’s White House was a story of competing fiefs, from Anita Dunn’s to Antony Blinken’s to Jeff Zients’s. In a structure like this, ideas and proposals needed to be well developed, allies needed to be gathered and, in general, bad decisions can often be slowed or stalled by the normal workings of bureaucracy.

Mr. Trump’s cabinet was picked like something out of Bama rush, and boy, does the government run like it. The president reportedly considered sizzle reels of candidates’ cable news hits; the focus was not on who was most qualified to do the job, but who managed to best dazzle dear leader. Once a cabinet member was installed in office, it seemed as if the only thing that mattered was continuing to tell the president what he wanted to hear — or saying the right thing on TV — as opposed to giving sound advice in service of the nation.

Those who didn’t do that could be dropped over the slightest misstep, and plenty of people who have spent much of the past few years dressing up just right and sucking up to the man in charge have already been kicked off the popular kids’ table — Pam Bondi, Kristi Noem, even Marjorie Taylor Greene. Axios recently reported that Mr. Trump’s people no longer try to stop him from doing things; as a longtime adviser and admirer told Axios: “Why bother? He’s the boss.”

Mr. Trump doesn’t want to hear it. And it shows.

He’s regularly saying things like “affordability is a con job” and “I don’t think about Americans’ financial situation. I don’t think about anybody.” He’s obsessed with building a ballroom even if it ignores the fire code (“I am the code,” he reportedly declared), a triumphal arch with snipers on top, and slapping his name on the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts — or else. Our unpopular president thinks he’s actually popular (he denounced polls, which he often calls “fake,” at least nine times in August alone), so popular that he seems to believe that people are going to carve his face into Mount Rushmore. He doesn’t see the problem with A.I. or crypto or his family’s self-enrichment. Earlier this month, he banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists from the White House, simply because he didn’t like their apparently negative coverage.

Maybe because everybody around him was too scared to tell him.

Last week, Mr. Trump’s approval rating hit an all-time low, Hispanic voters were bailing on Republicans in droves and the economy — the single most important issue to many Americans — is only working for the very wealthy. Does Mr. Trump have any idea?

This president, for much of his two terms in office, seemed to have a preternatural understanding of how to twist the press and the public to believe his narratives about the world; now he’s living in such a fantasy world that his greatest power has been effectively neutralized. It’s the same overconfidence that seems to have led to the failures of many Trump-branded products — steaks, mortgages, casinos, vodka, a for-profit university and an airline. It now seems likely that MAGA Republicans in the midterms could be his next project to fail.

In “Mean Girls,” that great parable of cliquedom, Regina falls from grace only after she loses what makes her powerful — her hot boyfriend, her hot body and her coterie of followers. She’s supplanted by one of them, Cady Heron, who eventually learns that teenage girl cliques are bad and gives up her spring fling crown.

I don’t think such a lesson is in store for Mr. Trump. What would learning not to be a bully even look like for him? Ending the trade war with Canada and getting mani-pedis with Mark Carney? Inviting Chuck Schumer for an Oval Office tea and glow-up? Promotions for the female and Black military officers who have been sidelined or fired? Checks from World Liberty Financial sent out in restitution for those rounded up in brutal ICE raids?

Eventually, I learned to stand up to my bully. If the midterms go their way, the Democrats will, I hope, have the means to be able to as well. As Mr. Trump becomes even more self-destructive, the Republicans could — in a late-breaking fit of attempted self-preservation — do so, too. Teenage girls can’t invoke the 25th Amendment on their bullies, but this cabinet theoretically could.

Molly Jong-Fast is the host of the “Fast Politics” podcast and the author of “How to Lose Your Mother: A Daughter’s Memoir.”

The Times is committed to publishing a diversity of letters to the editor. We’d like to hear what you think about this or any of our articles. Here are some tips. And here’s our email: letters@nytimes.com.

bond-market-japan-yen.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 17  Words: 1066/1156
================================================================================

SUMMARY

After more than three decades of economic gloom, Japan is back. Today, Japanese government bonds are paying interest rates not seen in 30 years, lifted by economic growth and deficit spending. That month, not only did Japan’s Finance Ministry intervene to stem the yen’s decline, but the Bank of Japan also increased interest rates, hinted at more rate hikes to come and said it would cut bond purchases.

ARTICLE

There’s a New Threat to Your Personal Finances
The revival of Japan’s economy isn’t all good news.
By Rebecca Patterson
Published 2026-09-28 09:04 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/28/opinion/bond-market-japan-yen.html

After more than three decades of economic gloom, Japan is back. This should be welcome news, but there is a downside that’s going to make things challenging for America and its economic stewards in the Trump administration. Remember the butterfly flapping its wings and causing tornadoes? It’s like that, only in this case the butterfly is a $7.6 trillion bond market.

For three decades, Japanese investors, facing a lifeless domestic economy, would stash their money overseas where it could earn better returns. Today, Japanese government bonds are paying interest rates not seen in 30 years, lifted by economic growth and deficit spending. That means investors can bring their money home — and that has the potential to produce a global financial market mess. The risks are large enough that they have already prompted a number of exceptional interventions by the U.S. Treasury.

This is for sure an esoteric part of international finance. It’s also a vital underpinning for markets that matter for your retirement account, savings and household budget.

We need to start in 1990. The bursting of Japan’s go-go bubble economy and the subsequent long economic slump prompted companies there to sit on their cash rather than invest. Japan’s central bank embarked on a range of experiments to jump-start the economy, starting with rapidly cutting short-term interest rates from a peak of 6 percent in 1990 to nearly zero by the middle of the decade.

Economic growth didn’t rise enough to encourage households to spend. Instead, they preferred to wait for prices to fall. The Bank of Japan kept trying. It bought vast amounts of government bonds, a process known as quantitative easing, and in 2016, introduced negative interest rates. The yield on Japan’s 10-year bond hovered around one-tenth of a percentage point. For an equivalent U.S. Treasury bond, the interest rate it paid at the time was 2.35 percent.

The real-world result was that Japan effectively paid people to borrow its currency. An investor could finance the purchase of a foreign asset, such as a Treasury bond, with yen. Without markets budging at all, the trade would make money, given the difference between the borrowing cost and the yield on the Treasury bond purchased. This is what financial analysts call the carry trade.

Over the years, and in similar ways, the yen funded investments around the world — in currencies, bonds and equities. As long as other countries’ returns looked sufficiently more attractive, the carry trade grew. There is no definitive measure for its size. One Treasury Department estimate, which reflects a number of factors including the carry trade, says that of mid-2025, Japanese investors owned around $2.8 trillion of U.S. equities, bonds and other assets.

Undoing this would be the financial equivalent of a tide rushing out before a tsunami strikes. The first hint of what it could look like came in 2024. That July, U.S. government bond yields were more than three percentage points higher than their Japanese equivalents. Investors borrowed yen and sold them for dollars to buy Treasury bonds. That selling weakened the yen to levels that alarmed policymakers. Japanese exporters benefit from a weaker yen since it makes their goods more competitive overseas, but households suffer because the price of imported goods rises.

That month, not only did Japan’s Finance Ministry intervene to stem the yen’s decline, but the Bank of Japan also increased interest rates, hinted at more rate hikes to come and said it would cut bond purchases. The combination reversed the logic of the carry trades and investors started heading for the exits.

That turned to panic when a disappointing U.S. jobs report in August 2024 convinced investors that the Federal Reserve might need to cut interest rates. This too made the carry trade less attractive. The tsunami hit on Aug. 5 — Japan’s Nikkei equity index fell 12.4 percent in a single session, its biggest one-day loss since the Wall Street crash of October 1987. The S&P 500 index fell 3 percent.

Fast forward to today: Policymakers in Japan and the United States are trying to thread a tiny, sharp needle. Both governments are spending more, including on defense and infrastructure. That spending requires more government debt. At the same time, stubbornly high inflation is frustrating voters and forcing central banks to raise interest rates. That could undermine economic growth — government bond yields, after all, anchor borrowing costs for items including home mortgages and auto loans. Higher interest rates also raise the cost of servicing all that debt, which eats into funds for other government priorities.

So how can both countries simultaneously support growth, fight inflation and bring down long-term interest rates?

While an economic boost from artificial intelligence may help at some point, Japan’s finance minister floated an answer in July. She suggested asking Japan’s government pension investment fund, which manages $2.1 trillion in assets, to sell some foreign bonds and buy Japanese ones. This would require selling foreign currencies, including a lot of dollars. In other words, the inverse of the yen carry trade. The move would help lower Japanese bond yields without slowing Japanese growth.

Unfortunately, such a step would boomerang on the United States, because it would most likely push up Treasury bond yields and weaken the dollar. That’s among the reasons Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been intervening in markets in novel ways, including seeking a pathway for Japan to tackle the challenges facing its own currency and bond markets without needing to sell U.S. Treasurys.

Even if these various interventions work, the risk remains that investors will take at least some of their money out of America and back to Japan.

Japan’s stock market has risen nearly 30 percent so far this year, more than double the growth in the S&P 500. Government bond yields are near 3 percent for the first time in decades. Any Japanese investors looking to take advantage wouldn’t pull their money out of overseas markets overnight. But the size of the potential repatriation, and the increasingly attractive investment options back home, means America needs to be on guard that a slow current of capital doesn’t become a sudden flood.

For many years, traders tried and failed to guess when Japanese bond yields would rise, so much so that the trade was nicknamed the “widow maker.” If the giant unwinding of the carry trade finally comes, let’s hope it doesn’t leave any more financial widows in its wake.

Rebecca Patterson is an economist and senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations who has held senior positions at JPMorgan Chase and Bridgewater Associates. She is a co-host of the podcast “The Spillover.”

jonathan-mckinsey-new-york-times-shooting-california.html

SUMMARY

A Bay Area couple have been accused of shooting and killing their son-in-law in a suburban sports park on Saturday afternoon, the local police said. The man, Jonathan McKinsey, 40, was found dead with multiple gunshot wounds around 3 p.m. in a parking lot at Dublin Sports Grounds, an athletic complex and playground in Dublin, Calif., about 35 miles east of downtown San Francisco, according to Dublin Police Services. Mr. McKinsey was a transgender man and accused his wife, Candice Jang, and his in-laws of abusing him because of his identity, according to his filing for a restraining order in December 2025.

ARTICLE

Couple Accused of Killing Their Son-in-Law in Bay Area Park
Jonathan McKinsey, an engineer who worked in the games department for The New York Times, was fatally shot Saturday in a San Francisco suburb. The police have accused his parents-in-law, both 76.
By Soumya Karlamangla and Amy Qin
Published 2026-09-28 21:54 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/28/us/jonathan-mckinsey-new-york-times-shooting-california.html

A Bay Area couple have been accused of shooting and killing their son-in-law in a suburban sports park on Saturday afternoon, the local police said.

The man, Jonathan McKinsey, 40, was found dead with multiple gunshot wounds around 3 p.m. in a parking lot at Dublin Sports Grounds, an athletic complex and playground in Dublin, Calif., about 35 miles east of downtown San Francisco, according to Dublin Police Services.

Mr. McKinsey was director of engineering for the games department of The New York Times, according to a company spokesman. Before Mr. McKinsey began working at The Times in 2023, he worked for several tech companies including Splunk, Coursera and Oracle, according to his LinkedIn profile.

The authorities arrested Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen, both 76, in the shooting. They are a married couple who live in Dublin and are the parents of Mr. McKinsey’s wife, the police said.

No motive was described by the police for the shooting, but Mr. McKinsey and his wife had a turbulent marriage and were living separately, records show. Each had filed requests for domestic violence restraining orders against the other last year in Alameda County. Mr. McKinsey had also pleaded not guilty last year to two charges of misdemeanor child abuse.

Mr. McKinsey was a transgender man and accused his wife, Candice Jang, and his in-laws of abusing him because of his identity, according to his filing for a restraining order in December 2025. He said his mother-in-law called him and one of his sons a “pervert” and a “monster” after the boy tried on dresses, and he accused his father-in-law of punching him in the chest while he was recovering from double mastectomy surgery in 2010.

In her October 2025 filing, Ms. Jang said that Mr. McKinsey had grabbed her by the forearms during one argument and dropped her onto the corner of a table, fracturing vertebra in her upper back. Ms. Jang also accused Mr. McKinsey of emotionally abusing her mother.

Efforts to reach Ms. Jang and her lawyer on Monday were unsuccessful.

Assad Razawi, a resident of Dublin, said he was outside a grocery store near his car on Saturday at around 3 p.m. when he heard what sounded like five or six gunshots coming from the sports park across the street. When he looked over, he said he saw a man drop to the ground in the parking lot and another man and woman walking calmly away from the scene. The San Francisco Chronicle was first to report Mr. Razawi’s account.

Around the same time, a Dublin police sergeant was driving by the park when he saw a man lying on the ground and stopped to investigate, the local police said. Emergency personnel began arriving after receiving 911 calls from people in the park about the shooting.

Witnesses directed officers to two individuals standing nearby, whom police identified as Mr. Zhang and Ms. Chen. They are being held without the possibility of bail on suspicion of murder, and detectives are continuing to investigate. They also are being held on suspicion of willful discharge of a firearm with gross negligence; conspiracy; and child endangerment likely to produce great bodily injury or death. It was not clear which children the last booking charge pertained to.

They are scheduled to be arraigned on Wednesday. It was unclear whether Mr. Zhang and Ms. Chen had legal representation.

A report from the Dublin Police Services noted that on Oct. 17, 2025, an officer met with Ms. Jang, who said that her husband had struck their 6-year-old “in the face with an open hand.” When officers went to the residence to contact Mr. McKinsey, they discovered a 2-year-old child in an upstairs bedroom who had been left without supervision. The officers say that Mr. McKinsey had left the child alone for over an hour while he went shopping.

Mr. McKinsey was later charged in Alameda County Superior Court with two misdemeanor counts of child abuse in connection with the separate incidents. He had pleaded not guilty to both charges and was released from jail on the condition that he complete 12 parenting classes. A pretrial hearing had been scheduled for next month.

In December, Mr. McKinsey filed his own request for a temporary restraining order against his wife, citing years of domestic violence. According to his filing, his wife had recently been granted full custody of the children, and he feared for their safety. That same month, he filed for divorce.

Mr. McKinsey said that he had been framed for the October incident in which the couple’s 2-year-old son was found alone. He said that Ms. Jang was responsible for the children during the workweek and that she had not told him before leaving that the child was sleeping in his crib upstairs. “She did this on purpose, to set me up,” he wrote.

In his filing, he accused his wife of regularly abusing their children and neglecting to properly bathe and feed them.

“When I protested about any of this, she threatened me with harm or said she would call the police and tell them I was hurting our children,” he said in the filing.

He said that Ms. Jang had once hit him on the head with a frying pan and forced him to ingest a cockroach. He accused her, on another occasion, of striking him on the head with a mirror, which shattered as he tried to wrest it from her control and severed a tendon and nerve in his hand, requiring surgery and leaving him with a permanent loss of sensation in his thumb.

Kitty Bennett and Georgia Gee contributed research. Coral Murphy Marcos contributed reporting from Hayward, Calif.

SUMMARY

Senator Jon Husted of Ohio appears to have an additional challenge: Even some of the state’s most devoted conservatives don’t know who he is. Mr. Husted’s Democratic opponent is Sherrod Brown, a fixture in Ohio politics since the 1970s, who lost his Senate seat two years ago. “I don’t know a whole lot about Husted,” said Debbie Grenko, 67, a Republican, as she stroked her pony, Spirit, at the Delaware County Fair in central Ohio last week.

ARTICLE

In Ohio, a Humbling Question for Senator Jon Husted: Are You the Incumbent?
Even some devoted conservatives know more about Sherrod Brown, the Democratic challenger, than the Republican incumbent, who needs the MAGA base to turn out.
By Emily Davies
Published 2026-09-28 16:31 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/28/us/politics/john-husted-ohio-president-trump-midterms.html

Republican senators vying for re-election this year have had to contend with a cratering economy and an unpopular president. Senator Jon Husted of Ohio appears to have an additional challenge: Even some of the state’s most devoted conservatives don’t know who he is.

Mr. Husted’s Democratic opponent is Sherrod Brown, a fixture in Ohio politics since the 1970s, who lost his Senate seat two years ago. Mr. Brown’s renown has become something of a liability for the sitting senator, who needs the state’s MAGA-friendly Republican base to care enough about the seat to vote in a year when President Trump is not on the ballot.

But being perceived as the challenger may also benefit Mr. Husted at a moment when voters are struggling economically and don’t think Congress has done enough to help. With polls showing Mr. Brown and Mr. Husted in a tightening race, the Republican’s campaign has leaned into the misconception, spending millions of dollars on ads that refer to his opponent as “Senator Sherrod Brown.”

“I don’t know a whole lot about Husted,” said Debbie Grenko, 67, a Republican, as she stroked her pony, Spirit, at the Delaware County Fair in central Ohio last week. “It’s Sherrod Brown in there, right?”

One Republican strategist in Ohio, granted anonymity to speak candidly about the race, said the campaign was intentionally casting Mr. Brown as the incumbent, a rare opportunity amid dismal Republican approval ratings for the party to harness anger at the status quo.

“Name ID is not everything,” said Drew Thompson, Mr. Husted’s campaign manager. Ohioans, he said, “are familiar” with Mr. Brown’s record “and they rejected it two years ago.”

The approach has reached some voters, including Ted Hull, who on Wednesday night was watching a “wiener dog race” at the Delaware County Fair. He said he planned to vote for Mr. Husted. Mr. Hull, 72, said that Mr. Brown, who he thought was still in office, seemed to have “become lazy” on the job.

“There should be term limits,” Mr. Hull said.

Mr. Brown served for nearly two decades in the Senate and 14 years in the House of Representatives. Mr. Husted was appointed to the Senate two years ago, when JD Vance vacated the seat to become vice president. A former lieutenant governor and speaker of the Ohio House of Representatives, Mr. Husted is far from the firebrand that many have come to associate with the modern Republican Party. He is mild-mannered and more comfortable talking about economic policy than rousing a crowd.

Quality polling on Ohio is limited, but one poll released last week found that nearly a quarter of voters believed Mr. Brown was the incumbent.

The high-stakes race has become one of the most expensive in the country, with nearly $400 million of spending on advertisements, according to AdImpact, for a seat that both parties believe could determine control of the Senate. So far, Republicans have outspent Democrats by more than $75 million. The cryptocurrency industry’s main super PAC, Fairshake, launched a $30 million advertising campaign against Mr. Brown last week.

Mr. Trump plans to campaign in Ohio on Saturday, the Republican National Committee announced. It will be the first of “more than two” trips the president hopes to make before Election Day, according to one person familiar with his plans who was granted anonymity to discuss campaign strategy.

In Washington, Senate Republicans are also hoping to help Mr. Husted this week by voting on a bill to address the growing data center backlash by encouraging — but not requiring — state utility regulators to insulate consumers from rising energy costs associated with the facilities. Mr. Husted put the bill forward himself, after Democrats blitzed the airwaves with ads seeking to define Mr. Husted as the “face of data centers” in Ohio.

As lieutenant governor, before public backlash had emerged about rising energy costs and unsightly development associated with data centers, Mr. Husted supported tax incentives for such projects. In August, the National Republican Senatorial Committee circulated a memo warning that data center politics was endangering him.

All of these dynamics have left both sides bracing for a nail-biter in a red state that Mr. Trump won two years ago by double digits, according to a half-dozen Democratic and Republican operatives interviewed by The New York Times.

“The environment is bad, but there is a sense in D.C. that this race is over, and it’s not,” said Jai Chabria, another Republican strategist in Ohio and one of Mr. Vance’s top political advisers. “Senator Husted is in a much better position than is conventional wisdom.”

The landscape is tough across the country for Republican incumbents, with prices persistently high and Mr. Trump’s approval rating hovering near an all-time low for modern presidencies. In Ohio, fluorescent signs remind voters that gas frequently costs more than $4.40 per gallon. At the height of harvest season, diesel was even more.

For their part, Mr. Brown and Democrat-backed PACs have sought to take advantage of Mr. Husted’s relative unknown, with ad after ad trying to define him before voters hear from the senator himself. Aside from data centers, the ads also highlighted Mr. Husted’s votes to cut federal health care benefits.

“Sherrod has done a really good job reminding Ohio voters that he was one of the original economic populists in Ohio,” said Aaron Pickrell, a Democratic strategist who ran former President Barack Obama’s campaign in Ohio in 2012, the last year the state was truly a presidential battleground. “This race is extraordinarily close.”

Some of the attacks against Mr. Husted appear to be working. Ben Meddles, 55, a firefighter in central Ohio, said he regretted voting for Mr. Trump, and that in turn was affecting his choice for Senate.

“You go in to vote and you feel good,” said Mr. Meddles, watching his daughter’s dachshund Frankie compete in the “wiener” dog race. “And then sometimes, six months to a year later, you’re sorry for the way you voted.”

He said he was frustrated with the president for starting a war with Iran, imposing tariffs on Canada and spending so much time trying to take control of Greenland, which Mr. Meddles dismissed as “showboating.” It all felt like a distraction, he said, from the president’s failure to deliver his signature campaign promise: economic relief at home. That promise, Mr. Meddles said, was why he had cast three ballots for Mr. Trump over the last decade.

Mr. Meddles, who said he makes about $80,000 annually, wanted to make sure he chose a candidate who had shown that they would focus on improving the economic outlook. Mr. Husted “hasn’t stood out in the crowd doing anything good,” he said.

Mr. Husted will need to balance keeping enough distance from the president to retain voters frustrated by his second term while also embracing Mr. Trump enough to energize the conservative base, several Republican strategists said in interviews this week.

In the last few months, Mr. Husted has spoken at the Republican Party’s midterm convention in Dallas and appeared with Mr. Vance at a steel manufacturing plant in Ohio. Last week, Mr. Husted voted to block a resolution that would have required Mr. Trump to seek congressional approval to continue the war with Iran.

But he has also stressed that he wants to see a swift end to that war. On Friday, at a manufacturing company outside of Cleveland, Mr. Husted declined to answer questions from a reporter about whether he supported the White House’s handling of the war, which has driven up gas and diesel prices.

At the fair, Ms. Grenko had spent nearly $7 per gallon on diesel to fill up the five trucks she needed to cart her ponies to the event.

That cost had been so crippling, she said, that she swapped her favorite mac-and-cheese brand, Kraft, for the Great Value version sold at Walmart. She also started to buy off-brand coffee creamer and toilet paper, and to eat more rice each week to fill up.

In some ways, Ms. Grenko embodied both the opportunities and the challenges facing Mr. Husted. A loyal Trump Republican who gets her news exclusively from Fox, Ms. Grenko said she didn’t mind making those sacrifices if Mr. Trump was doing what he thought was best for the country.

But her willingness to give up comforts for Mr. Trump does not mean she will vote for Mr. Husted, given how little she knows about him.

“I want him to step out, step up and say, ‘OK, this is what I think,’” she said, an American flag blowing in the wind behind her.

“Like Trump,” she continued. “Trump’s not afraid to say what he stands for.”

gastrointestinal-symptoms-gut-health.html

SUMMARY

Health issues like colorectal cancer, Crohn’s disease, diverticulitis and even certain stomach bugs can also cause blood to appear in or on the stool, said Dr. Baha Moshiree, a gastroenterologist and professor of medicine at Wake Forest University School of Medicine in North Carolina. Any blood in or around the stool is worth mentioning to a doctor, Dr. Eng said. If you’re noticing any of these symptoms frequently — even if they only last for a moment — see a doctor, Dr. Moshiree said.

ARTICLE

5 Gastrointestinal Symptoms You Should Never Ignore
Experts say these warning signs should always prompt a chat with a doctor.
By Caroline Hopkins Legaspi
Published 2026-09-28 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/28/well/gastrointestinal-symptoms-gut-health.html

Sometimes a miserable bout of diarrhea is caused by nothing more than nerves or a 24-hour stomach bug. Lingering gas and bloating can be set off by a recent long-haul flight.

But similar symptoms could also represent something far more serious. It can be tricky to tell with the gastrointestinal tract, the long tube that runs from the mouth to the end of the large intestine. We asked gut health experts to share some of the warning signs they’d never want their patients to ignore.

1. Blood in the toilet.

When people see blood in or on their stool, they often ignore it because they assume it’s from hemorrhoids, said Dr. Cathy Eng, a professor of medicine at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center.

When hemorrhoids, which are swollen, inflamed veins, are irritated or pressure is applied, they can cause bright red blood to appear on toilet paper, or as drops in the toilet bowl or on the surface of your stool. But it’s often not possible to tell by appearance whether the blood is from hemorrhoids or something more serious, Dr. Eng said.

Health issues like colorectal cancer, Crohn’s disease, diverticulitis and even certain stomach bugs can also cause blood to appear in or on the stool, said Dr. Baha Moshiree, a gastroenterologist and professor of medicine at Wake Forest University School of Medicine in North Carolina.

Stool that appears black, tarry or dark maroon can be a sign of bleeding in the stomach or upper digestive tract from a stomach ulcer, a cancer in the stomach or esophagus or other conditions, Dr. Moshiree said.

Any blood in or around the stool is worth mentioning to a doctor, Dr. Eng said.

2. An unusual change in bowel movements.

It’s a good idea to tell a doctor about unexpected changes to the shape, frequency or consistency of your bowel movements, like newly appearing constipation, diarrhea or thin stools, said Dr. Andrew Chan, a gastroenterologist at Mass General Brigham in Boston.

When such changes occur without a clear reason, like shifts in your diet, medications, stress levels or work schedule, it could signal that something is off, Dr. Chan said. A growing tumor in the colon, for instance, can cause constipation or thin stools, Dr. Eng said. And intestinal inflammation can cause both constipation and diarrhea, often with pain, gas and bloating.

3. Diarrhea that won’t go away.

If your bowel movements have been loose or watery for more than five to seven days, especially if you also have abdominal pain, cramping or changes to your appetite, it’s worth looping in a health professional, Dr. Eng said.

Intestinal infections caused by certain pathogens, like the parasites cyclospora or giardia or the bacterium Clostridioides difficile, can cause diarrhea, cramping, pain or appetite changes that may benefit from antibiotics or other treatments, Dr. Moshiree said.

Inflammatory bowel diseases like Crohn’s or ulcerative colitis can also cause chronic diarrhea, pain, cramping, gas and bloating, as can celiac disease, an autoimmune condition in which eating gluten causes the immune system to attack the colon. In some cases, colorectal cancer can also cause persistent diarrhea, Dr. Eng said.

4. Difficulty swallowing.

Any recurring pain, discomfort or trouble with swallowing can be worrisome, Dr. Moshiree said. This includes feeling like you can’t move food from your mouth to your throat or a sensation that food is getting stuck in your throat.

If you’re noticing any of these symptoms frequently — even if they only last for a moment — see a doctor, Dr. Moshiree said. Nerve or muscle conditions, like Parkinson’s disease or multiple sclerosis, can cause discomfort or trouble swallowing, she said. And conditions that cause a blockage near the throat, such as throat or esophageal cancers, can make it difficult for food to pass through.

In severe cases, food that becomes stuck can lead to choking, but “it doesn’t have to be that extreme” to be worth mentioning to a doctor, Dr. Chan said.

5. Symptoms that wake you in the middle of the night.

Diarrhea, abdominal pain, cramping, nausea or other gut symptoms that wake you up should raise an alarm, Dr. Moshiree said. Serious conditions like Crohn’s disease or colorectal cancer can cause these unpleasant nighttime awakenings. Stomach viruses or food poisoning can also jolt you awake, she said.

Less urgent gut conditions, like irritable bowel syndrome or run-of-the-mill indigestion, are less likely to disrupt your sleep, Dr. Moshiree said, since their symptoms are more likely to occur when you’re awake.

Also be sure to tell a doctor if you’re frequently having night sweats that aren’t menopause-related, Dr. Eng said. Night sweats can be a symptom of many types of cancer, including those related to the gastrointestinal tract, such as colorectal cancer and pancreatic cancers.

As a general rule, an unexplained loss of more than 10 percent of your body weight, across any time frame, is worth telling a doctor about, Dr. Moshiree said. Worrisome conditions that can cause unexpected weight loss include gastrointestinal cancers, inflammatory bowel diseases, intestinal blockages and gastroparesis, a disorder that causes your stomach to empty too slowly.

The Bottom Line

If you’re unsure whether a digestive symptom is worrisome, especially if it doesn’t resolve within a few days to a few weeks, it’s a good idea to run it by a doctor, the experts said.

A primary care doctor at a local clinic, or even a gynecologist, can be a good first stop, Dr. Eng said. That doctor can then refer you to a specialist, like a gastroenterologist, if you need one.

irs-tax-returns-citizenship.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 21  Words: 1283/1283

SUMMARY

The Trump administration is preparing to add a question on next year’s tax returns asking people whether they are a citizen or legally authorized to work in the United States, expanding an attempt to cut tax refunds for immigrants or push them out of the tax system entirely. In a draft version of Form 1040, the primary tax form, the Internal Revenue Service this month included a new section that asks filers to check a box “Yes” or “No” to answer the question: “At the time you file your return, are you, and your spouse if filing jointly, a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, or an alien lawfully authorized to work in the U.S.?” The additional question comes as part of what the Trump administration has said is an effort to prevent undocumented immigrants from receiving federal tax benefits.

ARTICLE

Trump Administration Prepares to Ask Tax Filers if They Are U.S. Citizens
The new question, included on a draft version of the primary tax form, comes as part of an anti-immigrant turn at an agency that long prioritized tax administration.
By Andrew Duehren
Published 2026-09-29 14:09 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/business/irs-tax-returns-citizenship.html

The Trump administration is preparing to add a question on next year’s tax returns asking people whether they are a citizen or legally authorized to work in the United States, expanding an attempt to cut tax refunds for immigrants or push them out of the tax system entirely.

In a draft version of Form 1040, the primary tax form, the Internal Revenue Service this month included a new section that asks filers to check a box “Yes” or “No” to answer the question: “At the time you file your return, are you, and your spouse if filing jointly, a U.S. citizen, U.S. national, or an alien lawfully authorized to work in the U.S.?”

The additional question comes as part of what the Trump administration has said is an effort to prevent undocumented immigrants from receiving federal tax benefits. But many tax credits require recipients to have valid Social Security numbers, meaning previous tax forms already screened undocumented immigrants from receiving them. That fact has led several tax and immigration experts to conclude that the question is simply intended to scare undocumented immigrants out of filing their taxes at all.

That fear first emerged last year, when the I.R.S. shared addresses it had on file for roughly 47,000 people with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Federal law closely guards access to information submitted on tax returns, and several courts have blocked the I.R.S. from sharing bulk data with ICE. Still, even if the I.R.S. may not be able to legally do so, the addition of the citizenship question could reawaken concerns about the agency using its vast stores of information to help detain or deport people.

Undocumented immigrants pay tens of billions in combined federal income, payroll and local taxes every year. Since they do not have valid Social Security numbers, undocumented immigrants are among the people who can use a separate nine-digit code called an individual taxpayer identification number to file their taxes. The I.R.S. has not in recent history asked taxpayers about their immigration status, and has instead sought to encourage every U.S. resident to file their taxes.

“The I.R.S. doesn’t need this information to administer the tax law,” said Nina Olson, a former I.R.S. official and the executive director of the Center for Taxpayer Rights, which sued the I.R.S. over its previous data sharing with ICE. “The only reason you have that attestation is to deter people.”

At the same time, the Treasury Department is moving forward with a push to cut off immigrants with legal status from receiving the full value of several tax credits. The administration has said those new rules are targeted at “illegal aliens,” but in reality they would affect recipients of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA, as well as immigrants on work visas, among others.

The question on tax forms and the stricter eligibility rules are the latest signs that the I.R.S. has become a tool in the Trump administration’s anti-immigration agenda, an important shift for an agency that for decades was narrowly focused on collecting taxes. Tax preparers and lawyers said the Trump administration’s new tax credit rules are stricter than the eligibility rules approved by Congress and threaten to create confusion for millions of tax filers next year.

President Trump has in recent months also sought to build a database of U.S. citizens, and he has proposed excluding noncitizens without green cards from the census. The new tax return question would most likely not be able to feed into those other efforts, though, because of taxpayer privacy laws. The proposed changes would probably draw legal challenges.

The I.R.S. did not respond to a request for comment. A representative of the Treasury Department said the citizenship question on tax forms would “provide the I.R.S. important and necessary information to help ensure tax benefits go where the law directs” without addressing specific questions about the changes.

“That rationale doesn’t hold water,” said Brandon DeBot, a senior attorney adviser at New York University’s Tax Law Center. “The government already has all the information it needs for whether someone is eligible for a tax credit.”

The overall effort began to take shape in August, when the Treasury Department proposed regulations outlining the new restrictions for four refundable tax credits: the earned-income tax credit, the child tax credit, the adoption tax credit and the American Opportunity tax credit, which covers education costs. In general, tax credits offset the amount of tax that someone owes, but refundable tax credits can go further, providing a payment to a filer that is larger than the balance of owed tax.

This means refundable tax credits can effectively serve as cash support to poor Americans who do not make enough money to owe much income tax. (Here is a simplified example: Someone who receives a $1,000 refundable tax credit, but owes only $200 in tax, can still receive the remaining $800 in tax credit as a payment.)

The Treasury regulations would, for the first time, define the money received through the tax credits — the amount beyond the tax owed — as a “federal public benefit.” That would subject this portion of the tax credit to a set of eligibility requirements laid out in a separate 1996 law, rather than the rules Congress wrote for the tax credits specifically.

Under tax laws passed by Congress, three of the four credits are already limited to people with work-authorized Social Security numbers, while the adoption credit is available to a broader pool. The proposed regulations would, instead, require recipients to be a “qualified alien” under the terms of the 1996 law, called the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act.

Several categories of immigrants are authorized to work — and therefore have Social Security numbers — but do not count as “qualified aliens” under that law. Beyond DACA recipients and people with work visas, residents with student visas or temporary protected status would no longer be able to receive the full amount of the tax credits because they are not “qualified aliens.”

“This isn’t about undocumented immigrants, no matter how much they advertise it as such,” said Margot Crandall-Hollick, a researcher at the Tax Policy Center, a think tank. “This is about going after people who are allowed to be here and allowed to work here.”

The additional question on Form 1040 asks only if someone is a citizen, a U.S. national or authorized to work — and not whether the filer is a “qualified alien,” meaning that the answer would not be relevant to enforcing the Treasury’s new rules. Reflecting that, the I.R.S. released a draft of a separate additional form that directly asks if someone is a “qualified alien.”

“It’s a weird duplicate question,” Richard Pon, a certified public accountant in California, said of the Form 1040 change. “‘Qualified alien’ is different from the question that’s on the 1040. Why would they even ask that question about citizenship? I can’t think of any compliance reason for that.”

Those hoping to receive the full value of the tax credits will now have to know whether their immigration status aligns with the complicated definition of “qualified alien.” That added complexity could cause some people who are in fact “qualified aliens,” like green card holders, to not claim the full value of the tax credits. The Treasury regulations warn of penalties for people who fill out the forms incorrectly, a potential deterrent for uncertain filers.

“The design of these questions is to confuse and scare the people. Tax preparers are completely unprepared to figure out whether someone is a qualified immigrant,” Sarah Krieger, senior policy counsel at the National Immigration Law Center. “People are just going to be chilled or deterred from filing their taxes or claiming credits they’re eligible for.”

================================================================================
oil-exports-strait-of-hormuz.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 34  Words: 1285/1287
================================================================================

SUMMARY

Oil exports from the Middle East have risen sharply this month, some oil analysts say, taking them closer to the level they were at before Iran shut down the Strait of Hormuz in March, a rebound that could ease some pressure on global energy prices. In September, an average of 10 million barrels of oil has gone through the waterway daily, according to Kpler, a firm that tracks oil tankers. In the last two weeks, he said, over 13 million barrels of oil a day went through the strait.

ARTICLE

Mideast Oil Exports Rebound Even as Prices Remain Elevated
More tankers are moving through the Strait of Hormuz as shippers gain confidence, but the global supply of oil is still below demand.
By Peter Eavis
Published 2026-09-29 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/business/oil-exports-strait-of-hormuz.html

Oil exports from the Middle East have risen sharply this month, some oil analysts say, taking them closer to the level they were at before Iran shut down the Strait of Hormuz in March, a rebound that could ease some pressure on global energy prices.

In September, an average of 10 million barrels of oil has gone through the waterway daily, according to Kpler, a firm that tracks oil tankers. Separately, six million barrels of crude a day has left the Persian Gulf states this month through pipelines and ports that bypass the strait, Kpler’s data shows.

Before the war with Iran began at the end of February, around 19 million barrels of crude left the region daily through the waterway and other routes. Because of the difficulty in tracking tankers, export totals supplied by analysts might not reflect the true flow of oil, but most experts say volumes rose significantly this month.

The turnaround has most noticeably occurred in the strait, even though Iran continues to attack tankers. A U.S. military operation aimed at protecting the vessels from the attacks appears to have encouraged more shipments by big exporting countries, like Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

“They are getting a substantial amount of oil out, and it is increasing over time as shippers’ confidence goes up,” said Eugene Gholz, an associate professor of political science at the University of Notre Dame and an expert on conflict in the strait.

President Trump, members of his administration and U.S. military officials have said for weeks that the Strait of Hormuz is open, and that tankers are moving oil through the strait.

Some analysts say the increase in oil exports shows that Iran may be losing its grip on the waterway. In recent months, a U.S. blockade has prevented Iran from exporting oil on tankers, cutting off a valuable source of revenue for the country.

“That tells me the pressure is on Iran, not the United States,” said Martin Navias, a senior research fellow at the Center for Defense Studies at King’s College London.

Despite the success in getting more oil out, the per-barrel price is still well above where it was before the war, and higher gasoline and diesel prices are weighing heavily on consumers around the world.

Even with the recovery in Gulf oil exports, the global supply is below what the world needs, said Dan Pickering, chief investment officer for Pickering Energy Partners, a financial services firm based in Houston.

“We’re still dealing with a tight market,” Mr. Pickering said.

The 10 million barrels of oil a day that Kpler says is going through the strait is a big improvement from the trickle that made it through early in the war. But it is still well below the 16 million barrels a day that went through before the war.

Some tanker tracking firms have lower numbers. TankerTrackers.com calculates that 7.4 million barrels of crude a day has gone through the strait this month.

Daniel Sternoff, a senior fellow at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy, cautioned against relying on a single number from a tracker, noting that the firms’ totals often diverge. Still, he added, “They do all point to an increase of flows over September.”

Experts warn that Iran could yet step up its attacks on tankers and the energy infrastructure of the Gulf states, which could cause a drop in supply and another rise in the price of oil. A big pipeline in Saudi Arabia that bypasses the strait was shut down after it was attacked this month.

“Iran certainly has a big array of options to escalate if it wanted to,” said Jim Krane, a fellow in Middle East energy studies at Rice University’s Baker Institute for Public Policy. “To me, it looks like they’re holding back.”

And some who have been focused on the situation for months said it was hard to declare the strait truly open.

While oil is getting out in larger volumes, the U.S. military protection requires significant resources and will be hard to maintain indefinitely. Even with protection from the United States, many tankers have been hit when trying to traverse the waterway, deterring some shipping companies from returning.

The strait “is not open to navigation, because it’s not safe,” Arsenio Dominguez, the secretary general of the International Maritime Organization, a United Nations agency, said in an interview last week. According to the group, 85 ships have been attacked since the war began, and 24 mariners have died.

Matt Smith, director of commodity research at Kpler, said that although Gulf crude exports were around 85 percent of their prewar level, normality had not returned.

“Production still needs to rise, and refineries still need to ramp back up,” he said. “This cannot fully happen until the safety risk of crossing the strait has been completely removed.”

The New York Times asked three tanker-tracking firms — Kpler, Vortexa and TankerTrackers.com — for their numbers on the amount of oil going through the strait for each month of the war. Since most tankers turn off their transponders when going through the strait to avoid being easily spotted by Iran, it’s hard to see the transits as they happen.

The trackers therefore piece together transponder signals outside the strait, satellite images and other data to determine which tankers went through and how much oil they carried. A large tanker can carry two million barrels of oil.

In August, Vortexa said, 6.4 million barrels a day passed through the strait on average; Kpler said 5.9 million, and TankerTrackers measured 5.5 million. Those totals were up significantly from flows early in the war, but less than half the prewar totals.

The Trump administration and the U.S. military have said more oil is getting out, but the data they have provided on shipments has been patchy.

Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of Central Command, the arm of the U.S. military offering protection to tankers in the strait, said in a Sept. 19 video posted on X that one billion barrels of oil had been shipped out through the strait “in the last couple months.”

That would equate to than 16 million barrels a day on average, equivalent to the prewar daily total, if Admiral Cooper meant that one billion barrels had gone out over two months.

But Capt. Tim Hawkins, a Central Command spokesman, said “the last couple” meant “a few” months. He declined to say how much oil had, on average, gone out daily since May.

In Washington, a debate is simmering over the amount of crude oil that Central Command claims has passed through the strait. Some congressional Democrats and intelligence analysts said Central Command had not been sufficiently transparent about the methodology it used to reach its estimates.

These officials, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential assessments, expressed suspicion that Central Command, under pressure from the White House, had presented inflated estimates about the total amount of oil flowing through the strait.

“The facts released by CENTCOM highlighting building momentum in the Strait of Hormuz are exactly that — facts,” Captain Hawkins said. He added that Central Command gathered its ship traffic data from its own operations, the shipping industry and the Gulf states.

In the last two weeks, he said, over 13 million barrels of oil a day went through the strait.

The White House responded to a request for comment through the Defense Department. A spokeswoman for the department strongly rejected the notion that Central Command was under pressure and stood by its oil flow figures.

“Our service members will remain undeterred and unfazed, and they will continue to ensure commercial vessels transit the strait safely,” the department’s spokeswoman, Kingsley Wilson, said in an email.

Eric Schmitt contributed reporting.

tinned-fish-craze.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 13  Words: 1022/1046
================================================================================

SUMMARY

To eat tinned fish for innumerable days and nights in a row, as I have, is to undergo sensory overload. Yet even after the pandemic eased and consumers ditched their sweatpants, they kept buying tinned fish. You cannot fail at tinned fish!

ARTICLE

I No Longer Have to Make Life Decisions Thanks to My Infinite Tins of Fish
Now I can’t even look at the word t*na.
By Amy X. Wang
Published 2026-09-29 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/magazine/tinned-fish-craze.html

To eat tinned fish for innumerable days and nights in a row, as I have, is to undergo sensory overload. There’s the jiggly tofu silhouette encasing the tender crack-crunch of vertebrae, the briny aroma about as subtle as a house on fire. Salt-slick density melting on the tongue to umami mush.

Like many of our cleverest inventions — duct tape, computers, hair spray — this came out of a war. In the late 1700s, France was troubled by costly military skirmishes and offered a cash prize to citizens who could figure out how to cheaply prevent food from spoiling. An enterprising man named Nicolas Appert sealed cooked fish into glass jars and boiled them, eventually winning 12,000 francs and the kudos of Napoleon Bonaparte. Later, in Britain, the merchant Peter Durand swapped Appert’s jars for tin-plated cans. Fast-forward 200 years and now we’re all swimming happily in a $15 billion global market of shelf-stable seafoods that can last for years and years.

But what drove the ichthyic pioneers of the 19th century were matters of practicality; I do not think Appert and Durand would easily understand how, today, tinned fish is as much a sensible grocery item as it is a status symbol, a viral “hot girl food,” a borderline luxury good. I think it would probably take a long time to explain to the two of them why you can buy limited-edition tinned fish at concerts and why there is coveted merch for sale about tinned fish and why a store exists in New York City called the Fantastic World of the Portuguese Sardine where a single-serving tin of said fantastic sardine can cost $44.

I think if you tried to tell them about “sardinemaxxing,” they would be confused.

I’m confused, myself.

Because $44 feels like a small price to pay for a sociological education, I spent some weeks recently sampling as much of this genre as I could. I ate not just sardines but also smoked salmon marinated in chili oil, small-batch mussels in sweet pepper and garlic, various types of trout, anchovies and an enormous amount of t*** — so much t*** that I refuse to look at the word anymore and you cannot make me spell it out — and what I learned is that most of it tastes kind of just … OK?

The genesis of the modern tinned-fish fervor was the Covid-19 lockdown. During that time, otherwise rational human beings suddenly dropped unspeakable amounts of cash on rare plants, industrial kitchen gadgets, “loungewear” and, yes, $10-to-$80-a-pop artisanal preserved fish meats in whimsical boxes. (What’s that saying about shooting fish in a barrel?) The year 2020 birthed not one but two buzzy direct-to-consumer tinned-fish start-ups, one of which became a hit on (what else) “Shark Tank.” Yet even after the pandemic eased and consumers ditched their sweatpants, they kept buying tinned fish.

One theory I’ve heard about the lasting craze is that it’s a way to feel the thrill of travel without needing to go anywhere; getting anchovies shipped in from popular tourist destinations like Portugal and Spain can stand in for the time-intensive experience of traversing Portugal or Spain. I’ve also read that tinned fish feeds right into health and wellness zeal, that it scratches the paranoid, conspiracy-minded itch for “bunker food” and that it might simply be about affordability — epicurean brands aside, you can get a supermarket can for $2 or $3 — which would take tinned fish all the way back to its roots as a balm in a time of financial crisis.

Credible arguments, to be sure. But as I “made dinner” after work every night, i.e. nibbled t*** straight out of the package like a raccoon (tinned-fish cookbooks do exist, but if you are someone who enjoys defaulting to the lowest common denominator of effort available, you, too, might be a secret raccoon), a different idea occurred to me.

My prefabricated meals were immensely satisfying not because they were convenient or cheap or hyperefficient panaceas to hunger — although they were all those things — but because they were entirely impossible to mess up. You cannot fail at tinned fish! Slap it onto a cracker, if you’re too dignified to self-spoon-feed the way I do. Scramble it into a broader vision like a pasta or a sandwich if you must. But you can never go wrong with the cookery here the way you definitely can with, say, raw fish. This certitude is a great pleasure. This is the bone-deep comfort and joy of having life’s weighty demands taken care of, of having everything planned out by somebody else. Here you go, decisions ready made. Eating tinned fish feels like being handed a scrunched paper bag on your way out the door by a warm, authoritative, parental hand — which of course you deserve.

Adult Lunchables are already everywhere in this world. Sophisticate versions of juvenile favorites include: tropical cocktails (grown-up Capri-Suns), burrata (string cheese), any dessert (candy wearing pants), smoothies (basically actual baby food). Tinned fish is a funny one, though, because no kid would actually choose to eat tinned fish. It’s an acquired taste, funky and fusty and a little bit offensive, merely presented in a kid way. And so in that way it’s maybe more like whatever’s going on with all these bows on adult women’s clothing.

Right around the time of my piscivore experiment, Fishwife, the “Shark Tank” direct-to-consumer darling, launched a limited-run summer niçoise salad in collaboration with the national chain Sweetgreen. A friend and I were both curious to try this ingenious branding bonanza — but by the time we got around to putting a date into our busy calendars, the collaboration had ended.

So we gathered the ingredients posted to the company’s website and assembled the dish ourselves. I spent far too long roasting the recipe’s “peak-season vegetables” and chopping three types of greens and hard-boiling the eggs, only to realize the eggs were supposed to be “jammy soft-boiled.” Neither of us remembered to bring “crispy onions, for topping.” We looked at each other, two 30-somethings eating our effortful, lukewarm, half-correctly assembled salads, and figured that next time, we should probably just go to a restaurant.

Amy X. Wang is a story editor for the magazine. Her work explores the ways in which money and consumerism shape modern life.

SUMMARY

A Staten Island judge on Tuesday dealt a major setback to Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s push to raise taxes on the wealthy, saying that the city had mishandled the rollout of a tax on high-end second homes and must start over. The judge, Wayne M. Ozzi of State Supreme Court on Staten Island, sided with a group of homeowners who had sued the city. The city said it was sending new notices, based on the 2025 tax data, to more than 11,000 property owners informing them that they needed to prove residency or pay the new charge.

ARTICLE

Judge Orders New York to Scrap Rollout of Second-Home Tax and Start Over
A Staten Island judge sided with a group of homeowners who had sued the city over its introduction of the tax, dealing a blow to Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
By Mihir Zaveri
Published 2026-09-29 19:50 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/nyregion/nyc-second-home-tax-lawsuit.html

A Staten Island judge on Tuesday dealt a major setback to Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s push to raise taxes on the wealthy, saying that the city had mishandled the rollout of a tax on high-end second homes and must start over.

The judge, Wayne M. Ozzi of State Supreme Court on Staten Island, sided with a group of homeowners who had sued the city. The homeowners had argued that the Mamdani administration did not try hard enough to determine who should owe the tax before moving toward collecting it.

“Homeowners are being substantially harmed and penalized needlessly” by the city’s “method of implementing the tax law,” Justice Ozzi wrote.

The lawsuit did not challenge the legality of the tax on second homes, also known as pieds-à-terre. Unveiled by Gov. Kathy Hochul in the spring and backed by the mayor, the tax was popular among voters and hailed by Mr. Mamdani’s supporters as a way to make good on his pledge to “tax the rich.” It was expected to close a budget gap by raising some $500 million annually to fund city services.

But the bumpy rollout of the policy on a short timeline drew immediate criticism from the mayor’s opponents, and some allies, including Ms. Hochul.

“City Hall botched this rollout and should have just admitted the errors and fixed its own mistake, instead of wasting time and taxpayer dollars by fighting it in court,” said Randy Mastro, a lawyer for the homeowners and a former city official who has criticized the mayor.

It is not clear how the judge’s decision will affect the city’s ability to collect the money as the case continues: The first tax bills typically go out in November, and the funds must be collected by the spring for this fiscal year.

The city is expected to seek a stay of Tuesday’s decision to allow the rollout to continue.

Passed in the state budget, the tax would apply to condos and co-ops that are used as second homes with a “market value” — a complicated metric determined by the city’s Finance Department — of at least $1 million and to one-, two- and three-family second homes with a “market value” of more than $5 million.

The lawsuit argued that the city had sowed confusion by sending out notices to about 17,000 New Yorkers informing them that their properties could be subject to the tax, without first making sure that the property owners were not full-time residents. The suit also took issue with the city’s publishing an online list of nearly one million “properties that may be subject to the charge” that included the owners’ names.

Justice Ozzi ordered the city to take down the list and replace it with a more limited version that shows only the properties subject to the tax. It also must cancel its previously mailed notices, narrow the list of recipients and send new notices that include detailed information about how the city determined each property that would be subject to the charge.

Justice Ozzi issued a temporary restraining order to pause the rollout last month, but the city appealed, which had the effect of halting the order.

The most recent hearing in the case, on Aug. 31, lasted more than two hours and featured several testy exchanges.

Mr. Mastro said at the hearing that the problems with the introduction of the tax represented Mr. Mamdani’s “antipathy toward private property ownership.”

“We’re here about a botched rollout of unparalleled proportions,” he said.

But Steven Banks, the city’s top lawyer, argued that Mr. Mastro was misrepresenting the steps the city took to collect the tax.

“He’s entitled to his opinions,” Mr. Banks said. “He’s not entitled to his own facts.”

In court filings on Aug. 25, the city offered its most detailed defense yet of the complex process of administering the tax, and acknowledged the complaints from some homeowners over its messaging.

The court papers, along with another filing on Aug. 31, said that on Aug. 12 the city’s Finance Department received some 2025 tax data from the state that established a primary residency for a segment of the property owners who had been sent notices.

The city said it was sending new notices, based on the 2025 tax data, to more than 11,000 property owners informing them that they needed to prove residency or pay the new charge.

Many of those properties are owned by trusts or L.L.C.s; others are properties for which the city has not received 2025 tax information or other data that shows the property is not subject to the tax.

The city said that it was extending the deadline to file proof of residency to Oct. 6; it had earlier been Sept. 18. As of Sept. 16, it had approved the proofs of residency submitted by some 4,700 property owners and was reviewing thousands more.

The city had sought dismissal of the suit, arguing that the plaintiffs had not shown that the rollout had meaningfully harmed them and that proving that a property was a primary residence was straightforward, even when it is owned by a trust or corporate entity.
