Police officers responding to a 911 call found Mr. Boahene unconscious near the tracks of the A train.

ARTICLE

Man Killed After Bag Gets Stuck in Subway Doors, Police Say
The man, a 57-year-old from Brooklyn, was pulled by the train and found near the tracks at the Utica Avenue station.
By Claire Fahy
Published 2026-09-29 14:15 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/nyregion/subway-backpack-dragging-death.html

A man died on Monday night after he was dragged by a train in Brooklyn because the bag he was carrying became stuck in a subway car’s doors, the police said.

The man, Yaw Boahene, 57, from Brooklyn, was exiting an express A train at around 6 p.m. on Monday at the Utica Avenue station when his shopping bag was caught as the doors closed, a Police Department spokesman said.

Police officers responding to a 911 call found Mr. Boahene unconscious near the tracks of the A train. Emergency medical workers pronounced him dead at the scene. An investigation into Mr. Boahene’s death is continuing, the police said.

In an interview on Tuesday, Demetrius Crichlow, the president of New York City Transit, a division of the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, said that a video of the incident shows Mr. Boahene unsteady on his feet and walking with a cane when he boarded the train at Rockaway Boulevard. He was also unstable when he got off at Utica Avenue, the video shows, and was carrying a thin, plastic shopping bag.

The subway train Mr. Boahene got on is called an R211, the newest class of cars in the transit fleet. According to Mr. Crichlow, those trains have sensors that will open the door if they detect objects above a certain size. A hand, a shoe, a large bag — all should prevent the door from closing.

“He was carrying a plastic bag, which has no real width to it,” Mr. Crichlow said. He added that “it’s a terrible situation, but we’re going to do whatever is possible to determine whether or not our equipment was part of it.”

The train entered service in July 2024 and was inspected as recently as July 29, he added. When it was inspected last night after Mr. Boahene’s death, a review of the mechanical operations of the door showed it was “operating as intended,” Mr. Crichlow said.

Driving a subway train longer than five cars — which A trains typically are — is a two-person job requiring an operator in the front to move the train and a conductor in the middle to control the doors, said John R. Ross, a former train service supervisor with the M.T.A., which runs the subway.

The conductor’s job is to “observe the platform as the doors close, and to observe the platform as he’s departing the station,” Mr. Crichlow said, adding that the conductor of the train that dragged Mr. Boahene has been removed from service while the investigation continues.

A spokeswoman for Transport Workers Union Local 100, which represents subway and bus workers, declined to comment.

Incidents of subway trains dragging commuters to their deaths are rare but do happen.

In October 2022, Joseph Ancona, 20, was killed at the 59th Street-Columbus Circle station after it appeared that his bag was stuck in a train door. He was dragged along the platform onto the tracks.

Earlier that year, in June 2022, Marcus Bryant, 37, was caught between a Q train and the platform in Brooklyn and fell onto the tracks. Early reports suggested his clothes were stuck in the train’s door, but subway officials later contradicted those accounts.

And in 2019, Vicente Alatorre, 39, was dragged into a tunnel by a train at Grand Central Station and died. In that case, it was initially thought that Mr. Alatorre’s clothes or a bag were stuck in the doors of a train, which authorities later denied.

Stefanos Chen contributed reporting.

adam-hamilton-kansas-senate.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 27  Words: 1706/1797
================================================================================

SUMMARY

Adam Hamilton has an unusual professional calling. Mr. Hamilton is also part of a cadre of Democrats whose politics are rooted in their Christian commitments — James Talarico in Texas is prominent among them — defying longstanding G.O.P. claims that their foes are hostile to people of faith. “I don’t really pay much attention to the national debate” among Democrats, Mr. Hamilton said in an interview.

ARTICLE

The Rev. Adam Hamilton Knows What’s the Matter With Kansas
This campaign could be a compelling model for Democrats.
By E.J. Dionne Jr.
Published 2026-09-29 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/opinion/adam-hamilton-kansas-senate.html

Political challengers tend to their day jobs when they can, but the Rev. Adam Hamilton has an unusual professional calling. So on a recent Friday afternoon, the Democratic candidate for the United States Senate from Kansas took time out from the campaign trail to perform a wedding. Two days later, he baptized a baby on the vast campus of Resurrection, a United Methodist Church he founded and leads.

Not a word of politics was spoken amid the prayers to Jesus and wonder at the mightiness of God. Instead, it was the insistent calls for selfless love and neighborly service echoing through Resurrection’s hallways and chapels that offered a quiet rebuke to the angry battles raging outside the sanctuary.

It may go too far to speak of the miraculous in an election, but it is a source of wonder and some amazement, for Democrats especially, that Kansas’ Senate race has joined the growing list of 2026 contests in which Republicans are vulnerable.

In a state that has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932, at least one recent poll, from Emerson College/Nexstar, gave Mr. Hamilton a two-point lead over the incumbent Republican senator, Roger Marshall. Those who rate Senate races have moved Kansas from a G.O.P. slam dunk to competitive status.

His campaign is important because it wraps together several trends visible across this year’s political map. They include a revolt against the Republicans in a farm belt hit hard by tariffs and rising diesel and fertilizer costs. The rebellion has affected Senate races in Iowa and Nebraska as well as Kansas, and some polls suggest it may be spreading to South Dakota. Mr. Hamilton is also part of a cadre of Democrats whose politics are rooted in their Christian commitments — James Talarico in Texas is prominent among them — defying longstanding G.O.P. claims that their foes are hostile to people of faith.

A former Republican himself, Mr. Hamilton embodies a nationwide shift in the allegiances of moderate Republicans toward the Democrats. And like many other candidates in the middle of the country, Mr. Hamilton is trying to balance blunt criticisms of Mr. Trump — on high prices, tariffs, the war in Iran, cuts in health care and nutrition programs and his handling of immigration — with promises of a less partisan, less angry, more cooperative politics on the other side of the Trump experience. Implicit is the idea that the opposite of Trumpism is not an equally in-your-face politics from the other side but a return to a degree of mutual respect.

This is why the often heated debate among Democratic factions that plays so prominently on the coasts and in the media seems so distant in places like Kansas that local Democrats are determined to make competitive.

“I don’t really pay much attention to the national debate” among Democrats, Mr. Hamilton said in an interview. “My focus is here in Kansas.” But if he prevails, the merits of his middle-of-the-road, values-based approach will become part of that debate. He speaks in fiercely moral terms of how much damage Mr. Trump’s cuts in safety net programs have done to Kansans living on the edge and how tariffs have hurt farmers and small businesses. But he is also running an ad calling out “socialism” and describes himself as “a moderate or independent-minded Democrat.”

The point, he told me, is “to differentiate who I am as a Democrat in Kansas,” noting that is “very different than, maybe, a mayor in Washington or New York City.”

Addressing a living room gathering in Overland Park in the suburbs of Kansas City that account for nearly a third of the state’s voters, Mr. Hamilton devoted considerable energy to detailing the costs of Mr. Trump’s policies and Mr. Marshall’s failure to challenge them. “Senator,” he said, “your job is to be a champion for the people of Kansas, not to be spokesperson for the White House to the people of Kansas.”

His stump speech always returns to a friendlier kind of politics. “I’m pretty sure in this room we have Republicans and we have Democrats and independents,” he told those gathered in Overland Park. “It’s not about that. It’s about decency. It’s about humanity. And what’s happening in Washington, D.C., is not normal. It’s not how things work. I’ve never seen it before.”

If you listen to Mr. Hamilton long enough, you learn that “normal” is both a very good thing and the counterpoint to all the country is experiencing now.

One other thing about Mr. Hamilton, and it may be the most important thing: He has built the largest Methodist congregation in the United States (24,000 members across nine sites in the Kansas City area and 22 services every Sunday) by preaching a Gospel that combines a thoroughly traditional promise of salvation through Jesus Christ with a call for community engagement and a dedication to those in need. He regularly notes that his congregation is divided roughly equally among Democrats, Republicans and independents.

In a state where 70 percent of adult Kansans identify as Christians, Mr. Marshall has taken to calling Mr. Hamilton “a megachurch C.E.O.” Mr. Marshall means it as a negative, even though a lot of Republicans frequent megachurches and respect executives. At the least, Mr. Hamilton can counter a favorite conservative talking point against Democrats “who never met a payroll": Resurrection has 461 employees.

To sharpen the attack, Mr. Marshall and ads on his behalf have added politically loaded adjectives, labeling Mr. Hamilton a “woke megachurch C.E.O.” or a “millionaire megachurch C.E.O.”

If “woke” is just an all-purpose right-wing epithet these days for anyone who believes in equal rights for Black and L.G.B.T.Q. people and for women, well, sure. But “woke” is a strange word for Mr. Hamilton, who has written dozens of books defending the Christian faith and urging readers to embrace it. The title and message of one of them, “Seeing Gray in a World of Black and White,” may best capture Mr. Hamilton’s disposition and his efforts to define what he calls a Christian “middle way.”

In his book, he argues that the use of Christianity in the culture wars has turned it into “a wedge that drives people away from Christ, rather than drawing them to him.” He also insists on “holding on to what is good in the past” and “retaining the historic doctrines of the Christian faith as articulated in the creeds.”

To walk Resurrection’s campus on a Sunday, attend a service and watch hundreds of families take advantage of its meeting rooms and coffee bars is to experience what you might call Heartland Homeyness. The Lord’s Prayer and — this being what Kansas City Chiefs’ fans call their kingdom — a whole lot of bright red Patrick Mahomes shirts take precedence over any kind of politics.

Republicans are finding it awkward this year to confront opponents such as Mr. Hamilton and Mr. Talarico whose faith defines them. The G.O.P.’s backup plan? To insist that their foes embrace defective or heretical brands of Christianity.

Campaigning for Mr. Marshall in mid-September, Vice President JD Vance accused Mr. Hamilton’s church of supporting a “devil-worshiping” drag group. The attack was false in just about all its specifics. The only actual fact Mr. Vance had to work with is that Resurrection joined dozens of other local sponsors of Kansas City PrideFest. Senator Ted Cruz of Texas on X accused Mr. Hamilton of being “heretical” for insisting that Muslims, Hindus and Jews are not condemned to an “eternity in hell.” Presumably, Mr. Cruz is prepared to explain to his non-Christian constituents that they face eternal damnation.

The attacks on Mr. Hamilton’s faith drew reproaches from his Methodist bishop and 120 Methodist ministers in Kansas, and Mr. Hamilton sees the onslaught as a sign of Republicans alarm: “We’ve got a real race on our hands, or they wouldn’t be here,” he told the Overland Park crowd.

Republicans should be worried. In a state Mr. Trump carried with 57 percent of the vote in 2024, his approval rating was down to 40 percent in the Emerson survey. It also found that 48 percent of voters had an unfavorable view of Mr. Marshall; just 41 percent saw him positively. Compounding his troubles, Mr. Marshall has come under scrutiny after The Times reported that he sued more than 700 patients for unpaid bills, the subject of a tough Hamilton ad that went up last week.

As for what Mr. Hamilton’s called his “inclusivist” view of salvation, he said in an interview that it is thoroughly orthodox, shared by, among others, the Roman Catholic Church and widely revered Christian thinkers such as C.S. Lewis and the early church father Justin Martyr. “God can give that salvation to anyone He chooses,” Mr. Hamilton said.

If this theological controversy seems strange in an election that for most voters is about economics, war and Mr. Trump, it reflects back on what makes Mr. Hamilton’s campaign a potentially compelling model: Because of who he is and what he believes, he is constantly linking values to policy.

This is where Democrats have historically fallen short, said Ashley All, a Kansas-based Democratic strategist. A veteran of two decades in Kansas politics who is not part of Mr. Hamilton’s campaign, Ms. All said Democratic campaigns and candidates did not ask often enough, “What are the things that connect people?” Mr. Hamilton does this regularly, she told me, “because building bridges has been his entire job for 40 years.”

He’s trying to prove that’s possible even in a fraught political moment. Recently he posted a video responding to a question he says he gets a lot — are you liberal or conservative? His answer was “Yes, of course!” He continued, “I think we can be both. To be a liberal means to be generous of spirit, open to seeing things with new eyes and open to reforming. And to be conservative means holding on to values or beliefs that are really important. We can be both of those things at the same time. … We need each other, we really do. We’re better together. And that’s how our system’s meant to work.”

A pastor who insists on seeing the grays in debates over politics and religion is making Kansas a laboratory for testing whether that’s still true.

E.J. Dionne Jr., a Times contributing Opinion writer, is the author of “Why Americans Hate Politics,” “Our Divided Political Heart,” “Why the Right Went Wrong” and, most recently, “100% Democracy,” with Miles Rapoport.

data-centers-democrats-republicans.html

SUMMARY

These tied Mr. Husted to the arrival of data centers in Ohio. Most data centers have been built near cities. Ohio Republicans are trying to mitigate the political fallout of data centers while protecting their continued construction.

ARTICLE

Republicans Are Struggling Everywhere. This State Is the Epicenter.
The problems of technology were there before Trump and will be there after.
By Christopher Caldwell
Published 2026-09-29 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/opinion/data-centers-democrats-republicans.html

At the start of this year, the largest underlying trend in national politics still seemed to be the transformation of longtime swing states into Republican bastions. Florida, Iowa, Ohio: The closer you looked, the more invulnerable President Trump’s party seemed.

The situation in Ohio was stark. In 2022, the governor, Mike DeWine, had beaten his Democratic opponent by 25 points. A year ago, the Trump-allied biotech billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy, who is running for governor, held nearly a double-digit lead over his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton.

Ohio’s high-tech industry was a big factor. A bipartisan enthusiasm spurred by President Joe Biden’s CHIPS and Science Act of 2022, it nonetheless played to the strengths of Republican incumbents. Intel was building a huge chip plant near Columbus. Mr. Ramaswamy was promising to turn the Ohio River Valley into the next Silicon Valley. “People talk about the Rust Belt,” he said in March of last year. “I don’t want to talk about the Rust Belt. I want to lead us to the platinum belt — the sectors of the future, from semiconductors to nuclear energy to even A.I.”

But times have changed. This month, a YouGov poll for Bowling Green State University found Ms. Acton leading Mr. Ramaswamy by three points. The incumbent Republican senator Jon Husted has fared similarly. Mr. Husted appeared likely at the start of the year to keep his seat. But since June, polls have shown him trailing the former senator Sherrod Brown, who was soundly defeated by the Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024.

A lot has happened to sour the public on Mr. Trump’s party, including the war with Iran and rising prices, but much of the discontent involves high-tech industries (like cryptocurrencies) and their needs (like H-1B visas for tech workers). Above all, Republicans are paying a political cost for the buildout of data centers for artificial intelligence.

Last month, Axios published a leaked memo from the National Republican Senatorial Committee that expressed alarm about the devastating effectiveness of video spots Mr. Brown had begun airing. These tied Mr. Husted to the arrival of data centers in Ohio. “More than any other thing in this race,” the memo said, “data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck. If he loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one.”

It’s not just Ohio. Mr. Trump has been dangerously dim on the subject of data centers. “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers,” he wrote on Truth Social, “is if they want to end up being backwards and poor.” He will probably hurt his party on Election Day, five weeks from now.

But it will not be easy for Democrats to lay a permanent claim to the moral high ground. The problems of high-tech industries were there before Mr. Trump arrived and will be there after he leaves. At present, the A.I. buildout is driving a large share of American economic growth. There are strong incentives for both parties not to restrain or regulate it. Neither Republicans nor Democrats have come up with a trustworthy set of policies for managing artificial intelligence, the multitrillion-dollar projects required to expand its use or the newfound political power this gives the tech industry.

Thousands of data centers have been built or are under construction in the United States. With 166 in operation, according to the Pew Research Center, Ohio has more than any state besides Virginia, Texas and California. Voters appear to think that’s enough. Gov. Kathy Hochul of New York has declared a moratorium on new construction. Other states are mulling outright bans.

What made Ohio so hospitable to tech expansion — and so vulnerable to a political backlash — is a long story. The state has lots of people, cheap open land, abundant water and weak zoning laws. Most important, it was devastated by deindustrialization like few other places, and has spent decades pursuing an industrial revival. Starting in 2011, Gov. John Kasich, a Republican, signed into law tax reforms and exemptions that would lure Amazon, Meta and Google to build new facilities in the state. In 2022, Intel committed to a $20 billion plant investment and the Biden administration bet heavily on tech in its CHIPS Act.

Last year, Ohio passed a bill that promised to fast-track data centers. In the New Albany International Business Park outside Columbus, there are already 40 data centers serving Amazon Data Services, Google, Meta and Microsoft, with 28 more planned. Last month Nvidia and partners announced an estimated $500 billion building project that will include a facility in Pike County, two hours east of Cincinnati, envisioned as one of the largest data-center complexes in the world.

All of this has costs. These vast installations are wrecking the landscape in unspoiled parts of Ohio, as they have done over the past two decades in Northern Virginia. And this is happening in a national real-estate market transformed by the Covid-19 pandemic, which led millions of Americans to move to more tranquil, nonurban surroundings. Ohio’s peak electricity demand is projected to rise by 56 percent over the next two decades.

Cheery projections made by Ohio politicians have not panned out. Tax exemptions intended to lure tech firms wound up costing $1.4 billion more than anticipated in 2025. Above all, the jobs have not come. Data centers are basically rows of computers sitting on racks — like a supersize version of that mysterious closet full of tangled wires and blinking lights at your workplace. Once construction is finished, no one but a couple of tech guys ever has any reason to go in there. Last year, The Wall Street Journal found that a large data center in Abilene, Texas, would employ about 100 people — a fraction of the jobs created by a cheese-packaging plant nearby. And cheese packaging doesn’t threaten to send residents’ utility bills through the roof.

Most data centers have been built near cities. But two-thirds of those projected for the coming years are being built in the sticks. The voters most up in arms now include a lot of Trump supporters. Ohio Republicans are trying to mitigate the political fallout of data centers while protecting their continued construction. In August, Mr. Ramaswamy called for free electricity for people living near data centers. Mr. Husted has sponsored a Senate bill urging big electricity users to cover their own electricity costs — legislation Senate Democrats criticized as toothless.

Outside of Ohio, Republican politicians appear even more worried. In August, Mike Rogers, a Senate candidate in Michigan who is not just a defender of data centers but an investor in them, called for a one-year statewide moratorium on new construction until better “guardrails” were in place. Last week, Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas, until recently an unflagging tech enthusiast, halted all permits for new data centers. Two new polls have shown the long-serving and perennially popular Mr. Abbott trailing his Democratic challenger, State Representative Gina Hinojosa.

Mr. Husted has cast the argument over data centers as one in which progress is at stake. “I mean, you can go back to the bunny-ear antenna on your TV,” he said on a recent podcast. “You don’t need a data center. But if you’re connected to a wire, you’re using the data center.”

That was true of the data centers that Amazon was building in 2006, but serving customers is less and less what data centers do now. Many of today’s monolithic structures exist only to train A.I.s — making models more powerful by carrying out operations that number in the trillions of trillions annually.

The result is a strange partisan landscape. It’s easy to think that data centers will become the Democrats’ issue, tying in to the party’s environmentalist commitments. But that is not what’s going on. The climate journalist Robinson Meyer told David Wallace-Wells of The Times recently that environmental arguments against data centers are sometimes overblown. The main reason people say they oppose them is water use, followed by electricity prices; but when a data center gets canceled, it is most often because of noise. In this respect the uprising against data centers resembles that against wind farms, a Republican movement if ever there was one.

Mr. Trump’s simple-minded online attacks on those who oppose data centers have led many partisan Democrats to deduce that the tech industry is “allying” itself with him. But the tech industry is merely taking pains, as it always does, to stay on the good side of its regulators. That effort has caused a good deal of quiet corruption through the years, and Mr. Trump’s demand for public avowals of fealty has made the corruption overt.

But all the Democrats have to do is win a presidential election, and they will rediscover that there is nothing — nothing at all — inherently Trumpian about the tech industry. They will inherit all the complexities that come with trying to push back against sector that is, for now, vilified and unpopular but vital to the economy.

Could they push back? Yes: If large numbers of Americans come to accept the argument of many A.I. experts that the technology itself threatens humanity with extinction, then Democrats might be emboldened to take extreme steps to rein in the industry, even on pain of economic upheaval. But in that case the party would be likely to lose its political advantage in another way: through an effort to stop A.I. that becomes bipartisan.

Seventy percent of Americans now oppose having a data center near them. That’s a problem for Big Tech — one that will persist even if Republicans are routed and better policies put in place. The costs of data centers are local, the benefits national. So entrenched has inequality become on the cutting edge of our economy that any promise of eventual top-down redistribution of those benefits will be met with skepticism.

This is especially true as voters grow more savvy about who gets what and from whom in the tech industry itself. There is a reason Mark Zuckerberg had to promise at least $12 billion to settle claims that his business fostered internet addiction: He is now dealing with parents who belong to his own generation — a less gullible bunch, when it comes to tech, than the analog-age parents who raised them.

As the baby boomers’ presence in the electorate wanes, the millennials and their successors will be called upon to weigh A.I.’s promises against the likelihood of human extinction. You can get a sense of how they are leaning by looking at the polls: The problem of data centers is not just the inconvenience they pose; it’s also the project they serve.

The Times is committed to publishing a diversity of letters to the editor. We’d like to hear what you think about this or any of our articles. Here are some tips. And here’s our email: letters@nytimes.com.

SUMMARY

Every week seems to bring a record high for diesel prices — and more trouble for the nation’s truckers. These rising fuel costs are going to make their way into your purchases until the world’s supply of diesel increases, which doesn’t seem likely anytime soon, given the Iran and Ukraine conflicts. There’s been a lot of talk about banning exports of diesel fuel, at least temporarily.

ARTICLE

$6 Diesel Is Hurting Small Truckers. It Could Hurt Trump, Too.
When fuel costs rise, the price of everything rises.
By Adam Wingfield
Published 2026-09-29 15:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/opinion/diesel-prices-truckers.html

Every week seems to bring a record high for diesel prices — and more trouble for the nation’s truckers. They’re hurting. Since January, diesel has increased more than 80 percent, to $6.53 a gallon.

Nearly everything that you buy rides on a big, diesel-burning truck at some point. Farmers are heavy users of diesel for their machinery, too, so diesel figures in twice at the supermarket. These rising fuel costs are going to make their way into your purchases until the world’s supply of diesel increases, which doesn’t seem likely anytime soon, given the Iran and Ukraine conflicts.

President Trump is reportedly considering banning diesel exports. It won’t help. Sure, some regions in the United States, such as the Southeast, would see prices subside for a short time, but prices elsewhere would increase.

For small truckers, the pain at the pump is threatening their businesses. About 92 percent of America’s trucking companies are small operations, with 10 or fewer trucks. If we lose too many of them, freight costs — and then your costs — will go even higher. I’ve been in this industry for more than two decades, as both a truck owner and now as a logistics consultant helping smaller operators. A lot of them were struggling even before we saw a $3 per gallon increase in diesel costs. It’s their largest variable expense.

We’re advising our truckers to be careful about the lanes they choose—as in, what destinations will yield the best outcomes. With truckers now spending as much as $1,400 per tank, you have to tightly control fuel burn. In California, the price is literally off the charts — the pumps were at their limit of $9.999 a gallon. We tell truckers going west to east to buy only enough fuel to get out of California. It’s worth it to add a stop in Nevada and fill up there. My clients generally buy fuel at the pump, often at a discount using a fuel card. But they can’t add a line item called a fuel surcharge.

In trucking, there are two different paths for moving cargo: One is by contract and the other is by the spot market. Contracted freight loads made by big fleets include a fuel surcharge that changes from week to week and is tied to the average diesel price. The spot market moves general freight through brokerages. Small carriers do most of their business this way; they generally don’t haul specialty items or perishables like pharmaceuticals. Truckers bid against one another on each load the brokers offer.

The spot market isn’t working well for a lot of them. This year, overall spot rates are up roughly 66 cents per mile to $3.41 per mile. But fuel costs are up 90 cents per mile. For a small trucking company, that can often become a losing proposition — they can’t hedge the cost of diesel prices as UPS and other large outfits can.

With diesel prices spiking, too often it means running a truckload at a loss, once you include costs such as maintenance, truck payments, insurance, registration and permits and disability coverage. You’ve got to worry about cash management, too. A small carrier running spot negotiates load by load but has to pay the fuel card bill in seven days whether that load is paid for or not.

To make matters worse, the trucking industry has dealt with a prolonged, post-pandemic freight recession that drove down rates and forced out thousands of trucking outfits. The current price spike could be a similar catalyst. That’s how exits happen in this business. Not a sudden collapse, but an owner-operator parking the truck, letting their interstate trucking authority lapse, and walking away because the next load won’t cover his bills.

Small trucking companies tend to drive in the right lane when it comes to politics. And they want immediate relief. Simple as that. If diesel rates keep rising, truckers will show up at the polls and let their complaints be known. They have been posting videos from truck stops and gas stations of their astonishingly high fuel bills, just in case the message isn’t getting across.

There’s been a lot of talk about banning exports of diesel fuel, at least temporarily. One Republican senator, Dan Sullivan of Alaska, said it out loud: “The cost of diesel is just too damn high.” Agreed. We need to get lower fuel prices for the sake of the entire economy. But a ban on diesel exports isn’t necessarily the right solution. We live in a global market. A ban will ultimately raise the cost of imports. It may provide temporary price relief to truckers in states such as Mississippi and Louisiana, close to the refineries that supply diesel, but it will raise prices in the Northeast, which imports diesel. Mid- to long term it could make things worse.

We all pay when there’s a sustained fuel price run-up like one we’ve experienced this year. It will probably push the next wave of small truckers out faster than many of us expect. Fewer trucks on the road means less capacity, and less capacity means higher rates. Those costs pass to the shipper, then the retailer, then to the register — where you will wonder why prices are going up again.

Everything on that shelf got there on a truck. And every one of those miles costs more to run today than it did in January.

Adam Wingfield is a former trucking company owner and founder of Innovative Logistics Group, a consultancy focused on small trucking firms.

The Times is committed to publishing a diversity of letters to the editor. We’d like to hear what you think about this or any of our articles. Here are some tips. And here’s our email: letters@nytimes.com.

Follow the New York Times Opinion section on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, Bluesky, WhatsApp and Threads.
