SUMMARY

In 1992, James Carville’s famous refrain — “It’s the economy, stupid” — compressed into four words what it might have taken a political scientist 400 words to explain: When family budgets feel tight, voters often go shopping for a new party to run things. Arguably, pocketbook issues led Donald Trump back to the White House for a second term: Poll after poll in 2024 showed the economy as the top issue and tended to show him with a significant advantage on who was more trusted to handle it. Today, President Trump and Republicans haven’t merely lost that advantage; they’re underwater on the cost-of-living issue by an eight-point margin.

ARTICLE

Trump Has Become Just Another Disappointing Politician
His winning brand — outsider businessman — has withered.
By Kristen Soltis Anderson
Published 2026-09-29 19:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/opinion/trump-republicans-economy-midterms.html

In 1992, James Carville’s famous refrain — “It’s the economy, stupid” — compressed into four words what it might have taken a political scientist 400 words to explain: When family budgets feel tight, voters often go shopping for a new party to run things.

So as we approach the 2026 midterm elections, it’s hardly a unique insight for a pollster like me to say the election will hinge on the issues of our fragile economy and the high cost of living. Arguably, pocketbook issues led Donald Trump back to the White House for a second term: Poll after poll in 2024 showed the economy as the top issue and tended to show him with a significant advantage on who was more trusted to handle it.

Today, President Trump and Republicans haven’t merely lost that advantage; they’re underwater on the cost-of-living issue by an eight-point margin. And this year a second issue has been rising in my polling, ranking below the cost of living but ahead of other concerns. It’s not just the economy: “It’s the corruption,” too.

Voters don’t think the economy is working for them, and they think it’s being rigged more and more in favor of a precious few who are cozied up to our nation’s leaders. The combination of these two worries is putting Mr. Trump and Republicans in a terrible position on the eve of an election.

It’s also eating away at the winning brand that Mr. Trump cultivated over many years.

When Gallup asked Republicans back in 2016 what made Mr. Trump appealing, one in six alluded to his experience as a businessman. This was a product of his years in the public eye as a real estate mogul and as the star of “The Apprentice.” The top response? Mr. Trump was an “outsider.” A decade ago, that branding was understandable: He had never held elected office and was quite obviously not beloved by the G.O.P. establishment. His brand was so strong that in 2023, more than six years after he first took the oath of office, he was still considered an “outsider” by nearly seven in 10 Republicans.

Some of his voters are wondering if that’s still true. Robert, one of the Trump-voting Texas swing voters in a recent Times Opinion focus group for which I was a moderator, put it this way: “You used to think that you could count on the Republicans to be able to help out with the economy.” Now, he said, it feels as if “it’s going to be the top class or the certain friends that are getting the benefit of the economy, not the general folks.”

In my own polling, nearly two-thirds of voters say “most politicians are corrupt or just looking out for their own interest.” To borrow a phrase Mr. Trump used to be particularly fond of, voters think there’s a swamp that needs a lot of draining. Republicans howled, rightly, when President Bill Clinton was alleged to have traded stays in the Lincoln Bedroom for campaign contributions. They raised hell over Hunter Biden’s unseemly income streams during his father’s vice presidency.

For years, Mr. Trump got a lot of mileage out of his supporters thinking of him as a singular figure — a tycoon who put his glitzy life on hold in order to fix a broken Washington. Today, they see headlines about memecoin scams, inexplicable pardons and the enormous wealth that the president’s family and close associates are accumulating, and some of them are beginning to draw a different conclusion.

It would be one thing if Americans thought Mr. Trump were focused on fixing the economy and just hadn’t had enough time to deliver results. Sometimes voters give points for effort: In 2012, my research on young voters found that though they felt President Barack Obama’s economic record was lackluster, they still gave him credit for “trying.”

In January 2025, I asked voters what they hoped Mr. Trump would focus on in his second term, and they were clear that they wanted to see efforts to lower the cost of living and secure the border. By November 2025, more than seven in 10 said he had given a lot of attention to the latter, but only 43 percent said he had made reducing the cost of living one of his highest priorities. Today, that figure is down to four in 10, fewer than the number who think he has prioritized projects such as building a White House ballroom or renovating the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. Even among Republican voters, only six in 10 think he has made the cost of living a top priority.

Many of Mr. Trump’s supporters grumble that he’s out chasing pet projects and feeding his ego, busy renaming buildings and bodies of water. As Pam, another of my focus-group participants, put it: “Those things to me are a waste, instead of spending time on what’s going on here in the U.S. and the fact that people are struggling.”

On its own, an economy that feels like it is leaving people behind would be a political problem for any incumbent. But add to it the gold leaf and vanity projects, and you wind up with a politically perilous one-two punch.

Some of the people who’ve believed in Mr. Trump over the past decade seem to be coming to the conclusion that the outsider businessman they voted for is just another typical politician. And while there are surely plenty of disillusioned Trump voters who wouldn’t dare cast a ballot for a Democrat, there’s no guarantee that they’ll bother to turn out on Election Day if they feel their own side is behaving poorly. Come November, that’s a slice of their coalition that Republicans can’t afford to lose.

Kristen Soltis Anderson is the author of “The Selfie Vote: Where Millennials Are Leading America (and How Republicans Can Keep Up).”

SUMMARY

Most college professors I know believe that students learn to think — critically, creatively, reflectively, tenaciously — only by writing. At Williams College, where I am a professor, writing skills are among the very few general education requirements. If I do not treat writing as essential for achieving thought, it is not clear why I should force my students to.

ARTICLE

I’m a College Professor. Writing Isn’t as Important as We Think.
If I do not treat writing as essential for achieving thought, it is not clear why I should force my students to.
By Joe Cruz
Published 2026-09-29 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/opinion/writing-thinking-college-ai.html

Most college professors I know believe that students learn to think — critically, creatively, reflectively, tenaciously — only by writing. At Williams College, where I am a professor, writing skills are among the very few general education requirements.

It’s no surprise, then, that universities see artificial intelligence as an existential threat, and have launched an arms race of countermeasures: more proctored essay exams; test-taking rooms shielded from the internet; requirements that essays be composed on platforms that track all edits, so the word-for-word genealogy can be verified. I’ve heard professors rejoicing when they see typos or grammatical errors in an essay, as if they proved that a student wrote it without any help from A.I.

But what if we are mistaken in treating writing as the highest cultivation of thought? The evidence that supports this belief is thin at best. Writing can be useful cognitive scaffolding for memory and self-regulated learning, but the notion that it is the best process for developing thinking skills is a fairly recent idea, traceable to the 1970s writing-across-the-curriculum movement.

In 1980, James Britton, an educator, hypothesized that we discover what we think in the act of writing. “Hypothesized” is the correct word here, since Mr. Britton’s anecdotal and introspective suppositions never amounted to proof of a stronger claim, and studies since have been limited or inconclusive.

In Plato’s “Phaedrus,” Socrates offers a startling criticism of writing. Written words, he claims, are not the true children of knowledge, because writing cannot speak, answer questions or come to its own defense. Only through conversation among minds, he suggests, does reason yield real insight. For the past two millenniums, this appraisal has seemed like a failure to appreciate the power of writing. But perhaps Socrates was right, and we think best by speaking, answering and defending our ideas.

I don’t rely on prepared scripts when I teach, and few of the teachers I most admire do. Instead, I engage my seminar students through messy, searching conversation, responding to their presence in the classroom to gauge whether we’re understanding one another. I want to make new connections in the immediacy of our back-and-forth. I want to recall a thread from two class meetings ago spontaneously and weave it into my improvised lecture while snapping into new ways of thinking about it in the moment.

If the only way that I could teach my courses was to sculpt written paragraphs, I’m not sure I would actually know the material. If I do not treat writing as essential for achieving thought, it is not clear why I should force my students to.

Writing assignments serve practical needs of colleges and universities. When we receive a batch of 10-page essays, we can take them home, read a few, put them aside and grade the rest when the opportunity arises. If our minds wander, we can reread the prose before us. If we need to justify a grade, we can cite the record. Writing is a portable, compact trace of mind that is more manageable in a bureaucracy than is a conversation. But none of these conveniences is about developing the best thought.

Last semester I permitted my students to use A.I. tools on their final essays in accordance with specific guidelines. They then had a 45-minute oral exam in which I could audit their understanding of their claims and push them further in their analyses. I was reassured by the results. In no case did I suspect that an A.I. had written a student’s paper in the substantive, objectionable way that we are all concerned about. The students were all too sharp on the ideas, too deft in reconfiguring their thoughts and extending them dynamically. Moreover, at least half of the class was more agile, more reflective and clearer during oral exams than they were in their papers.

I believe colleges can permit the use of A.I. writing tools without undermining the next generation of thinkers. But to get there, we need to embrace a different image of a university education — one in which ideas are expressed in real time and analytical thought unfolds as a debate or an oral defense or a group discussion. It will take courage to demand that students demonstrate active, participatory mastery of ideas. And it will take courage on their part to abandon the safe recursion of revision and narrative refinement. To be sure, there will be challenges of scale, and not every kind of institution will be able to adapt. The benefits, however, may be enormous.

Pursuing an alternative path where we think aloud together, vigorously and sharply, won’t yield a world in which nothing is written. Socrates was wrong if he was suggesting that there should be no writing at all. Writing has an important function: It summarizes and compresses our thoughts into a shareable, durable medium. Writing remains an essential life skill, and we will continue to do it. A.I. will write summaries of our thoughts and may contribute some of its own. But we shouldn’t always force students to maintain a written record of knowledge. Universities have forgotten that archiving and thinking are separate.

Consider what we might gain if we practiced speaking more and carrying around the resources of mind through our own attention, memory and engagement with one another. We may end up spending less time isolated, gain more practice resolving disagreement and find ourselves a clearer sense of what we believe. This is the moment to claim critical thought back.

Joe Cruz is the chair of the philosophy department and the program on cognitive science at Williams College.

SUMMARY

Fourteen years ago, a venture capital firm created a program for college students to invest in their peers, called Dorm Room Fund. This month, Dorm Room Fund raised a new $50 million fund to keep investing in companies created by college students and the 500 members of its alumni network. Dorm Room Fund and several other alumni also invested.

ARTICLE

College Students Flex Their Power in A.I. Investment Frenzy
Dorm Room Fund, a program that lets college students invest in their peers, raised a new $50 million fund as the competition for young founders ramps up.
By Erin Griffith
Published 2026-09-29 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/technology/dorm-room-fund-ai-investment.html

Fourteen years ago, a venture capital firm created a program for college students to invest in their peers, called Dorm Room Fund. Some dismissed the effort as risky and a little bit crazy. After all, could you really trust students to make good investments?

Now the fund’s network has its tentacles all over the artificial intelligence boom.

Dorm Room Fund’s alumni have gone on to establish major A.I. companies like the coding start-up Cursor and the defense tech company Shield AI. Others have become investors at top firms including Sequoia Capital, Andreessen Horowitz and Lightspeed Venture Partners. They share deals, advice and industry banter.

This month, Dorm Room Fund raised a new $50 million fund to keep investing in companies created by college students and the 500 members of its alumni network. That is four times the size of its last fund, a sign of how much investor attitudes about the program have changed.

Silicon Valley investors have long courted college students, including paying them to drop out, as Peter Thiel’s Thiel Fellowship famously does. But the wooing has gotten more aggressive in the A.I. boom, where dropouts and recent graduates are finding overnight success in growing numbers.

Last week, Andreessen Horowitz announced the Horowitz Andreessen Academy, a free and unaccredited one-year program in San Francisco for high school graduates to “learn at the speed of Silicon Valley.” The start-up accelerator Y Combinator last year introduced Early Decision, where founders who are accepted to the accelerator can “defer” joining until after they graduate from college.

“When there are big tech shifts, it advantages first-time builders,” said Molly Fowler, 39, a partner at Dorm Room Fund, which is based in New York. “It’s those moments that level the playing field.”

Dorm Room Fund was created as part of the venture capital firm First Round Capital, before being spun out in 2021. The program works by choosing students from a pool of undergraduate and graduate school applicants, creating a team of 60 student investors on roughly 30 campuses — including Stanford University and the University of Waterloo — each academic year.

The students are trained on venture capital basics and meet weekly to evaluate potential deals. They also travel to an annual off-site meeting described as a junior version of Allen & Company’s Sun Valley Conference, a gathering of tech and media power players.

Many of Dorm Room Fund’s student investors wind up at big venture firms, where they rely on their network from the program to find their next investment. Others are inspired to start companies. At least 118 Dorm Room Fund student investors have become entrepreneurs, and many have raised funding from their Dorm Room Fund peers.

Ms. Fowler said she had initially targeted $30 million for the latest fund but had enough interest for $50 million. She joined the firm in 2019 and used her experience as a political campaign fieldworker to deepen the engagement and community-building aspects of the program. This is critical, she said, because students won’t show up to a club if they aren’t getting anything out of it.

This points to another challenge of investing in students: They can be flaky, or worse. The amount of money sloshing around start-ups can attract opportunists who might try to get money for a class project or because they didn’t get the internship they wanted. Ms. Fowler said program participants had a keen sense of people’s reputations on campus, which she views as an advantage.

“It’s not like, ‘Here’s $100,000, go give it to your friends,’” she said.

Once the student investors have identified an investment deal, Ms. Fowler and her colleague, Madison Jacox, help with diligence and negotiating deal terms. Ms. Fowler’s team also leads investments in companies founded by alumni of Dorm Room Fund.

While not all the fund’s investments have produced hits, the portfolio includes eight $1 billion start-ups — such as Shield AI, worth $13 billion, and Vulcan Technologies, which provides A.I. technology for government agencies and is worth $2.5 billion — and 30 companies worth more than $300 million.

Claire Smilow, 35, an investor at the venture capital firm BoxGroup, participated in Dorm Room Fund from 2018 to 2020 while at Harvard Business School. There, she overlapped with Michael Truell, who joined the program while attending M.I.T. They stayed in touch.

In June 2022, BoxGroup invested $750,000 in Mr. Truell’s new company. The start-up did not have a product, but Ms. Smilow was impressed by Mr. Truell and eager to back “anything he built,” she said. Dorm Room Fund and several other alumni also invested.

Mr. Truell’s company became Cursor, the A.I. coding start-up. It sold to SpaceX this year for $60 billion, the largest acquisition of a venture-capital-backed company.

Ms. Smilow has backed at least two other founders she met through the network. She has stayed active in the community, attending alumni meet-ups, visiting campuses and speaking to new student investors.

“The Dorm Room Fund community has been more impactful on my career than the Harvard Business School community,” she said.

The firm’s latest fund shows the way the money often flows in Silicon Valley. Aryan Shah, 22, joined Dorm Room Fund while at Emory University from 2023 to 2025. Talking to founders inspired him to start his own company, so in 2025 he dropped out and co-founded Metis, which makes software for A.I. agents. His first call was to Ms. Fowler, who wrote a $300,000 check and advised him on fund-raising. Mr. Shah’s first three hires were Dorm Room Fund alumni.

In March, DoorDash bought Metis for more than $100 million in cash. Mr. Shah told Ms. Fowler that he wanted to put some proceeds into her new fund, so he wound up investing in the fund that had backed his company. Thirty percent of the new fund’s investors are Dorm Room Fund alumni or firms that employ them.

Investing in the fund felt like a way to give back, Mr. Shah said, and he wanted to support others having the same experience.

“It is truly the biggest cheat code any college student can have coming out of school if they want to do venture or start-ups,” he said.

SUMMARY

OpenAI now has artificial intelligence agents that act as personal digital assistants. Announced at the company’s annual developer conference on Tuesday in San Francisco, the agents, called dots, will compete with Meta’s A.I. agent, called Muse, which was also released this month; Google’s Gemini Spark, which came out in May; and Instinct, an A.I. agent start-up that raised $1 billion in its latest funding round. OpenAI’s new agents were introduced as the company faces growing questions about the safety of its technology and increasing calls for government regulation of the A.I. market.

ARTICLE

A New A.I. Agent Enters the Marketplace: OpenAI’s Dots
The ChatGPT maker unveiled agents that act as assistants, just weeks after Meta released Muse, as it faces scrutiny over incidents involving its technology.
By Emmy Martin
Published 2026-09-29 17:15 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/technology/openai-dots-ai-agents.html

OpenAI now has artificial intelligence agents that act as personal digital assistants.

Announced at the company’s annual developer conference on Tuesday in San Francisco, the agents, called dots, will compete with Meta’s A.I. agent, called Muse, which was also released this month; Google’s Gemini Spark, which came out in May; and Instinct, an A.I. agent start-up that raised $1 billion in its latest funding round.

“You may have seen early signs of what this could look like in virtual assistants that help you book a reservation or buy a plane ticket, and these things are useful to hand off,” Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, said, “but they are trivial relative to what the technology can do — and so we wanted to be way more ambitious.”

Dots are OpenAI’s most aggressive push to create a product out of A.I. agents, which are bots that can autonomously perform tasks for users, such as booking restaurant reservations or managing finances. Silicon Valley is betting A.I. agents will be how people next use the technology in a major way, moving consumer A.I. products away from answering questions to completing tasks.

OpenAI’s new agents were introduced as the company faces growing questions about the safety of its technology and increasing calls for government regulation of the A.I. market.

Over the summer, OpenAI’s A.I. agents went rogue and meddled with several U.S. federal government websites, and attacked Australian government websites and the infrastructure of the A.I. start-up Hugging Face. While A.I. agents from Anthropic, Meta and Google have also breached or tried to hack outside organizations, what is known so far about OpenAI’s agents has dwarfed issues that other companies have caused.

On Monday, OpenAI also said it would not release its newest A.I. model, known as GPT-6.1 Astra, because of safety concerns. Dots are powered by the company’s prior model, GPT-6 Astra. An OpenAI spokeswoman said the company “conducted additional safety testing” of dots and was “confident rolling this out.”

Users can message their dot agent, which they can name, in ChatGPT, Slack or Microsoft Teams or through text and connect to third-party apps. They can also talk to the agent on a phone call. The agents will be available starting Tuesday to subscribers of ChatGPT’s pro plans, except for those in some parts of Europe, and business premium and enterprise customers. Each user will get one agent, though OpenAI said it planned to increase that number.

OpenAI said users could set rules for what the agent could do on its own and what required permission. The agent must get approval before sensitive actions like changing a password or installing software, and it would not message people or change anything in a user’s apps without being asked.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

OpenAI also released GPT-6.1 Sol, a cheaper model that it said approached the abilities of its top system, GPT-6 Astra, at one-fifth of the price.

openai-warnings-security.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 31  Words: 1302/1304

SUMMARY

The exchanges between OpenAI employees and executives — which have not been previously reported — were part of a pattern where the San Francisco company did not prioritize security, according to employees and independent security researchers. Independent security researchers said they found bugs in recent months that allowed them to view the internal communications of OpenAI employees. OpenAI is not the only company that has recently disclosed A.I. security incidents.

ARTICLE

OpenAI Ignored Employees Who Warned It Wasn’t Doing Enough About Security
Employees and security researchers said that they had cautioned the company on safely testing its A.I. models and strengthening its corporate infrastructure, but that OpenAI did not listen.
By Sheera Frenkel, Dustin Volz and Dylan Freedman
Published 2026-09-29 16:55 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/technology/openai-warnings-security.html

Months before OpenAI’s artificial intelligence went rogue, two employees raised an alarm with top executives. They were ignored.

In emails, the employees said they worried that OpenAI’s newest artificial intelligence models were not being appropriately monitored during testing to gauge the technology’s sophistication and to secure the models, according to messages viewed by The New York Times.

In response, OpenAI executives told the employees that the tests needed to move forward as quickly as possible to release the A.I. models on time. No additional security protocols were instituted, said the workers, who were not authorized to speak publicly on sensitive matters.

OpenAI’s models later broke out of their testing environments and attacked the A.I. start-up Hugging Face and other organizations, setting off a global debate about A.I. safety.

The exchanges between OpenAI employees and executives — which have not been previously reported — were part of a pattern where the San Francisco company did not prioritize security, according to employees and independent security researchers. That approach not only was evident with the testing of A.I. models, they said, but also showed up in other areas of the company, which makes the ChatGPT chatbot.

Independent security researchers said they found bugs in recent months that allowed them to view the internal communications of OpenAI employees. They also found other vulnerabilities that would enable them to see the company’s internal computer code and view the chat logs of ChatGPT users. When the researchers contacted OpenAI about their findings, they said, the company initially disregarded them.

“OpenAI’s security seems to be about what you’d expect from a research lab that scaled at a blistering pace over four years and focused more on beating its competitors than securing its infrastructure,” said Joshua Saxe, the chief technology officer of the A.I. security firm Abundant Security.

OpenAI employees said that many of the day-to-day decisions about security were made by Greg Brockman, the company’s president, and Dane Stuckey, the chief information security officer. Sam Altman, the chief executive, is not closely involved in security, they said.

OpenAI is not the only company that has recently disclosed A.I. security incidents. Google, Meta and Anthropic have also revealed that their most advanced A.I. technology escaped testing environments and autonomously attacked other computer infrastructure without their knowledge.

But OpenAI’s handling of security is under particular scrutiny because its A.I. models have been involved in the biggest known number of instances of what the company has called “concerning” behavior — and in instances that experts have said were the most troubling.

In a dozen or so incidents, OpenAI’s systems hacked or tried to breach organizations, including the websites of U.S. government agencies; the technology also hid its mistakes, made up data, tried to message other chatbots and moved files onto the open internet without permission. In all of these cases, the A.I. acted without being instructed to do so.

“In some sense, this is an OpenAI-specific problem in that it seems like they had very bad security, and also sloppy model training practices that led to the models having this sort of propensity,” said Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI employee who has criticized the company’s safety and leads a research nonprofit called the AI Futures Project, though he added that other A.I. companies were not much better.

Drew Pusateri, an OpenAI spokesman, said the company was committed to safety and took any security reports or concerns seriously. The lab has internal channels for reporting safety issues, he said, and took immediate action on flaws brought up by independent security researchers.

“As frontier models have become more capable, we continue to evolve our security practices, but recognize a need to move faster,” Mr. Pusateri said. He added that OpenAI had slowed some A.I. development and was making changes to strengthen security in research and testing.

(The Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

Two OpenAI employees said workers had raised concerns for months about potential safety issues with testing A.I. models, including not enough monitoring. Employees also asked about vulnerabilities in the type of software the company was using to manage day-to-day safety, according to messages viewed by The Times. Each time, their questions were brushed aside or acted on too slowly, they said.

Security researchers said they had been met with a similar reception when they told OpenAI about other vulnerabilities.

In July, researchers at the security company Hacktron said they told OpenAI about how they had found a way to break into the company’s systems with the help of an A.I. model created by its rival Anthropic. OpenAI initially took issue with their approach, they said.

In a shared channel on the messaging platform Slack, Mr. Stuckey of OpenAI wrote that it was “pretty sad” that Hacktron’s researchers had gone to such lengths to demonstrate the company’s vulnerabilities, according to copies of the communications seen by The Times.

“We just felt like they were angry at us,” Mohan Pedhapati, a Hacktron researcher, said of OpenAI. He added that the company appeared to still be using the security practices of a start-up, leveraging the software services of others for critical infrastructure instead of building its own tools.

“Why are you using Slack to build your nuclear Manhattan projects?” Mr. Pedhapati asked. Hacktron’s hack could have granted him full access to the Slack messaging platform to see what OpenAI employees were saying, he said.

Mr. Stuckey later apologized to Hacktron, and OpenAI awarded the researchers $6,500 for disclosing the flaw.

“We thank the researchers for contacting us and sharing their findings,” Mr. Pusateri said.

In September, researchers at the Objective-See Foundation, a nonprofit that studies security and privacy risks, including those posed by A.I. agents, reported a bug to OpenAI that would give people access to a ChatGPT user’s entire private chat logs on a compromised device and allow them to invisibly interact with the user’s browser sessions.

Patrick Wardle, a software analyst at the Objective-See Foundation, said that when his team initially submitted what it found to OpenAI’s official bug bounty program — where researchers report bugs or vulnerabilities they find in exchange for recognition or financial rewards — its report languished. The research was escalated to the appropriate engineering unit only when Mr. Wardle reached out directly to friends at the company and Mr. Stuckey, who were all responsive, he said.

OpenAI gave $500 to the group for its work, which Mr. Wardle said was low compared with what he would expect from other companies given the severity of the flaw. OpenAI fixed the bug, he said, and acknowledged it this week in its public software release notes without disclosing details.

It was “not the mature security program you’d expect from a security-centric company,” Mr. Wardle said.

OpenAI employees said that more such disclosures were probable. The company is not only reviewing actions taken by its new models during testing but is still receiving warnings from hackers about open security vulnerabilities, they said.

On Friday, an independent report released by a group of engineers and researchers revealed new alarming behavior from the Hugging Face incident, including instances in which OpenAI’s agents tried to message Anthropic’s Claude and use other A.I. models to beat anti-robot protections on a website.

OpenAI also revealed last week that new safeguards had failed to prevent its latest A.I. model from breaking through them to gain access to the internet. A retrospective review found other instances of unauthorized internet access that had gone undetected. OpenAI announced that it was pausing training for its most advanced models and was engaged in an extensive review of unexpected behavior by the technology.

On Monday, the company went even further. It said it would not release its newest A.I. model, GPT-6.1 Astra, because of security concerns raised by its researchers.

home-mortgage-program-birthrate-decline.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 23  Words: 808/807
================================================================================

SUMMARY

What they found sheds new light on how personal finances affect the decision to have children: Homeownership increases the birth rate. Dr. Kearney and Dr. Dettling found a policy that did: government-backed home mortgages, mostly issued under the postwar G.I. “This mortgage program was not meant as a pronatalist policy, but it seems to have had that effect,” Dr. Kearney said.

ARTICLE

Could Homeownership Reverse the Decline in Birthrates?
Researchers looked back at the baby-boom era and found that federal mortgage programs played a part in the country’s population upswing after World War II.
By Sabrina Tavernise
Published 2026-09-28 15:21 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/28/us/home-mortgage-program-birthrate-decline.html

Puzzling over the reasons for today’s baby bust, a pair of economists went back to the last baby boom for answers.

What they found sheds new light on how personal finances affect the decision to have children: Homeownership increases the birth rate.

Experts have long been skeptical that the two-decade decline in the birthrate was related to people’s pocketbooks. They reason that as the birthrate has been falling, household income has been rising and poorer women have been more likely to have more children than richer women.

But Melissa S. Kearney, an economics professor at the University of Notre Dame, and Lisa J. Dettling, an economist at the Federal Reserve Board, found an economic connection that was less about price and more about ownership.

The finding, published in its final version by the National Bureau of Economic Research in September, offers new insights into what policies could actually raise the birthrate, which has hit historic lows around the world. Governments have tried multiple strategies, including tax credits, subsidized child care and paid maternity leave, to encourage people to have more children, but nothing has made much of a difference.

Dr. Kearney and Dr. Dettling found a policy that did: government-backed home mortgages, mostly issued under the postwar G.I. Bill.

“This mortgage program was not meant as a pronatalist policy, but it seems to have had that effect,” Dr. Kearney said.

The finding comes as the cost of living has taken center stage in midterm election campaigns. Housing in particular has felt increasingly out of reach for younger Americans: The median age of first-time home buyers rose to 40 in 2025, a historic high. Last week, mortgage rates jumped to 7 percent, the highest since January 2025, raising the hurdle to home buying even higher.

The baby boom began in 1946, after the Allied victory in World War II. By 1957, the total fertility rate had risen by about 30 percent, reaching 3.7 children per woman, a modern high.

Researchers over decades have tried to explain that burst of fertility. Hypotheses included the economic security that families felt in contrast to the war years and the sharp drop in health risks during pregnancy.

But Dr. Kearney and Dr. Dettling wanted to look for new clues. They decided to examine homeownership, which also expanded during that time. The G.I. Bill in particular gave millions of returning soldiers the ability to buy houses with low or no down payments.

That policy was transformational, helping to build the American middle class. Young families, in particular, benefited: Among Americans of childbearing age, homeownership rose to 50 percent in 1960, from 20 percent in 1940.

But how could economists figure out if rising homeownership had fueled the baby boom? They discovered that the Federal Reserve held a trove of data: thousands of pages of mortgage records.

Undergraduate research assistants digitized them over two years. The researchers then linked them with demographic data from each state to test if there were any effect.

“We kept cutting the data and looking at it,” Dr. Kearney said. “It kept lining up.”

The result was startling: For every 1,000 new mortgages issued through the government programs, there were about 300 additional births the following year.

The mortgages were not the only driver, nor were they predictive for everybody: Black women, whose families were unfairly shut out of the postwar mortgage program, also had increases in childbearing.

The findings also help explain a related shift in the demographics of the era, Dr. Kearney said. Women married younger, and started to have children earlier than previous generations. They also went on to have larger families.

She emphasized that the effect of the government programs on births was not related to housing costs, but to homeownership. Having your name on a deed represents a certain kind of emotional and financial security, one that can create confidence in the future. Women today often say they want that before having children.

Other researchers who looked at the study said it was sound, but that it was historical.

“The empirical work seems pretty strong and they find a pretty good-sized effect,” said Phillip Levine, an economics professor at Wellesley College who has written papers with Dr. Kearney but was not involved in this one.

But, he added, it is not clear how much the past can be applied to the present. “Does that mean that we would get the same result today? We don’t know.”

Dr. Kearney said the findings are relevant today, but the context is different. Making it easier for young families to get a mortgage could still spur earlier and more childbearing. But such a policy today could also push up home prices, given that today’s supply of housing is far more restricted, compared to the mid-20th century when the suburbs were forming. That, she said, is the challenge for policymakers.

SUMMARY

A super PAC supporting Dan Osborn, the independent candidate for Senate in Nebraska, is airing a graphic new 60-second ad attacking his opponent, Senator Pete Ricketts, the Republican incumbent, for pardoning a man convicted of sexual assault nearly three decades after the assault. Pete Ricketts cast the deciding vote to pardon this man.” Mr. Ricketts and Mr. Peterson ultimately voted for the pardon.

ARTICLE

A Tough Ad Reminds Nebraska Voters About a Brutal Crime and a Pardon
A group supporting Dan Osborn, the independent Senate candidate in Nebraska, is airing an ad attacking Senator Pete Ricketts, a Republican, for pardoning a man convicted of sexual assault.
By Lisa Lerer
Published 2026-09-29 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/us/politics/ad-watch-nebraska-senate-race.html

A super PAC supporting Dan Osborn, the independent candidate for Senate in Nebraska, is airing a graphic new 60-second ad attacking his opponent, Senator Pete Ricketts, the Republican incumbent, for pardoning a man convicted of sexual assault nearly three decades after the assault.

Here’s a look at the ad, its accuracy and its major takeaway.

On the Screen

The ad opens with a “content warning” about sexual assault and the phone number for the National Domestic Violence Hotline.

It cuts to a narrator, called “Jody S.,” who says she has a “story to tell” about Mr. Ricketts.

The woman describes being violently assaulted by an intruder in her home.

The style is spare, with limited music and images of an empty home. Some of the woman’s words are rendered in white type over a black background.

The ad pans to a series of newspaper headlines from the 1990s showing that the woman’s attacker pleaded guilty to sexual assault and was sentenced to prison.

Later, a black-and-white image of a smiling Mr. Ricketts flashes on the screen. The woman says that the senator, then serving as governor and as a member of the state’s pardon board, had voted to pardon her assailant.

Viewers next see a mug shot of the woman’s attacker on Nebraska’s official sex offender registry, part of the state government website. The man’s image then disappears. His pardon, the woman explains, meant that his name was removed from the registry.

The Script

“I have a story to tell about our senator, Pete Ricketts. On April 30, 1993, John Arias broke into my home, tied me up with parachute cord and violently raped me. My children heard everything that happened. He was caught, pled guilty and went to prison. He said I should watch my back for the rest of my life. Pete Ricketts cast the deciding vote to pardon this man.”

“Governor Ricketts.”

“Yes. But with that, you’ve got your pardon.”

“That pardon brought back all the nightmares. I found out just totally by accident. I thought impossible that anyone would make that decision without contacting the victim. Because of Pete Ricketts, my attacker is now allowed to own a gun and had his name removed from the sex offender registry. I have no idea why Senator Ricketts chose my rapist over me.”

“Nebraska Values PAC is responsible for the content of this advertising.”

Accuracy

The assailant, John Arias, pleaded guilty to first-degree sexual assault and was sentenced to 15 to 30 years in prison. He was released in April 2008, after serving nearly 14 years, according to state records.

In September 2022, he requested a pardon from the state board of pardons, which included Mr. Ricketts, who was then governor; Doug Peterson, then the state attorney general, and Bob Evnen, the secretary of state. A pardon would not erase the crime from state records but would remove his name from the state’s sex offender registry.

According to an audio recording of his 28-minute pardon hearing, Mr. Arias did not deny the assault, though he appeared to question some of the details of the victim’s account.

Mr. Ricketts and Mr. Peterson ultimately voted for the pardon. Mr. Evnen opposed it, saying that he didn’t think Mr. Arias had “fully come to grips with what happened that night.”

Mr. Peterson described the request as “on the bubble,” but cited Mr. Arias’s military service and volunteer work with the American Legion.

“We historically have taken these types of criminal acts, like sexual assault and child abuse, very seriously,” he said.

Mr. Ricketts agreed that Mr. Arias’s request was “on the bubble” but announced “you’ve got your pardon” — the line clipped in the ad.

Weeks after granting the pardon, Mr. Ricketts issued a statement defending his decision, saying that Mr. Arias “has shown to be remorseful.”

A few months later, the victim, who said she was not notified about the pardon or invited to participate in the hearing, testified before the State Senate in support of a bill to ensure that crime victims are notified of Nebraska Board of Pardons meetings.

“His rights were restored,” she told the legislators. “I ask you, where do my rights fit in?”

The Takeaway

Mr. Osborn, a union leader and Navy veteran, is in a tough race against Mr. Ricketts, who served two terms as governor and won his Senate seat in a 2024 special election. While Mr. Osborn is an independent, Democratic candidates cleared the field to ease his path, and he has been endorsed by the Nebraska Democratic Party.

The spot is an effort by Democrats and their allies to gain traction in a red state, where registered Republicans outnumber Democrats nearly two to one. Mr. Osborn has repeatedly cast Mr. Ricketts, one of the richest members of the Senate, as uninterested in the concerns of everyday Nebraskans. The ad is an effort to undermine his character and reinforce that image.

SUMMARY

Democrats in Congress are increasingly adopting a more punitive approach to dealing with Israel, taking a series of steps in recent days that suggest they would pursue sanctions for building new settlements and other actions against the Jewish state should they win majorities in November’s elections. Last week, Senator Chris Coons, the Delaware Democrat who would be in line to become the chairman of the Foreign Relations Committee if his party were to win control of the Senate, introduced legislation that would impose sanctions on Israel for the construction of settlements in the E1 area of the West Bank, a strategically significant patch of land that would split the West Bank in two and complicate the potential creation of a Palestinian state.

ARTICLE

Democrats in Congress Embrace a More Punitive Posture Toward Israel
Nearly every Democratic senator voted to advance a measure calling for a human rights report on Israel’s conduct in the West Bank, as some in the party propose punishing settlement activity with sanctions.
By Robert Jimison and Annie Karni
Published 2026-09-30 00:12 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/us/politics/democrats-congress-israel.html

Democrats in Congress are increasingly adopting a more punitive approach to dealing with Israel, taking a series of steps in recent days that suggest they would pursue sanctions for building new settlements and other actions against the Jewish state should they win majorities in November’s elections.

On Tuesday, all but one Senate Democrat voted to advance a measure that would force the Trump administration to produce a human rights report examining violence by Israel in the West Bank, including the deaths of Palestinian American citizens, in a rebuke that would once have seemed unthinkable.

The bid failed, but the near-unanimous level of Democratic backing for it reflected the party’s new willingness to embrace steps that had long been considered anathema given the relationship between the United States and its closest Middle East ally.

At the same time, top Democrats in the House and Senate have proposed legislation that would impose sanctions on Israel for building settlements, making it clear to Israeli companies and banks that if they were involved with settlement building they would be penalized. The steps, months after almost half of House Democrats voted to cut off aid to Israel, are the latest sign of an expanding appetite in the party to move beyond expressions of disapproval and toward measures that could reorder the U.S.-Israeli relationship.

“While I was pleased so many of my Democratic colleagues joined this effort, it’s clear the United States must do more,” said Senator Chris Van Hollen, Democrat of Maryland and the author of the human rights measure. “It is our responsibility to ensure recipients of U.S. taxpayer dollars act in line with our laws and our values.”

He added that “this resolution was an opportunity to shed light on a reality that flies in the face of that principle.”

The measure was blocked on a vote of 51 to 47. But it attracted support from almost the entire Democratic caucus, including from Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the minority leader and a staunch supporter of Israel. The sole Democratic “no” vote was from Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, who is an unequivocal backer of Israel.

One Republican, Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, voted with Democrats in favor of the resolution.

The issue of Israel and Gaza has repeatedly exposed divisions in the Democratic Party throughout this year’s midterm campaign. But in this case, the vote demonstrated near unity on an issue that drew far less support just two years ago.

In 2024, when Senator Bernie Sanders, the Vermont independent, forced a vote on a similar resolution seeking a State Department report on whether human rights violations had occurred in Gaza, just 11 Democrats voted to move the resolution forward.

Mr. Van Hollen’s measure invoked a never-tested section of the Foreign Assistance Act that allows Congress to demand information about the human rights practices of countries receiving U.S. security aid, and to cut off the money if an administration refuses to disclose it.

It would have required the State Department to produce an unclassified report examining Israel’s human rights record in the West Bank, including any effort to investigate the cases of nine U.S. citizens “killed by violent Israeli settlers or Israeli security forces.”

Coming just weeks before the midterm elections that have been shaped by Democratic voters’ mounting hostility toward Israel, it was seen by some senators in the party as a way to register opposition to the conduct of Netanyahu government without going as far as cutting off military aid. Still, it marked a clear break with the past, when most Democrats would reflexively vote against any measure that challenged Israel.

“That we’ve gotten to the point of a unanimous rebuke is astounding,” said Jeremy Ben-Ami, the president of J Street, the center-left lobbying group. “It used to be there was unanimous Democratic support for every pro-Israel resolution. Now it’s unanimous to take on their human rights violations.”

The debate has taken on new urgency during another burst of violence in the West Bank, where attacks by Israelis and Palestinians have fueled an increasingly volatile cycle.

Earlier on Tuesday, more than 100 Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians and soldiers in the West Bank when the military tried to return a Palestinian family to its home months after being forced out following a long campaign of violence.

As the violence continues, some Democrats are moving beyond investigations and are instead seeking to impose direct consequences on Israelis involved in expanding settlements.

Last week, Senator Chris Coons, the Delaware Democrat who would be in line to become the chairman of the Foreign Relations Committee if his party were to win control of the Senate, introduced legislation that would impose sanctions on Israel for the construction of settlements in the E1 area of the West Bank, a strategically significant patch of land that would split the West Bank in two and complicate the potential creation of a Palestinian state.

The move was notable for Mr. Coons, who has joined with Republicans to oppose his party’s bids to block U.S. weapons sales to Israel, saying that he would not “abandon our steadfast ally.”

Representative Joaquin Castro of Texas, a senior Democrat on the Foreign Affairs Committee, on Thursday is set to introduce a broader bill that would punish Israel for the construction of any new settlements throughout the West Bank and Gaza, as well as the expansion of existing ones. It also would prohibit the import of goods made in the settlements.

The bill is expected to be cosponsored by Democratic Representatives Don Beyer of Virginia, Madeleine Dean of Pennsylvania, Greg Casar of Texas and Sara Jacobs of California.

In a statement to The New York Times, Mr. Castro said that the record expansion of West Bank settlements was one of the top impediments to peace.

“Democrats must face this with urgency — act now or watch the prospect of Palestinian self-determination slip away forever,” he said. “Congress should and can be using every tool we have available, including sanctions.”

The recent moves come just weeks after Britain, France and Canada announced coordinated sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

democrats-voter-turnout.html

SUMMARY

From the first primaries in March through the final ones in September, Democrats’ turnout outpaced Republican voters in many key states that will decide congressional majorities next year. This primary season, perhaps the starkest example of Democratic enthusiasm came in Texas, a state Mr. Trump carried by 14 percentage points two years ago. Even in 2018, during the last Democratic wave election, 500,000 more people voted in the Republican Senate primary than in the Democratic one.

ARTICLE

Democratic Turnout Surged in the Primaries. Will It Matter in November?
A voter enthusiasm gap provides another signal that Democrats are favored this fall, though Republicans still have key advantages.
By Reid J. Epstein, Ashley Wu and Christine Zhang
Published 2026-09-29 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/us/politics/democrats-voter-turnout.html

From the first primaries in March through the final ones in September, Democrats’ turnout outpaced Republican voters in many key states that will decide congressional majorities next year. In red states like Texas, battlegrounds like Georgia and bluer ones like New Hampshire, Democrats have raced to the polls to choose their nominees, while Republicans have not kept up.

“There’s been historic enthusiasm gaps this cycle, that are real reasons to be optimistic,” said Meredith Kelly, who was a top official for the House Democratic campaign committee in 2018, the last midterm election with President Trump in office.

Furious Democratic voters emerged during that campaign’s primary season and maintained their energy into November. The party flipped 42 House seats, taking the majority. Republicans gained Senate seats that year in deep-red states like Indiana, Missouri and North Dakota where they ousted Democrats who had been elected during Barack Obama’s second presidential campaign.

This primary season, perhaps the starkest example of Democratic enthusiasm came in Texas, a state Mr. Trump carried by 14 percentage points two years ago. Both parties had hard-fought and expensive Senate primary campaigns there this year.

About 150,000 more people voted in the Democratic primary between James Talarico, the victor, and Representative Jasmine Crockett than in the Republican contest between Senator John Cornyn and the state’s attorney general, Ken Paxton, who would go on to win in a runoff.

That’s a major change from four years ago, when there were 900,000 more votes in the state’s Republican primaries for state offices than in its Democratic contests. Even in 2018, during the last Democratic wave election, 500,000 more people voted in the Republican Senate primary than in the Democratic one. That year, the last midterm election with Mr. Trump in office, Democrats flipped seats across Texas as Beto O’Rourke came the closest any Democrat had gotten in decades to winning a Senate race in the state.

The lopsided Democrat turnout didn’t extend to every state, and was most notable in battleground states.

Compare 2022 to 2026: Twenty-two states held contested primary elections in both parties for governor or Senate. Democratic turnout increased in three-quarters of those states this year over four years ago, while dropping in two-thirds of those states for Republicans.

Going back farther, Michigan and Wisconsin held competitive Democratic primaries in both 2018 — which drew record turnouts at the time — and 2026, and both saw huge turnout increases this year.

In Wisconsin, David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, narrowly defeated Francesca Hong, a state legislator from Madison, in a race that saw turnout jump by more than 250,000 votes — a 47 percent increase. Both the winning and losing candidates got more votes than the winner in the 2018 primary.

Michigan’s numbers were nearly as striking. The state’s 2018 competitive Democratic primary for governor drew 1.1 million voters. The Senate contest last month had 1.5 million.

Eight years ago, on the eve of the 2018 primaries, Nate Cohn wrote in The Times that the vote in primary races generally provides “a rough if imperfect indicator of the national political environment.”

But Republicans are better prepared for a wave of Democratic enthusiasm than they were during the “blue wave” in 2018. Republicans redrew House districts across the country to create more potentially safe seats for their candidates, and the party has a large cash advantage. As in 2018, this year’s Senate battleground is being fought in red states Mr. Trump carried two years before, giving his party a distinct advantage.

Tom Perez, who was the Democratic National Committee chairman in 2018, acknowledged that voter enthusiasm among Democrats wouldn’t go as far in the new political environment.

“I really do believe that people are going to come out in abundance,” he said, but he added that it would require more financial investment in potentially competitive races.

“You don’t want to wake up the day after and see that you lost by three points somewhere because you didn’t do anything,” he said.

jack-smith-congress-testimony.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 39  Words: 1468/1470

SUMMARY

It was meant to be a dramatic confrontation, a public accusation of perjury against Jack Smith, the special counsel who investigated Donald J. Trump. During a four-hour Senate Judiciary Committee hearing, Mr. Schmitt, a Republican from Missouri, struck a conspiratorial tone and asked Mr. Smith if he had attended an Atlanta Hawks home game in February 2024. Mr. Schmitt focused on the basketball game in the hopes that he could show Mr. Smith had perjured himself and was involved in a conspiracy with local Atlanta prosecutors to ensnare Mr. Trump.

ARTICLE

As Jack Smith Testifies, a Senator’s Accusation of Perjury Falls Apart
A Republican eager to prove the former special counsel was dishonest appeared to instead demonstrate his own confusion over basic facts.
By Devlin Barrett and Charlie Savage
Published 2026-09-29 09:30 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/us/politics/jack-smith-congress-testimony.html

It was meant to be a dramatic confrontation, a public accusation of perjury against Jack Smith, the special counsel who investigated Donald J. Trump. Instead, Senator Eric Schmitt’s amateur sleuthing into basketball led him to the wrong game, league and state.

During a four-hour Senate Judiciary Committee hearing, Mr. Schmitt, a Republican from Missouri, struck a conspiratorial tone and asked Mr. Smith if he had attended an Atlanta Hawks home game in February 2024.

Mr. Schmitt focused on the basketball game in the hopes that he could show Mr. Smith had perjured himself and was involved in a conspiracy with local Atlanta prosecutors to ensnare Mr. Trump. In a hearing where Republicans repeatedly accused Mr. Smith of lying, what Mr. Schmitt first presented as smoking-gun evidence against Mr. Smith turned out to be a misfire.

During his testimony, Mr. Smith appeared deeply confused by Mr. Schmitt’s question. “I definitely did not go to a Hawks game,” he said. “I’m sure of that.”

Mr. Schmitt seemed confident he had just caught Mr. Smith in a lie. It was part of a broader effort by Mr. Trump’s Republican allies to characterize Mr. Smith as politically partisan, a man with an ax to grind not just against a former president, but also the Republican establishment. Mr. Smith has already defended his work before Congress, and Republicans have claimed that his past testimony included perjury.

On Tuesday, Mr. Schmitt argued that Mr. Smith had lied again, this time about a basketball game. If the prosecutor was in Atlanta, Mr. Schmitt suggested, he might have met with the local district attorney, Fani Willis, who also pursued a criminal case against Mr. Trump.

Mr. Schmitt’s Republican colleague from Louisiana, John Kennedy, stood next to him helping hold up a poster board showing text messages among members of Mr. Smith’s special counsel team from Feb. 3, 2024, discussing seats at a basketball game.

“I don’t think you know we have this stuff, so I’ll give you a second to process it so you don’t perjure yourself,” Mr. Schmitt said, even as the poster board was swiftly taken down, too quickly for most in the room to read it.

When the former special counsel insisted he had not gone to see the Atlanta Hawks play in that time period, Mr. Schmitt declared, “I think you’ve already perjured yourself,” and called Mr. Smith a “dirtbag.”

The accusation appeared to unravel almost immediately.

Invited to respond by Senator Amy Klobuchar, a Minnesota Democrat, Mr. Smith said he had, in fact, attended a basketball game on that day, but it was to see the Iowa Hawkeyes at the University of Maryland. That night, Caitlin Clark, the star point guard who now plays in the W.N.B.A., scored 38 points and had 12 assists.

Ms. Klobuchar suggested that Mr. Schmitt’s accusation was rooted in the senator’s confusion between the “Hawks” of Atlanta and the “Hawkeyes” of Iowa.

Mr. Schmitt declared that he still stood by calling Mr. Smith a “dirtbag,” then left the hearing.

The exchange took up just four minutes of the hearing. But it showed how eager the Republicans were to paint Mr. Smith as an out-of-control partisan — and to find a basis to accuse him of a crime at a time when the Justice Department has proved receptive to pursuing the people who investigated Mr. Trump.

A central issue was Mr. Smith’s subpoenas for lawmakers’ phone records as he and his team sought to trace Mr. Trump’s pressure campaign on Congress to block Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s Electoral College certification.

As part of that effort, investigators also examined whether Mr. Trump had defrauded his supporters when he raised vast sums after the election promising to expose fraud that did not happen. They also subpoenaed financial records of Republican-aligned groups as they traced what actually happened to the money.

That effort did not result in charges.

Senator Ted Cruz, Republican of Texas, and others argued that when Mr. Smith subpoenaed phone records of Republican lawmakers, and sought court orders keeping those subpoenas secret, he showed that his prosecutorial ambitions extended far beyond Mr. Trump.

“Is it a crime to be a Republican?” Mr. Cruz asked angrily. “Absolutely not,” replied Mr. Smith.

Senator Darline Graham, the sister of Senator Lindsey Graham, who died in July, also confronted Mr. Smith over a subpoena of her brother’s phone records. Like Mr. Cruz, she focused on how an application for nondisclosure order to the phone companies raised the risk that if the subpoena became public, a target could destroy evidence or intimidate witnesses.

“Do you really believe that Lindsey was going to destroy evidence that was not even in his possession?” she asked.

“No, I believe your brother was a patriotic public servant. He was not a target of our investigation, and in fact he likely would have been a witness in our case” against Mr. Trump, Mr. Smith replied.

He told both Mr. Cruz and Ms. Graham that his team sought the records to investigate the conduct of Mr. Trump, not the lawmakers. The concern was not whether the lawmakers would destroy evidence or intimidate witnesses, but whether Mr. Trump or his associates would seek to do so.

Democrats countered Republican accusations by pointing to the evidence Mr. Smith gathered against Mr. Trump, leading to indictments for his efforts to undo the results of the 2020 election, and for his handling of classified documents at his Mar-a-Lago home in Florida.

Senator Adam Schiff, Democrat of California, said the G.O.P. anger directed at Mr. Smith and the F.B.I. was a smoke screen for facts they would rather not face — that the former president had engaged in wrongdoing, and that the witnesses against him in both cases were largely Republicans.

Senator Cory Booker, a New Jersey Democrat, called the hearing “a farce.” The Republicans attacking Mr. Smith, he added, “choose Trump over truth, corruption and crimes over the Constitution, and I’ve had enough of it.”

For his part, Mr. Smith maintained a measured, even meek, tone as lawmakers on the panel alternated between describing him as a pinnacle of his profession and a poster boy for improper conduct.

“If asked whether to prosecute a former president today, based on the same facts, I would do so regardless of whether that president was a Republican or a Democrat,” he said, adding: “I will not be silenced by continued threats of prosecution from the president or others.”

In early 2022, the Justice Department opened two investigations involving Mr. Trump. One was into his campaign’s plan to create false slates of electors as a pretext to block Mr. Biden’s certification, and the other was into Mr. Trump’s hoarding of classified documents while out of office, and his obstruction of efforts to retrieve them.

In November 2022, after Mr. Trump announced he would run for president again, Mr. Smith, a former prosecutor of federal corruption and international war crimes, was tapped to take over the inquiries as a special counsel. The next year, Mr. Smith brought two indictments against Mr. Trump.

Mr. Smith insisted that he brought charges because Mr. Trump “engaged in criminal activity,” and not because of any political agenda to stop Mr. Trump’s resurgence, as the president’s Republican allies have asserted. Mr. Trump triumphed over the two federal cases by winning re-election in 2024, leading to Mr. Smith’s resignation.

Since leaving government, Mr. Smith has said that the Justice Department has been “corrupted” by Trump loyalists who have wrecked its credibility and sought to undermine the rule of law.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, in testimony to Congress in July, suggested the department would investigate Mr. Smith to determine if he had lied to Congress.

Much of Tuesday’s hearing covered familiar ground — including whether investigators’ effort to collect lawmakers’ call records violated the Constitution’s “speech or debate” clause, as Republican lawmakers insisted.

That issue is contested. Everyone agrees members of Congress cannot be prosecuted or forced to testify about their legislative acts. But appeals courts have disagreed about whether it also creates a confidentiality shield, and no court has interpreted it as barring subpoenas to phone companies for call logs.

The Justice Department’s public integrity section signed off on the subpoenas, Mr. Smith said. But while he defended the investigation’s work as carefully following the law, Justice Department rules, and best practices for prosecutors, he did offer one regret for how he had done the job.

Mr. Smith noted that he had come from a generation of prosecutors who spoke almost exclusively in courtrooms, and not in public, even to defend the integrity of the work or the prosecution team.

Following that tradition proved costly in the cases against Mr. Trump, he said.

“I do agree that prosecutors in the future need to learn to be able to communicate to the outside world,” Mr. Smith said.

Glenn Thrush contributed reporting.

ARTICLE

Top Democrats, Long Hesitant to Spend Money in Texas, Start to Back Talarico
The main super PAC for Senate Democrats will begin to run digital ads in the state’s Senate race, in a sign of the party’s growing confidence.
By Theodore Schleifer and Lauren McGaughy
Published 2026-09-29 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/us/politics/james-talarico-ken-paxton-texas-senate-race-money.html

Top national Democrats are preparing to make an initial investment in the Texas Senate race, a strategic shift that speaks to the party’s growing confidence in a state that has dashed its hopes for decades.

The main super PAC for Senate Democrats, Senate Majority PAC, said on Tuesday that it would begin an advertising effort meant to help James Talarico, the Democratic nominee, by targeting his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton.

The super PAC, which is aligned with Senator Chuck Schumer, the minority leader, had so far resisted spending money in Texas, viewing the party’s path to a majority as running through smaller states where advertising is cheaper.

The group declined to provide a figure or a range for its planned spending in Texas. For now, it will run statewide ads only on YouTube and other digital and streaming platforms and forgo more expensive television ads that could drain the super PAC's resources. That suggests that national Democrats are not yet prepared to go all-in for Mr. Talarico.

Mr. Talarico has narrowly led in polls and his campaign has raised much more money than Mr. Paxton’s, but national Republican groups have begun spending enormous amounts to prop up their nominee, giving him an overall financial advantage. G.O.P. groups have reserved about $167 million in ads for the final two months of the race.

Because the cost of political advertising in Texas is so high, with its large size and many media markets, both parties have been reluctant to invest in the state, worrying that doing so could divert resources from other top Senate races. When Senate Majority PAC announced its initial advertising plans this year, it focused on eight states and left out Texas.

Unless Democrats sharply ramp up their spending, Republicans are likely to hold an advantage on television in the final weeks of the race. As of Monday, Mr. Talarico was set to be outspent by nearly five to one on all advertising in the final two months before Election Day, with only about $35 million booked on his behalf, according to AdImpact, a media tracking firm.

Lauren French, a spokeswoman for Senate Majority PAC, said that its ads would run through Election Day and “focus on Paxton as a corrupt, dangerous individual.”

The first ad, which will come from an allied super PAC that was created last week and is called Texas Forever, targets Mr. Paxton, the state attorney general, over his office’s handling of a prominent child abuse case.

Adam Hoffman, a lawyer in Waco, Texas, was accused of sexually abusing a local boy for years. After the victim declined to testify again when the trial resulted in a hung jury, lawyers in Mr. Paxton’s office cut a deal in which Mr. Hoffman served less than a month behind bars and did not need to register as a sex offender in Texas.

The arrangement set off a local outcry and allegations that Mr. Paxton had given Mr. Hoffman a sweetheart deal. Mr. Paxton has denied any wrongdoing and defended his office’s work on the case, saying it was the best deal possible while honoring the victim’s wishes. Gerry Morris, a lawyer who represented Mr. Hoffman, told The New York Times in June that while he disliked Mr. Paxton, it was “an absolute 100 percent lie” that the attorney general had done anything to sway the case’s outcome.

Some Democrats have privately pined for Senate Majority PAC to get involved in Texas. Mr. Talarico’s fund-raising emails have pointed to the challenge he faces, using words like “beyond ridiculous” to describe the tens of millions of dollars flooding into the state for his opponent.

Garry Jones, who leads a different pro-Talarico super PAC, Lone Star Rising, argued that money alone would not swing the race for Mr. Paxton.

“We’re a few weeks into the deluge, and what we’re seeing is that there isn’t enough money in the world to make Texans forget they hate Ken Paxton,” Mr. Jones said.

Lone Star Rising said it planned to spend at least another $10 million for Mr. Talarico.

Mr. Paxton, who won a hard-fought Republican primary on the back of his support from President Trump and the party’s right-wing base, has long been trailed by scandal. He was indicted in 2015 on felony fraud charges, but cut a deal in 2024 to avoid trial without admitting guilt. He was impeached in 2023 over allegations of corruption but was acquitted in a State Senate trial. His wife, a state senator, has filed for divorce, citing adultery.

Anthony Holm, a longtime Republican consultant who once worked for Mr. Paxton, said that for the better part of a year, Mr. Talarico had been the one with an advantage in fund-raising, and therefore in messaging.

But now that Mr. Paxton has the financial edge, Mr. Holm said, he can use the influx of cash to target the meaningful chunk of voters who are still undecided.

“As long as Paxton has the money,” Mr. Holm said, “he’ll be fine.”

ARTICLE

In Nine Key Senate Races, Five Republicans Won’t Commit to Campaigning With Trump
Three campaigns left their positions unclear, and two said they would not join the president on the trail.
By Tim Balk
Published 2026-09-29 17:40 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/us/politics/republicans-senate-midterms-trump-campaign.html

President Trump has said he plans to campaign for dozens of Republicans running in competitive races in the lead-up to the midterm election on Nov. 3.

Mr. Trump has several stops scheduled in the coming days, including visits to heavily Republican states such as Oklahoma, Alabama and Tennessee. But the president is deeply unpopular, and some Republicans in battleground states have started to separate themselves from his administration, his costly war with Iran and his polarizing immigration policies.

For Republicans running in the most competitive Senate races, Mr. Trump can pose a dilemma. His super PAC is flush with cash that could help them, and he remains popular with the Republican base. But he could be toxic with swing voters.

Among the nine Republicans whose races are expected to be crucial in determining Senate control, four would like Mr. Trump to join them on the trail ahead of the election, or are open to the possibility, according to their campaigns. Three campaigns left their positions unclear, and two said they would not join the president on the trail.

Here’s where the candidates stand on whether they would campaign with Mr. Trump in their home states. (These nine candidates are running in races that the nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates as the most competitive: tossups and races leaning toward Democrats or Republicans.)

Yes

Senator Dan Sullivan of Alaska

Mr. Sullivan has “every intention” of campaigning with Mr. Trump in Alaska at some point in October, said a campaign spokesman, Nate Adams. Mr. Trump said at a news conference this month that he would visit conservative-leaning Alaska in the last 30 days of the campaign.

Plans for a visit have not been firmed up, Mr. Adams said.

Mr. Sullivan is trying to fend off former Representative Mary Peltola, an independent-minded Democrat who finished first in the all-party primary in August.

Michael Whatley of North Carolina

Perhaps more than any Republican running in a competitive Senate race, Mr. Whatley has stood by Mr. Trump. Two weeks ago, the two campaigned together in Gastonia, N.C., near Charlotte, where Mr. Whatley declared, “I am still with that guy,” referring to the president.

A spokesman for Mr. Whatley, DJ Griffin, said the candidate would welcome further opportunities to campaign with the president.

Mr. Whatley faces former Gov. Roy Cooper, a popular Democrat, in a swing state that Mr. Trump carried narrowly in 2024. Mr. Cooper leads in the polls.

Senator Jon Husted of Ohio

Mr. Husted is scheduled to be joined by Mr. Trump at a rally on Saturday in Vandalia, which is north of Dayton. “We look forward to hosting President Trump in Ohio this weekend,” Amy Natoce, a campaign spokeswoman, said in a statement.

Mr. Husted is trying to fend off Sherrod Brown, a Democratic former senator and longtime fixture of Ohio politics.

Ken Paxton of Texas

Mr. Paxton, the scandal-plagued Texas attorney general, has aligned himself closely with Mr. Trump, campaigning with the president more than once this year and speaking at Mr. Trump’s midterm convention this month.

A spokesman for Mr. Paxton, Nick Maddux, said in a text message that Mr. Paxton would “of course” be open to campaigning with Mr. Trump again in the lead-up to the election.

Mr. Trump is visiting Denton, Texas, on Thursday for an event focused on his economic agenda, said Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman. Mr. Paxton will be in West Texas for previously scheduled events, including a rally in Amarillo, Mr. Maddux said.

Mr. Paxton is in a tight race with James Talarico, a Democratic state lawmaker and seminarian.

No

Senator Susan Collins of Maine

Ms. Collins, a centrist who has had a turbulent relationship with Mr. Trump, has long ruled out campaigning with him in her Democratic-leaning state.

“That’s just not going to happen” Ms. Collins said in an interview in June, adding, “I’m happy running my own campaign.”

Ms. Collins is running against Troy Jackson, a Democratic former state lawmaker who was once was president of the Maine Senate.

John E. Sununu of New Hampshire

Mr. Sununu’s campaign has signaled he has no interest in being joined by Mr. Trump on the trail in Democratic-leaning New Hampshire.

“John’s focus the entire campaign has been on New Hampshire,” Mike Schrimpf, a campaign spokesman, said in a statement, adding that Mr. Sununu “doesn’t plan to campaign with anyone from outside New Hampshire.”

Mr. Sununu is running against Representative Chris Pappas, a four-term Democrat.

Unclear or no comment

Mike Rogers of Michigan

Mr. Rogers, who joined two rallies with the president during the summer, is walking a general-election tightrope in Michigan, a swing state that went narrowly for Mr. Trump in 2024.

A spokeswoman for Mr. Rogers, Abby Ronson, said the campaign had no comment on whether Mr. Rogers would be open to campaigning with Mr. Trump before the general election.

Mr. Rogers faces Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive Democrat running as a populist outsider.

Representative Ashley Hinson of Iowa

Ms. Hinson received Mr. Trump’s endorsement for Senate last September, early in the election cycle, and defended him earlier in 2025 at testy town halls where she was heckled. She also appeared with Mr. Trump in the Oval Office on Monday, where she expressed appreciation for his agenda.

At the same time, Ms. Hinson, whose race is considered a tossup, has sought distance from Mr. Trump and called for an “immediate” end to the Iran war.

At the White House, Mr. Trump told Ms. Hinson that he planned to campaign with her at a “great rally” in Iowa. Ms. Hinson, nodding, replied, “We’ll save you a good Iowa pork chop, sir.”

Still, Ms. Hinson’s representatives did not respond to numerous requests for comment on whether she would be open to campaigning with Mr. Trump. When Vice President JD Vance visited the state for a campaign rally this month, Ms. Hinson did not join him.

She is running against Josh Turek, a Democratic state lawmaker.

Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas

Mr. Marshall, a first-term senator, has generally been a reliable defender of Mr. Trump, braving boos to defend the president’s tariffs during a candidate’s debate this month. He also appeared with Mr. Vance at an event in the Kansas City area this month.

But Mr. Marshall’s campaign did not respond to requests for comment on whether he would be open to campaigning with Mr. Trump before the election.

Mr. Marshall is trying to fend off the Rev. Adam Hamilton, a Democrat, in a traditionally conservative state. Kansas’s agriculture-heavy economy has been hit hard by the war with Iran and the administration’s tariff policies.
