SUMMARY

The Supreme Court on Tuesday gave President Trump a temporary victory on a central piece of his mass deportation agenda, agreeing the administration can, for now, resume rapidly deporting immigrants to countries other than their own. The court, she said in a statement, “has allowed the administration to resume sending people to third countries where they face persecution or torture.” Since then, the Trump administration has continued to deport immigrants under the program, including to authoritarian countries with histories of human rights abuses.

ARTICLE

Supreme Court Allows Rapid Third-Country Deportations, for Now
The court also announced it would hear arguments in December on the legality of the Trump administration policy to swiftly deport immigrants to countries not their own.
By Abbie VanSickle
Published 2026-09-29 19:15 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/us/politics/supreme-court-deportations-third-country.html

The Supreme Court on Tuesday gave President Trump a temporary victory on a central piece of his mass deportation agenda, agreeing the administration can, for now, resume rapidly deporting immigrants to countries other than their own.

Although the justices cleared the way for the policy to continue, they also announced that the court would fast-track the case and hear oral arguments about it in December, setting up a final ruling on the issue next year and a new test for presidential power at the court.

The one-page emergency ruling was unsigned and gave no vote count, as is typical in such cases.

On the line in December will be Mr. Trump’s policy of sending people to countries where they have no ties, including nations that have faced allegations of human rights abuses. Among the countries migrants have been sent to are Liberia, Equatorial Guinea, Costa Rica, Honduras and the Central African Republic.

The court’s three liberal justices noted that they would have denied the government’s request to resume the deportations.

The justices asked the lawyers for the administration and the immigrants who challenged the policy to focus their briefing for the December argument on whether the lower court judge who had paused the swift deportations had the authority to do so, and whether the policy violated the Constitution and international protections against torture.

James Percival, the top lawyer at the Department of Homeland Security, celebrated the court’s ruling. In a statement, he called it a “victory.”

“A bad day for criminal illegals and open borders activists alike,” he said. “It’s not too late to get $3,000 and a flight home.” He ended his statement with a link to department instructions for immigrants on how to self-deport.

Trina A. Realmuto, a lawyer for the National Immigration Litigation Alliance and part of the team representing the immigrants, called the emergency decision “a devastating result.” The court, she said in a statement, “has allowed the administration to resume sending people to third countries where they face persecution or torture.”

But she pointed out that the court had agreed to hear full argument in December, saying that Tuesday’s decision “does not decide that the policy is lawful.”

The deportations had been blocked recently after a federal court ruled the administration could not deport migrants to third countries unless they were given an opportunity to contest their removals, including to voice concerns that they might be persecuted or tortured abroad.

The justices’ ruling means that the administration can, for now, continue its program and conduct rapid deportations including to countries like Equatorial Guinea, where U.S. deportees were hooded, bound and beaten by the police, according to reporting by The New York Times.

The justices had weighed in previously on the administration’s efforts to send immigrants to third countries.

In May 2025, the Trump administration asked the justices to step in and clear the way for third-country deportations after a federal judge in Massachusetts temporarily blocked the administration from sending people to countries not their own — in that case South Sudan — without the chance to object.

In a one-paragraph ruling, the court’s conservatives allowed the administration to continue the deportations over the noted dissents of the three liberals.

Since then, the Trump administration has continued to deport immigrants under the program, including to authoritarian countries with histories of human rights abuses. So far, the administration has sent more than 25,000 people to third countries as part of its mass deportation efforts, according to a social media post by Mr. Percival.

Some immigration and human rights experts have asserted that the third-country deportations may be part of a broader strategy by the Trump administration to encourage undocumented immigrants to leave on their own, rather than face the fear of being sent to a country where they have no ties.

In his brief, Solicitor General D. John Sauer characterized the third-country deportation program as “an essential tool to remove certain aliens, including some of the worst criminal aliens.”

Mr. Sauer wrote that the appeals court ruling had “created substantial logistical problems with ongoing removal operations,” including canceled deportation flights and disrupted delicate diplomatic negotiations with other countries.

Lawyers for a group of immigrants challenging their removals said in a brief that the Trump administration had ignored “the significant harm resulting from deporting thousands of longtime U.S. residents, many with no criminal history, to third countries without regard to the persecution or torture they face there.”

They argued that the Trump administration could avoid any delays in its deportation program simply by “providing the notice and opportunity to be heard that the law requires.”

SUMMARY

President Trump, staring down a rough midterm season for Republicans, unveiled plans for an Iowa steel mill project on Monday that he said would plug billions into the economy and create construction jobs in a state hit hard by his policies. In the Oval Office on Monday, Mr. Trump, several cabinet members and Iowa Republicans said the project would remind voters that Mr. Trump’s policies have created jobs.

ARTICLE

How a Planned Steel Mill in Iowa Reveals Trump’s Midterm Strategy
As President Trump travels the country, he is expected to focus on his economic accomplishments at a time when Americans have expressed deep frustration with his policies.
By Katie Rogers and Farah Stockman
Published 2026-09-29 00:19 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/28/us/politics/trump-steel-plant-iowa-midterms.html

President Trump, staring down a rough midterm season for Republicans, unveiled plans for an Iowa steel mill project on Monday that he said would plug billions into the economy and create construction jobs in a state hit hard by his policies.

Voters in Midwestern states were crucial to delivering a second election win to Mr. Trump, but now, those voters are among the hardest hit by tariff-driven manufacturing costs and a rise in fuel prices driven by the war in Iran. When a reporter in the Oval Office asked him on Monday why several Republican candidates in Iowa were working so hard to protect their seats, Mr. Trump seemed mystified.

“I don’t know,” said Mr. Trump, who is traveling to several states this week ahead of the midterm elections. “I love Iowa. I’ve always been very strong with Iowa.”

The project in Iowa is one of several job-creation announcements Mr. Trump is expected to make as he traverses the country. He will travel to several reliably conservative states this week, including Oklahoma and Alabama. He is also scheduled to visit Ohio this weekend in support of Senator Jon Husted, an embattled incumbent facing several challenges, including a lack of name recognition among some of the state’s most devoted conservatives.

Mr. Trump said on Monday that he would also visit Iowa, where he hopes the planned steel mill will boost prospects for Republicans in tight races — and perhaps his own fortunes as a kingmaker who has asked supporters to pretend he is on the ballot in November. Americans have signaled that they are doing just that, but in a way that could backfire on him. The war in Iran and the cost of living have both eroded his support.

So Mr. Trump has leaned into the promise of the mill, which is part of an $18 billion investment from Mesabi Metallics. Supporters of the project say it will be one of the largest steel mills in the world when it is completed.

In the Oval Office on Monday, Mr. Trump, several cabinet members and Iowa Republicans said the project would remind voters that Mr. Trump’s policies have created jobs. Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks, who is facing a tough re-election race and who last week voted to curb Mr. Trump’s war powers, appeared to be behind Mr. Trump, telling reporters that the steel mill could create some 6,000 construction jobs and 1,750 permanent jobs, with salaries that could exceed $100,000 a year.

“We’re going to mine it in America. We’re going to mill it in America, and we’re going to make it in America,” Ms. Miller-Meeks said.

Mesabi Metallic is owned by Essar Group, a Mumbai-based conglomerate controlled by one of India’s wealthiest families. The Iowa mill project follows another initiative led by Mesabi: a $2.5 billion iron-ore mine and pellet plant in Nashwauk, Minn.

That project, described as the first new operation of its kind in the state in about 50 years, has been supported by EXIM Bank, a U.S. federal import-export bank that announced it would extend loans to the company worth up to $10 billion. Some analysts consider the EXIM loan to be risky, because Mesabi has faced financial problems and significant delays over the years.

Alec Varsamis, a spokesman for EXIM, said that Mesabi had so far been granted a $770 million loan for the iron-ore mine in Minnesota.

“We are operating at no cost to the taxpayer, and we are on track to repay our congressional appropriations to the U.S. Treasury,” Mr. Varsamis said.

In the Oval Office on Monday, Mr. Trump said that the project would go forward even if control of Congress changed hands, or if a “less friendly” president took over. Rewant Ruia, chairman of Mesabi’s executive board, and Ravi Ruia, co-founder and vice-chairman of the Essar Group, were also in the Oval Office for the announcement.

The company filed for bankruptcy protection in 2016, and has been entangled in a lawsuit with Cleveland-Cliffs, another steel manufacturer.

Mesabi executives have leaned on a Trump-world insider as the company has sought to expand its footprint in the United States. The company hired Jason Miller, a longtime Trump adviser, as its lobbyist, paying him at least $240,000 through his company SHW Partners, according to lobbying disclosure records. The government of India also hired Mr. Miller’s company, paying $150,000 per month for “strategic counsel, tactical planning and government relations assistance on policy matters before the U.S. government,” according to federal filings under the Foreign Agents Registration Act.

Mr. Miller said in text messages that he had stopped his work as a lobbyist for Mesabi, adding that he deregistered with the company at the end of July, and deregistered as a lobbyist for India in June. He has since joined the administration as an unpaid special government employee. He was not present in the Oval Office and said he had “recused” himself from Monday’s announcement.

Robert Weissman, co-president of Public Citizen, a nonprofit consumer advocacy organization that tracked Mr. Miller’s lobbying on behalf of Mesabi and the Indian government, said that the extension of potentially billions in taxpayer-backed loans from EXIM Bank deserved more scrutiny because of Mr. Miller’s role.

“In any other administration, this would be treated as a monumental scandal,” Mr. Weissman said. “But in this one, it’s just another day.” Rewant Ruia, chairman of Mesabi Metallics, spoke in the Oval Office on Monday, and said the new steel plant in Iowa “will use the latest technology and will compete head-to-head with any steel plant in the world on size, quality and on cost.”

Gov. Kim Reynolds of Iowa, a Republican who attended the Oval Office event, said in a statement that the deal would be transformative for her state.

“Our commitment in Iowa to fiscal responsibility, tax competitiveness, and long-term economic stability has created one of the nation’s strongest environments for business investment,” she said. “Now, this opportunity will fundamentally change the economic trajectory of our state and the entire region for decades to come.”

The steel mill project is part of a broader election-season attempt by Mr. Trump to push back against widespread voter frustration with his policies, including tariffs that have been punishing for American manufacturers, particularly in the Midwest.

Mr. Trump and his advisers believe that any polling predicting a blowout for Democrats is overrated, and to some degree, they have history on their side. On Monday, Mr. Trump again called recent polling “fake,” and complained that the news media had not appropriately trumpeted employment numbers, 401(k) account gains and a host of other accomplishments.

“Nobody talks about all of the incredible things,” Mr. Trump said.

But this is not 2016, or 2024. In 2026, Americans are deeply unhappy with the cost of living and frustrated with the war in Iran, which has driven up prices further. In response, Mr. Trump has taken to calling the concept of affordability a Democratic hoax, while promising that prices will come down as soon as the war ends.

“We’re going to win that war very soon. That’ll be over, and the gases, gas prices, will come tumbling down,” Mr. Trump said. “So nobody else could have done that. Nobody else.”

Mr. Trump’s self-congratulatory messaging on the war has done little to help G.O.P. candidates in tough races across the country. In the past week, Republicans running for Senate seats in Iowa and Michigan have called on Mr. Trump to end the conflict. A slate of other candidates, including two running for governor in Wisconsin and Michigan, and Mr. Husted in Ohio, also have said that the war needs to end, and soon.

SUMMARY

On the morning of Aug. 4, two Russian guided bombs, each weighing more than 1,000 pounds, struck the residential block where I grew up in Kramatorsk, eastern Ukraine. Russian forces have been advancing on Kramatorsk slowly but steadily, and I long knew that my childhood home would eventually find itself in the fight. Two months after the war broke out, I returned to Kramatorsk to report on Russian advances in the eastern Donetsk region.

ARTICLE

Bomb by Bomb, the Slow Death of My Hometown in Ukraine
It was possible, for a time, to think that Kramatorsk, where I was born and raised, would survive the war mostly unscathed. Not any more.
By Olha Konovalova
Published 2026-09-29 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/world/europe/ukraine-kramatorsk.html

On the morning of Aug. 4, two Russian guided bombs, each weighing more than 1,000 pounds, struck the residential block where I grew up in Kramatorsk, eastern Ukraine.

I learned of the attack from social media, scrolling through videos until I recognized a neighboring building in flames. Then came the frantic search for any piece of information on whether my home had also been destroyed.

Finally, a man who still lives in my building sent me a video, filmed from inside my flat. The fire had spared it, but not the blast. Shards of glass covered the floor. In the kitchen, the window frame had been torn from the wall. In the living room, the windowsill was gone entirely. Even the bathroom tiles had cracked.

Russian forces have been advancing on Kramatorsk slowly but steadily, and I long knew that my childhood home would eventually find itself in the fight. Still, nothing prepares you for seeing the place you were born torn apart by bombs.

This is an experience shared by millions of people across Ukraine over four and a half years of war — those now watching their homes being damaged by the approaching fight, and those who’ve already lost them.

As a journalist, I have covered such stories repeatedly, watching city after city being destroyed: Sievierodonetsk, Bakhmut, Avdiivka, Pokrovsk, Kostiantynivka. Now, it’s my hometown’s turn.

Kramatorsk is a small city filled with parks and childhood memories. I remember splashing in a fountain in the city center on hot summer days and sledding down the hill near my school in winter. On weekends, my mother and I would walk to the local farmers’ market to buy fresh milk and homemade cheese that we would devour with breakfast. A Georgian restaurant near our home became a favorite spot for family evenings over a khachapuri and wine, a birthday celebration or just a cup of coffee.

Everything changed on Feb. 24, 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale invasion. Explosions woke my parents in Kramatorsk and they called me in a panic to ask what they should do, where they should go and what they should take with them.

I was in Mariupol that day, more than 100 miles to the south, working as a producer with a CNN team. Trying to organize my parents’ evacuation over the phone, I told them to pack the essentials — documents, a change of clothes and our cat — and get out of town.

They left the apartment tidy, expecting to come back soon. They’re still in Norway today, under refugee status.

Two months after the war broke out, I returned to Kramatorsk to report on Russian advances in the eastern Donetsk region. Russian troops were closing in, capturing village after village. Shelling had become an almost daily occurrence. It seemed like my last chance to see home.

When I opened the door, the first thing I noticed was the smell. Our apartment used to smell of my mother’s cooking. Now it smelled empty. Everything was covered in dust. Knowing I might not be able to return, I wanted to take as much as I could: family photo albums, my father’s chessboard, my grandmother’s hand-embroidered bedsheet. But it turned out a life doesn’t fit into a suitcase, and I had to leave much behind.

Outside my flat, though, Kramatorsk carried on a life that was both strange and strangely ordinary. There were constant reminders of the war, of course, like gasoline shortages and the absence of Coca-Cola from supermarket shelves; we managed to get both on the black market. But food delivery services still ran, and hotels were full of journalists.

Ukrainian forces pushed the Russian troops back and the city grew safer. Residents began to return. Kramatorsk became a rear base for journalists and humanitarian group staffers working at the front. Businesses reopened, including our favorite Georgian restaurant. As I began visiting Kramatorsk more often, I had lunch there.

Sitting in the same place my family used to gather, it was easy to believe that Kramatorsk had escaped the fighting. The same town, the same restaurant, the same me.

That, it turned out, was an illusion.

I had seen it play out before, in the town of Pokrovsk, about 40 miles southwest of Kramatorsk. Pokrovsk, too, had returned to something resembling normal life after the initial Russian invasion. For the news media teams I worked with, Pokrovsk was a safe place, somewhere to sleep and eat a good meal at the end of a day at the front.

But as the fighting closed in, guided bombs started to hit Pokrovsk more often. Starting in the fall of 2024, the streets grew emptier as people evacuated and shuttered their homes and businesses. Within months, Pokrovsk had emptied out, inhabited only by the soldiers preparing for the coming street fighting.

On my trips back to Kramatorsk, I began to recognize the same pattern in the past few months. As Russian forces pushed closer, their drones began reaching the city, flying through my neighborhood on the eastern edge of the city.

Bombs hit areas I have known my whole life. This spring, an airstrike hit the street I used to walk down to go to art school as a child, where I would stop at a little shop to buy a chocolate bar and cherry juice before class. The bomb landed a few meters away from the shop.

Finally, on Aug. 4, bombs landed near home. One struck the building next to mine; the other reduced the Georgian restaurant where I had spent so many happy family moments to rubble. All around, trees were uprooted and burned-out cars lay overturned in the street. In my own building, alongside blown-out windows, damaged balcony frames hung from the upper floors. Then, in late September, another attack sparked a large blaze that ravaged several dozen flats next to mine.

My home has survived, but will I have anywhere to return to, when the war is over? Deep down, I know how this story will end.

Constant Méheut contributed reporting.

SUMMARY

In China’s latest push to reduce its dependence on American artificial intelligence technology, DeepSeek, one of the country’s leading A.I. companies, announced Wednesday that it had developed software tools for chips made by Huawei Technologies. The partnership targets one of the biggest obstacles to China’s ambitions to build a homegrown A.I. industry — software that can extract the best performance from its chips. And Huawei has become a corporate linchpin of Beijing’s drive to develop a domestic alternative to the American chips, computing systems and software that underpin much of the global A.I. industry.

ARTICLE

Leading Chinese Tech Firms Target Nvidia’s A.I. Dominance
In China’s push for self-reliance in artificial intelligence, DeepSeek and Huawei have teamed up to develop software tools for advanced chips.
By Steve Lohr
Published 2026-09-30 10:41 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/business/china-ai-deepseek-huawei.html

In China’s latest push to reduce its dependence on American artificial intelligence technology, DeepSeek, one of the country’s leading A.I. companies, announced Wednesday that it had developed software tools for chips made by Huawei Technologies.

The partnership targets one of the biggest obstacles to China’s ambitions to build a homegrown A.I. industry — software that can extract the best performance from its chips.

Advanced semiconductors alone are not enough to power A.I. systems. Computer hardware and chip-level software must work together for artificial intelligence to do anything useful, from training frontier models to developing applications that companies and consumers use daily.

That software can also be a powerful competitive weapon and moat against rivals trying to make inroads.

Though China is catching up, Silicon Valley companies remain leaders in A.I. technology, with Nvidia, whose chips power the most advanced A.I. systems, at the forefront. Nvidia’s semiconductor designs are the most advanced in the world. But its dominance rests on more than chips. The company also benefits from having an estimated four million software developers worldwide who use CUDA, a software platform for Nvidia chips.

In an announcement Wednesday on its official WeChat site, DeepSeek presented its work with Huawei as a potential alternative to CUDA. To build a successful A.I. ecosystem, specialized software must be a “universal, easy-to-program language that can also reach the upper limit of hardware performance,” DeepSeek said.

DeepSeek said its programming language, TileLang, was designed to meet that challenge, offering “a simpler programming model” than Nvidia’s CUDA. Programming languages are how humans — and more recently A.I. systems — instruct computers to do things.

The company said the version of TileLang it designed for Huawei’s A.I. chips was open source, meaning freely available for others to use and modify. DeepSeek said it tested the programming language on older Nvidia chips and now uses TileLang as the “core tool” for working on artificial general intelligence, systems that will match or exceed human intelligence in all tasks.

The partnership brings together two companies playing central but different roles in China’s efforts to narrow the A.I. technology gap with the United States.

DeepSeek has emerged as one of China’s most prominent developers of A.I. models. And Huawei has become a corporate linchpin of Beijing’s drive to develop a domestic alternative to the American chips, computing systems and software that underpin much of the global A.I. industry.

China’s advances in A.I. software models, led by companies including Z.ai and Moonshot AI, have so far outpaced progress by its domestic chip makers. Huawei is trying to close that gap.

At a company event in Shanghai this month, Huawei announced plans for larger, more powerful A.I. computing systems and new generations of its flagship Ascend chips in 2028 and 2029.

Huawei executives also said the company could not meet China’s demand for A.I. chips and related equipment and planned to restrict overseas sales as it prioritized its domestic market.

The company made clear that American export controls have added urgency to China’s drive for technological self-sufficiency. Those restrictions have limited Chinese companies’ access to Nvidia’s most advanced chips as well as sophisticated equipment needed to manufacture cutting-edge semiconductors.

“We cannot accept a destiny where we cannot control our fate,” Eric Xu, Huawei’s current chairman, said at the conference. Or have that fate “being determined by others in terms of willingness to sell chips to China or not.”

Huawei uses an unusual management system in which senior executives rotate through the chairman’s position for six-month stints.

Xinyun Wu and Amy Chang Chien contributed research from Taipei.

ARTICLE

Bracing for More Inflation Volatility
Consumers, business owners and investors are growing increasingly concerned about rising inflation, and its potential repercussions.
By Andrew Ross Sorkin, Bernhard Warner, Sarah Kessler, Michael J. de la Merced, Niko Gallogly, Brian O’Keefe, Sri Muppidi and Ian Mount
Published 2026-09-30 11:45 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/business/dealbook/inflation-pce-interest-rates.html

Andrew here, back from D.C. The White House meeting between tech leaders and President Trump drew some skepticism over its voluntary self-policing pact — and fairly so. Still, getting top companies aligned on artificial intelligence safety is a step in the right direction. Conspicuously absent from the table was Apple, prompting questions about its position in the A.I. race despite Tim Cook’s close ties with Trump. Finally, take a look at the news below on Ken Griffin’s record $3 billion gift to help build a Carnegie Mellon campus in Miami. Bringing a premier research institution to Miami could give the city a major boost.

Price pinched

The fast-growing U.S. economy has been a global outlier. But rising fuel prices and borrowing costs have consumers and business owners feeling increasingly gloomy.

So far, the bull market rally is holding up. Yet investors are bracing for new economic data — beginning with the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, set to be released at 8:30 a.m. Eastern — that could heap more pressure on the Fed to raise interest rates.

The prospect of higher rates is already jolting the I.P.O. market.

The latest:

- The yield on the 10-year Treasury note was trading around 5.23 percent on Wednesday. The yield on the 30-year Treasury bond on Tuesday hit its highest level since June 2002.
- S&P 500 futures are under pressure. The benchmark index is on pace for a monthly loss.
- Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, rose above $103 on Wednesday. The average price of diesel in the U.S. is at $6.41. A glimmer of hope: Oil exports from the Middle East have begun to rebound.

Watch Wednesday’s P.C.E., the Fed’s preferred inflation measure. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones forecast that core inflation last month rose by 3.3 percent on an annualized basis — in line with the July number.

- An update to how P.C.E. is calculated is expected to lower the final numbers slightly. “But that shouldn’t alter the underlying trend” that inflation is running well above the Fed’s 2 percent target, Mike Reid, head of U.S. economics at RBC Capital Markets, wrote to investors this week.

Traders on Wednesday saw a 57 percent chance of the Fed leaving rates unchanged at its October meeting. But a hot P.C.E. number on Wednesday could push the odds for a rate increase higher.

High inflation is weighing on sentiment. U.S. consumer confidence fell to its lowest level since 2014, the Conference Board reported on Tuesday. Respondents said they saw interest rates and inflation climbing over the next year.

Business owners are feeling the pinch, too. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce and Justworks, a payroll processing firm, on Wednesday published their latest small-business survey. Only 27 percent of respondents described the national economy as being in “good health,” a sharp drop from a year ago; 54 percent said inflation was their biggest challenge.

Could findings such as these put more pressure on the Trump administration to enact measures like, say, a ban on diesel exports to potentially bring down prices?

HERE’S WHAT’S HAPPENING

Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s tax on high-end second homes is dealt a blow. A.I.’s ‘morally binding’ moment

The artificial intelligence sector’s no-guardrails camp appeared to exit a White House luncheon on Tuesday with a clear victory.

President Trump said his dining companions, a who’s who of tech titans, backed “tremendous self-regulation” of a technology that has drawn increasing security worries from many corners of the globe, including in Silicon Valley. But the details were scarce, and big questions loom.

When asked by reporters who would scrutinize A.I. labs, Trump said that they would essentially be “policing each other” and that such an accord would be “morally binding.”

Who was there? (See seating chart below)

- Dario Amodei of Anthropic, who has been among the most vocal in urging formal regulation;
- Jensen Huang, the C.E.O. of Nvidia, who has called proposed new regulations “completely unnecessary”;
- Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and David Sacks, the venture capitalist and former Trump administration A.I. czar, who have also bristled at Amodei’s calls for more regulation;
- Elon Musk, the C.E.O. of the rocket and A.I. company SpaceX;
- Jeff Bezos, the founder of Amazon;
- Sundar Pichai of Google;
- And Greg Brockman, the OpenAI president who along with his wife, Anna Brockman, gave $25 million to MAGA Inc., a pro-Trump super PAC, in 2025.

What was agreed, according to Trump’s social media post? The A.I. executives committed to:

- “Implement robust internal controls” of their A.I. models during training and deployment, especially on issues of cybersecurity and biosecurity.
- Call on independent evaluators or auditors to ensure that companies are adhering to the safety protocols.

Worth noting, the commitments mirrored voluntary ones A.I. companies made during the Biden administration.

Left unaddressed: How will the companies contend with a thicket of state regulations in the works, as well as measures from other countries? And what about the labs’ exposure to potential legal liabilities?

OpenAI’s big bet on dots

Artificial intelligence agents are the hottest new product category in Silicon Valley — and increasingly a big business.

OpenAI’s take on them was the star of the A.I. lab’s developer conference on Tuesday in San Francisco, as the company stakes its claim in the agent industry, Sri Muppidi reports from the event.

Meet dots, agents powered by OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra model. Think digital assistants that are meant to proactively take actions — say book restaurant reservations or write code on behalf of users (within user-set limits).

OpenAI is wading into an increasingly crowded field populated by Meta (Muse), SpaceXAI (Grok Bot) and the popular start-up Instinct.

Driving the competition is the idea that A.I. tools are evolving from answering users’ queries to doing things for them — and the hope that they can drive, and disrupt, big business. Like Meta, OpenAI is pitching its agent software to professionals.

- Some of the roughly 2,500 conference attendees were impressed. “Anything that can be more proactive in my life — and less time me sitting at a keyboard and asking Codex to do something — is good for me,” Max Aitel, a university student, told DealBook.
- Others are reluctantly adapting. “Do I have a choice? Do I have a say?” Bhavani Kola, a math teacher at a community college, told DealBook.

Dots is part of OpenAI’s effort to remake its business as it prepares for an eventual I.P.O. and seeks to catch up with rivals like Anthropic. The company has claimed that GPT-6 Astra beat the competition at tasks like coding. That said, it shelved a newer Astra model because of safety concerns.

And it has talked up its strides in winning over business users, some of which are reflected in its latest financials. It is nearing $70 billion in annualized revenue, according to a person with knowledge of the company’s financials. The person, who spoke on the condition of anonymity and wasn’t authorized to discuss confidential data, confirmed a report by Axios. That’s up about 70 percent from July.

OpenAI’s other big moves: It’s in early discussions to raise $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation, the person added. (Bloomberg first reported the talks.)

The fund-raising effort would help OpenAI pay for its huge computing power costs, as it leans toward putting off its public offering until next year to shore up its finances and focus on safety.

- “I want OpenAI to be a public company someday,” Sam Altman, the company’s C.E.O., said at the conference. “But I don’t want to put additional pressure right now as we’re going through this significant change,” he said, referring to the company’s safety push.

Ken Griffin’s recording-setting college donation

Since moving the headquarters of his financial empire to Miami from Chicago in 2022, the hedge fund executive Ken Griffin has become a major booster for his new home base.

Now, he is making a giant donation to help bring a world-class university to Miami.

Griffin has pledged $3 billion to Carnegie Mellon University, the largest single donation in the history of American higher education, Alan Blinder reports for The Times:

Some $2 billion of Mr. Griffin’s contribution involves a new 35-acre outpost in Miami’s artsy Wynwood neighborhood, where students are expected to enroll beginning in 2028. The university, which already has locations in Qatar and Rwanda, is forecasting that the Miami campus will eventually accommodate more than 3,500 students. The campus is the latest top university outpost planned for South Florida, where wealthy residents have long argued that the region needs to expand its ranks of well-trained college graduates to attract and retain businesses. Vanderbilt University, for instance, is planning a campus in West Palm Beach, and Northwestern University runs a graduate business program in Coral Gables.

Griffin went to Harvard, and has donated more than $500 million to it. But he broke with the school after the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and the ensuing turmoil at Harvard’s campus.

Miami has become a philanthropic focus for Griffin. In February, he and Stephen Ross announced a campaign to promote the so-called Gold Coast region of Florida to companies.

SUMMARY

The Federal Reserve’s internal watchdog found no evidence of illegal behavior or administrative misconduct associated with the central bank’s nearly $2.5 billion project to overhaul its headquarters in Washington, D.C., even as it concluded that the renovations were poorly managed and lacked sufficient budget constraints. In a sweeping 120-page report, the Fed’s independent inspector general on Wednesday provided the most comprehensive overview to date of what caused extensive cost overruns on the project, which has been underway since 2022. The inspector general report found that the board did not obtain a project cost estimate until January 2026, three and half years after construction began and after more than $2 billion in costs had been earmarked.

ARTICLE

Fed’s Watchdog Finds No Misconduct or Illegal Activity in Costly Renovations
A new report by the Federal Reserve’s independent inspector general concluded that a nearly $2.5 billion construction project was poorly managed but made no referrals to the U.S. attorney general.
By Colby Smith
Published 2026-09-30 17:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/business/fed-renovations-trump-powell-report.html

The Federal Reserve’s internal watchdog found no evidence of illegal behavior or administrative misconduct associated with the central bank’s nearly $2.5 billion project to overhaul its headquarters in Washington, D.C., even as it concluded that the renovations were poorly managed and lacked sufficient budget constraints.

In a sweeping 120-page report, the Fed’s independent inspector general on Wednesday provided the most comprehensive overview to date of what caused extensive cost overruns on the project, which has been underway since 2022. It identified a range of missteps, including the Board of Governors’ failure to obtain a total cost estimate until the work was well underway or to establish a “guaranteed maximum price.”

The project last year became a major front in President Trump’s campaign to pressure the Fed into lowering interest rates. Mr. Trump repeatedly criticized Jerome H. Powell, who served as Fed chair until May, for the cost overruns and frequently raised the question of whether he had committed fraud as he floated the idea of firing him.

The Federal Reserve Act stipulates that the president can remove a sitting Fed official only “for cause,” which has long been interpreted to mean gross negligence or a dereliction of duty. Mr. Trump’s attacks on Mr. Powell culminated in a criminal investigation led by the Justice Department over whether Mr. Powell misled Congress about the project.

The inspector general’s report undermined the Justice Department’s investigation, which was abandoned in April after a number of legal setbacks. The watchdog found no wrongdoing by Mr. Powell or his colleagues, and it affirmed that no referrals were made to the U.S. attorney general.

The report’s findings are significant given that Jeanine Pirro, U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, had threatened to reopen the investigation at any point based on the inspector general’s findings. That possibility contributed to Mr. Powell’s decision to stay on as a governor after his term as chair expired, a position he can hold until January 2028. Kevin M. Warsh, whom Mr. Trump handpicked to replace Mr. Powell, took over in May.

In a social media post on Wednesday, Mr. Trump said that Mr. Powell should be “forced to resign” from the board in the wake of the report.

“He can’t manage a Building, and he certainly shouldn’t be allowed to manage his High Interest Rate Policy (only on “TRUMP!”),” the president wrote.

Mr. Trump added that he had asked Todd Blanche, the attorney general, to study the findings. If Mr. Powell does not resign, Mr. Trump said he “should be sued, at the highest level, by the United States Government, for either corruption or incompetence, both of which are completely unacceptable.”

In a statement on Wednesday, a spokesman for Ms. Pirro said she was in the process of reviewing the report.

The watchdog’s report, which Mr. Powell commissioned in July 2025, was led by Michael Horowitz, who served as inspector general of the Justice Department before moving over to the Fed earlier that year. The document made clear that the Board of Governors, which has seven politically appointed, Senate-confirmed officials, was not engaged in the “day-to-day management of the renovation project.” Instead, those duties were delegated to staff members on the board’s Facility Services team.

The inspector general report found that the board did not obtain a project cost estimate until January 2026, three and half years after construction began and after more than $2 billion in costs had been earmarked. A guaranteed maximum price was never set, meaning there was no cap on spending or built-in incentives to minimize costs.

One aspect of the construction project that received significant criticism was the inclusion of certain design features in a 2021 proposal such as new marble, a rooftop terrace and private dining rooms for top policymakers. When pressed at a congressional hearing in June 2025, Mr. Powell denied that many of those features were part of the latest proposal.

“There’s no V.I.P. dining room. There’s no new marble. We took down the old marble, we’re putting it back up. We’ll have to use new marble where some of the old marble broke. But there’s no special elevators. There’s just old elevators that have been there,” he said at the time.

The inspector general’s report corroborated Mr. Powell’s statement, concluding that its investigators “did not find that these design features materially contributed to the substantial construction cost increases.”

They acknowledged that some of the cost overruns were tied to inflation, which the Fed had flagged as a primary reason. But they also cited substantive design changes throughout the project, including the shift from an open-seating office plan to a closed-office arrangement, as well as the need for major mechanical, electrical and plumbing items that ran up the budget.

In a statement on Wednesday, Senator Tim Scott, Republican of South Carolina, described the Fed’s cost overruns as “egregious” and said that “inflation does not change the Fed’s responsibility to manage its resources prudently and be accountable to Congress.” He vowed that the Senate Banking Committee, which he leads, would “continue rigorous oversight to ensure the Fed is transparent and stays focused on its mission.”

His Democratic counterpart on the committee, Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, said in her own statement that the watchdog’s findings confirm that there is “no basis to restart the president’s witch hunt” against Mr. Powell.

In a letter to Mr. Horowitz on Tuesday, Mr. Warsh said he had retained the help of the General Services Administration, which is the agency responsible for managing federal work spaces, to work with the Fed “in the task of finally bringing the renovations to a speedy and successful completion.” He also said that the Fed would work with an independent auditor to examine the construction costs and, in keeping with the recommendations provided by the inspector general, that he would “promptly complete negotiations for a guaranteed maximum price for the project.” He also said staff would establish fixed metrics for the project’s budget and schedule.

Mr. Warsh’s arrival at the Fed has to some extent reset relations between the central bank and the White House, at least with top leadership. Mr. Trump has so far refrained from criticizing Mr. Warsh, even after the chairman voted with his colleagues to raise rates in September.

Mr. Trump directed his anger instead at other members of the Board of Governors, whom he accused of being “hostile” and “political.”

One of those governors, Lisa D. Cook, is involved in an extensive legal battle with Mr. Trump, who in August renewed his efforts to oust her after the Supreme Court ruled against the administration’s earlier attempts. Michael S. Barr, a governor nominated by President Joseph R. Biden Jr., also appears to be under heightened scrutiny for the implosion of Silicon Valley Bank, which happened under his watch in 2023 when he was serving as vice chair for supervision.

An external report on the bank’s failure released this month, which was commissioned by the current vice chair for supervision, Michelle W. Bowman, concluded that the central bank’s regulators “knew, or should have known,” about the mounting vulnerabilities at the lender. Instead, they failed to intervene in a timely fashion because of a “fear of taking action that may later be viewed as mistaken and being held accountable for such,” the report said.

trumps-new-tariffs-face-a-familiar-court-challenge.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 21  Words: 1099/1099
================================================================================

SUMMARY

Just hours after the Supreme Court struck down President Trump’s original roster of punishing global tariffs, he defiantly proclaimed that he would stop at nothing to somehow bring them back. This time, the cases concern the use of Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the administration to investigate unfair trade practices and impose tariffs if it finds that American businesses were harmed. The expansive nature of the tariffs prompted state officials and small businesses to file a series of lawsuits, arguing that the Trump administration failed to marshal the evidence required to issue the duties.

ARTICLE

Trump’s New Tariffs Face a Familiar Court Challenge
For the third time in less than two years, the Trump administration is set to return to court on Wednesday to defend its power to wage a punishing global trade war.
By Tony Romm
Published 2026-09-30 09:03 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/business/trumps-new-tariffs-face-a-familiar-court-challenge.html

Just hours after the Supreme Court struck down President Trump’s original roster of punishing global tariffs, he defiantly proclaimed that he would stop at nothing to somehow bring them back.

Seven months later, the work to revive those duties is well underway. But their return is about to land the administration back in the federal courthouse in New York where its legal troubles first began.

The latest phase of Mr. Trump’s ever-evolving trade war rests in the familiar hands of a panel of federal judges, who on Wednesday will hear the third major case in less than two years challenging the president’s ability to tax imports from around the world. Each of the fights has centered on different legal justifications, but the root cause is the same: Mr. Trump’s reliance on decades-old laws to issue duties that opponents see as a harmful overreach.

This time, the cases concern the use of Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the administration to investigate unfair trade practices and impose tariffs if it finds that American businesses were harmed. In July, the government relied on the statute to impose tariffs on 86 countries at once, claiming that they had failed to stamp out “forced labor” and had put U.S. firms that better protect workers at a competitive disadvantage.

The expansive nature of the tariffs prompted state officials and small businesses to file a series of lawsuits, arguing that the Trump administration failed to marshal the evidence required to issue the duties. Instead, they framed the process as one motivated by politics and pretense, citing past statements from Mr. Trump and his deputies promising to resurrect a set of policies that had been declared illegal.

The administration has vigorously contested the claims, setting the stage for another complicated hearing in front of the Court of International Trade in downtown Manhattan. Judges on that specialized circuit have twice ruled against Mr. Trump in major tariff cases. Another defeat could again force the administration to surrender any money it has collected, though the administration appears to be hoping that the third time is the charm.

“Changing the statute, when you lose on a previous statute, doesn’t change the law,” said Sara Albrecht, the chairman of the Liberty Justice Center, a legal group representing two of the suing small businesses. The center helped to lead successful challenges against the president’s past tariffs.

“As long as they continue to file and abuse the statutes on the books, we’re going to continue to challenge them,” Ms. Albrecht said.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

The legal onslaught has hardly impeded Mr. Trump’s trade brinkmanship. Despite two years of economic shocks and uncertainty, the president still sees sky-high tariffs as the most potent tools for courting U.S. investment, protecting domestic industries, extracting new revenue and pressuring allies and adversaries into making concessions.

At every turn, however, Mr. Trump has faced stiff opposition and defeat.

Originally, Mr. Trump tried to impose steep, country-by-country tariffs using the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, or IEEPA. But the trade court last year found those duties to be unconstitutional, a decision upheld by the Supreme Court in February. That decision required the Trump administration to refund more than $160 billion in illegally collected tariffs while forcing the president to return to the drawing board.

Mr. Trump then tried to impose a temporary 10 percent tariff on nearly all goods arriving in the United States. That, too, faced lawsuits — and similarly was struck down by judges on the Court of International Trade. The tariffs eventually expired, but the case itself remains on appeal.

For its third try, the Trump administration turned to Section 301, the provision of law targeting unfair trade practices. In contrast to Mr. Trump’s previous efforts, there is “no doubt that Section 301 gives the president power to impose tariffs due to foreign practices that are unreasonable or burden or restrict U.S. commerce,” said Timothy C. Brightbill, a top trade lawyer at the law firm Wiley Rein.

In fact, presidents of both parties successfully invoked Section 301 in the past to target trade practices by individual countries, including China. But the expansive way in which Mr. Trump applied the law this summer triggered swift lawsuits from groups of small businesses and state officials, many of which had been involved in those past fights against the president’s earlier duties.

In their newest filings, each of the opponents proffered a similar set of arguments. While condemning forced labor, the lawsuits claimed that the administration had failed to conduct rigorous investigations and had not amassed sufficient evidence about the abuses in question in each country and the harms caused to American industry.

Under Mr. Trump’s approach, the 86 targeted countries faced tariffs ranging from 10 to 12.5 percent. But there was little differentiation in the rates that applied across a wide range of U.S. trading partners that have vastly different laws and human rights records. In the eyes of state officials, led by the attorney general of Oregon, there was “no rational fit” between Mr. Trump’s concerns and the “blanket global tariffs” he ultimately imposed.

The disconnect led many of Mr. Trump’s opponents to conclude that the tariffs were not supported by the facts — but, instead, served only to recreate the rates struck down by the Supreme Court. As evidence, they pointed to a series of past statements from top administration officials. One example included Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who previously proclaimed on CNBC that the “the tariff rates are going to go back to exactly where they were.”

Lawyers for the Justice Department vigorously disputed each of those characterizations as they sought to convince the court that its tariffs are legal. The arguments underscored the extent to which the administration hoped to use Section 301 as its primary trade tool, with work underway to issue a second battery of tariffs targeting dozens of additional countries for engaging in “excess capacity” and flooding markets with cheap goods in the coming weeks.

In a filing submitted in early September, the government framed its tariffs as a “moral and economic imperative.” The administration also defended its investigative process and argued the court had no right to review its determinations about forced labor, while dismissing the notion that past comments from public officials suggested anything untoward.

“Even if they could be considered, the cited statements would merely reflect that the Trump administration believes that tariffs are an effective tool for protecting American businesses against unfair trade practices,” the Justice Department wrote in one of its filings. “This is no revelation.”

attention-infidelity-ruin-romance.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 15  Words: 1308/1308
================================================================================

SUMMARY

A few weeks ago the independent movie “Before Sunrise” popped into my mind. Drawing on large surveys, books and qualitative interviews with young people, Cox reveals how fearful they are of being vulnerable, because any misstep can lead to global and permanent humiliation on social media. In a phone call, Cox told me that while there have been gender divides in every era, what is new for Gen Z-ers is the way the algorithms of social media are warping their views of all kinds of interactions and reinforcing “initial biases.”

ARTICLE

‘Attention Infidelity’ Is Ruining Romance
Your full attention is a gift. Give it more often.
By Jessica Grose
Published 2026-09-30 09:08 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/opinion/attention-infidelity-ruin-romance.html

A few weeks ago the independent movie “Before Sunrise” popped into my mind. A 1990s classic and the first in a trilogy, the film is about two cerebral 20-somethings, Céline and Jesse, who meet cute on a train to Paris. They decide to hop off in Vienna, and spend a day together bantering, interacting with locals, wandering the beautiful city without purpose and falling in love.

They relate in spite of cultural differences (he is American, she is French, they both talk to Austrians) and gendered ones, too. As I was replaying the movie in my mind, I had a thought that made my stomach drop: My children may never get to experience this. By “this” I mean the uninterrupted attention, general serendipity and conversational vulnerability that I got to experience before smartphones.

“Before Sunrise” even somewhat presaged our screen-addled present. In her review of the film in The New York Times, Janet Maslin notes Jesse’s commentary on the “dubious spiritual value of technology,” when he states, “You never hear somebody say, ‘Well, you know, with the time I’ve saved by using my word processor, I’m going to go to a Zen monastery and hang out.’”

Mine is not a new fear, and I realize it is born out of a kind of nostalgia. From the pollster and public opinion researcher Daniel Cox’s forthcoming book, “Generation Uncoupled: America’s New Gender Divide and the Crisis of Human Connection,” I learned a new term: “attention infidelity.” Cox defines it in a somewhat unusual and expansive way: when a partner’s digital life intrudes on an in-person connection.

This kind of “infidelity” can include looking at sexually explicit material or engaging in suggestive social media interactions, but more often it is just the banal distraction of dead-eyed scrolling. “Instead of reaching for each other,” Cox explains, “we snatch up our digital devices that flood us with an endless stream of hyper-curated content.”

Though couples of any age experience this to some degree — my husband and I try to leave our devices in the kitchen after dinner so we can actually talk to each other — people like us who got together before the smartphone at least had the benefit of cementing our bonds with long stretches of concentrated attention. That kind of sustained focus breeds deeper understanding across differences and more grace.

Some may dismiss this kind of worry about young people’s nascent relationships as a technological moral panic. But Cox, who is the director of the Survey Center on American Life at the right-leaning American Enterprise Institute, has compiled a list of sobering statistics that show that screens are a driving factor in how disconnected teenagers and 20-somethings are from one another.

Gen Z-ers, the first generation that can’t remember a world without smartphones, participate less in “embodied social experiences” than their counterparts in every other generation. They’re less likely to work, go to church, attend parties, date or play sports, Cox notes. About half of teenagers describe themselves as “almost constantly” online. There is no other change that has occurred in the past few decades that would explain this unique decline.

Young people’s very online isolation, which was worsened by the Covid lockdown, means they have much less practice interacting with new people and navigating the usual friction and established norms. This, Cox writes, has left them lonely, unmoored and distrustful of each other.

While dating has always been challenging and provided fodder for complaint, today’s teenagers and 20-somethings have a starting point of greater suspicion, which can be poison for the creation of romantic relationships. Drawing on large surveys, books and qualitative interviews with young people, Cox reveals how fearful they are of being vulnerable, because any misstep can lead to global and permanent humiliation on social media.

The example of “West Elm Caleb” came to mind when I was reading Cox’s book. Caleb was a New Yorker who went viral in 2022 because a few women posted about how he would ghost them instead of breaking up with them properly. What followed in the wake of his virality was “a massive online harassment campaign against a fairly average 25-year-old whose biggest crime so far is being a bad communicator,” as Rolling Stone’s Brittany Spanos put it. The rise of online dating, where relationships start on digital territory, only exacerbates this dynamic.

This kind of technologically driven apprehension particularly affects heterosexual coupling. In a phone call, Cox told me that while there have been gender divides in every era, what is new for Gen Z-ers is the way the algorithms of social media are warping their views of all kinds of interactions and reinforcing “initial biases.” Cox cited a 2025 Washington Post analysis of over 1,000 users, which found that “gender is one of the biggest predictors of what’s in your feed.”

In the worst cases, gender-specific feeds lead to misogynistic manosphere influencers gaining a foothold in young men’s minds, which Cox rightfully condemns as toxic in his book. But our feeds are also creating news silos that may affect our perception of the world in more subtle ways. At minimum, they mirror a lack of a shared reality that might provide a basis for conversation and connection. (I saw this in action when I discovered that my husband knew nothing about the Lindsay Clancy verdict, even as I had been served wall-to-wall content about it for weeks.)

Two things give me hope about the social and romantic lives of young people. One is that at least some Gen Z-ers seem to know what they’re missing. Ethan Hawke, who played Jesse in “Before Sunrise,” told The Times in 2020 that his daughter watched the movie with friends, “and there was a certain envy they had for a time where you didn’t have email. Life insisted that you live in the moment more.” Having seen technology colonize their lives, they refuse to give another inch to A.I.

The other is that Americans in a wide variety of demographics are disgusted by the way screens have come between them and other people, and want to create a better world for our children. Cox is most certainly to the right of me, and while I did have some partisan quibbles with his book, I overwhelmingly agreed with his broad analysis and specific dismay with the status quo. He understands something I also hold to be true: giving another person your full attention is a gift, one we should all be more conscious of giving each other.

End Notes

- I am sick about the sexual assault allegations at Cornell. Beyond blind rage I don’t have anything particularly coherent to say about it for now, but I have been doing a lot of reading. First, I recommend this article from May in The Times about New York State’s unfair and outdated rape laws, and how they make it “difficult to charge people with rape if the accuser chose to become intoxicated.” I also recommend reading this New York magazine interview with two editors from The Cornell Daily Sun about their reporting on the case.
- Finally — in a sadly related issue — The 74, a nonprofit newsroom focused on education, recently published an investigation into almost 2,000 child sex abuse claims involving New York State K-12 schools. These claims were made because of a 2019 law that “allowed any living survivor of childhood sexual abuse to bring a civil case during a two-year look-back window and permanently extended the statute of limitations from age 23 to 55 for future civil cases,” explained the reporter, Amanda Geduld. Nearly one-fifth of these claims were made against adults who had access to their victims through schools. “Multiple teachers were credibly accused of sexual abuse in one school, and then permitted to quietly move on to a new one,” Geduld found. Feel free to drop me a line about anything here.

john-maynard-keynes-ai-economist.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 47  Words: 1548/1921
================================================================================

SUMMARY

Nearly a century ago, the legendary economist John Maynard Keynes predicted that technology would significantly increase productivity and reshape how we live. But what would Keynes say about this moment? Narrator: There are numerous biographies on Keynes.

ARTICLE

What Would John Maynard Keynes Say About A.I.? The Keynes Bot Told Us.
Nearly a century ago, Keynes predicted that technology would liberate us from work. To imagine what he would think of artificial intelligence today, a Princeton economist used A.I.
By Markus Brunnermeier, Sarah Kramer and Mehron Abdi
Published 2026-09-30 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/opinion/john-maynard-keynes-ai-economist.html

To understand how A.I. will affect our future, we’re looking to the past.

Nearly a century ago, the legendary economist John Maynard Keynes predicted that technology would significantly increase productivity and reshape how we live. Today, as A.I. capabilities accelerate, technologists have similar claims.

But what would Keynes say about this moment?

The Princeton University economist Markus Brunnermeier set out to answer this very question. Using an A.I. agent trained on more than 12,000 pages of Keynes’s writings and transcripts, along with the few available recordings of him, Brunnermeier and his team built a bot designed to answer questions in Keynes’s voice and style. He then had an in-depth conversation with the Keynes bot about the future of work and what happens to society when technology changes what people do for a living. Times Opinion, in collaboration with Brunnermeier, distilled those conversations into a short exchange.

The result is a revealing conversation with a Keynes who never lived to see the A.I. age — and a trenchant warning from his A.I. bot.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement. The companies have denied those claims.)

How the Keynes bot Was Created The economist Markus Brunnermeier and the researcher and Ph.D. student Pablo Balsinde built a bot using ChatGPT to create the Keynes A.I. The bot was instructed to draw primarily from Keynes’s seminal essay “Economic Possibilities for Our Grandchildren” (though the model was also provided with his larger body of work) and to answer questions in his style, which the pair described as “first-person, early 20th century British cadence, restrained wit.”

According to the team behind the bot, its initial responses were often long-winded and unclear. To improve them, the researchers “asked the GPT to rephrase, prompted it to reply using famous quotes from Keynes and cut parts of responses.” While the language was generated by the model, the responses were edited by the research team for clarity and brevity.

For the visuals, the team uploaded a public domain image of Keynes and used DeepSeek to alter the environment, placing him behind a desk. To create audio resembling Keynes’s voice, the team used a recording of Keynes from the BBC as a reference.

Below is an edited transcript of this video. We recommend watching it in its original form for the full effect. You can do so using the video player above.

Narrator: This is John Maynard Keynes, one of the most famous economists who ever lived.

He died in 1946. Yet in the last century, we have looked to his teachings many times. And if you stick around for the next five minutes, maybe he’ll have something to teach you about how A.I. might change our lives. But first, a little background.

According to the Encyclopaedia Britannica, John Maynard Keynes revolutionized economic theories. He is widely considered the founder of modern macroeconomics.

Archival clip of John Maynard Keynes: It is a wonderful thing for our businessmen to taste hope.

Narrator: There are numerous biographies on Keynes. But Lord Robert Skidelsky is considered to have written the definitive account of Keynes’s life and work — in three volumes.

Keynes’s essays and books have been cited in numerous articles. There’s a Keynes rap.

Clip of “Fear the Boom and Bust: Keynes vs. Hayek”: John Maynard Keynes wrote the book on modern macro. The man you need ——

Narrator: There are many groups dedicated to Keynes’s philosophy around the world. Harald Hagemann is the honorary chairman of the German-speaking society.

Archival clip of Harald Hagemann: Welcome to all of you.

Narrator: John Maynard Keynes was Charles Darwin’s granddaughter’s brother-in-law. And Keynes’s great-great-nephew starred in the 2005 smash hit movie “The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe.”

Tilda Swinton as the White Witch: I would very much like to meet the rest of your family. Skandar Keynes as Edmund Pevensie: Why? They’re nothing special.

Narrator: In 1930, Keynes published a paper that predicted that technology would dramatically increase productivity in what he called “progressive countries” over the next century. At the time, people were skeptical of his argument. Sound familiar?

It’s 2026, and again, there is a fierce debate raging as to where technology is taking us.

Archival news clip: The people building A.I. earnestly believe it could kill us all ——

Narrator: Uh — not that debate.

Archival news clip: A.I. is rapidly reshaping the workplace. Clip of Allie K. Miller on “The Mel Robbins Podcast”: You are going to expand your capabilities and your superpowers. Clip of Gael Breton on “Authority Hacker Podcast”: The models got so good that the gain in productivity is undeniable at this point.

Narrator: So what would Keynes say about what A.I. means for our economy?

Up in the north tower of the Bendheim Center for Finance at Princeton University, the economist Markus Brunnermeier has been trying to answer this very question. And he’s taken an unorthodox approach to finding out what Keynes might think.

Markus Brunnermeier: So with the help of A.I., I built an avatar of him. I used his writings, along with an archival photo and interviews with him. Welcome, Lord Keynes.

A.I.-generated bot of John Maynard Keynes: Well, thank you, Professor Brunnermeier. For someone born in 1883 to be reanimated as an artificial intelligence is, I confess, an unexpected form of life after death.

Narrator: So you may not all approve of this. We don’t know for certain that Keynes would approve. But we did run it by his family. Remember Edmund?

Clip of Skandar Keynes: They’re nothing special.

Narrator: Well, he, along with his sister, great-aunt and great-uncle, gave us the go-ahead.

Keynes: Today I have the curious privilege of speaking with you, those very grandchildren I was speculating about 100 years ago.

Narrator: Sorry, sorry — last interruption, we promise. Keynes was British and spoke and wrote more formally than we speak today, so we’ve updated some of the language to more contemporary English and modified the conversation for brevity and clarity. You’re welcome.

Brunnermeier: Professor Keynes, when you wrote your essay “Economic Possibilities for Our Grandchildren,” it was the start of the Great Depression. A majority of Americans were poor. Education was a luxury. Yet a handful of folks were so rich, they didn’t need to work at all.

Keynes: Indeed. I predicted that by 2030, the United States could be as much as eight times richer per head. America beat that prediction: Your society is already eight times richer, and it’s only 2026.

Brunnermeier: Our lives are not perfect, but overall, we are much better off than we used to be. Technological advancements lifted more than one billion people out of poverty, even as the world’s population quadrupled.

Keynes: Absolutely. I also predicted that in four years, you would be living lives of such material abundance that everyone would need to work far less, perhaps 15 hours a week. From what I can tell, that has not come to pass.

Brunnermeier: Correct. But now we have artificial intelligence. Do you think A.I. could fulfill your prediction of a 15-hour workweek? And in four years our lives could be predominantly ones of leisure?

Keynes: Unfortunately, I see the emergence of A.I. introducing new challenges. I fear you may end up with skilled and overworked professionals with money but no time, and the rest of society with time but no money.

Brunnermeier: Why?

Keynes: Due to the concentration of A.I.’s potential, as A.I. takes over tasks that are more and more qualified and sophisticated, it will bring an increased concentration of expertise into the hands of a limited few. Those people might, in the future, be managing the whole economy by themselves.

Narrator: At this point in the video ——

Clip of “Once in a Lifetime” by Talking Heads: You may ask yourself.

Narrator: Which group will I belong to? Well, tighten your seatbelts, because the Keynes Bot is about to get darker.

Brunnermeier: There’s something else in your 1930s essay that haunts me. You warned that humanity might suffer a “nervous breakdown.” That we have been bred to struggle against scarcity and when that struggle is removed, we won’t know what to do with ourselves. Does that still hold?

Keynes: Yes, though it might split the population into two groups, each suffering differently.

The first — those still employed and dominating the new technology — burn out. They make work their whole identity, and so when A.I. absorbs more of what they do, they do not step back. They grind harder at whatever the machine cannot yet handle, trying to prove they are still essential.

The second group troubles me more. The displaced lose something money cannot replace: the quiet daily reassurance that someone needs them to show up. They may question their own worth. And it can take a very long time — perhaps a generation — to find a new purpose. If the gains are not shared, they will also suffer materially. So the struggle against scarcity would not end for them. It would just be exacerbated by a lack of purpose.

In any case, there might be not only widespread unemployment, but a deeper risk: the strain on democracies, and the fraying of the bonds that hold a society together.

Narrator: According to the Keynes Bot, the haves and have-nots both could have serious nervous breakdowns. Are you wondering if there’s an overlooked Option C? Markus?

Brunnermeier: Is this terrible future inevitable?

Keynes: Not at all. Whether A.I. ends up as a source of broadly shared prosperity and purpose or a machine for manufacturing a new dominant class of wealthy and powerful is not preordained by the technology itself. It will be determined by your government and whether it has the political courage to use its laws and its tax systems to ensure that A.I. will work to the benefit of all of society’s citizens.

Brunnermeier: Thanks a lot for your insights, Lord Keynes.

Keynes: Thank you, Markus. The central question remains the same: What shall be done with the growing powers of production and invention? The outcome is up to you to decide.

Narrator: OK, so what have we learned? Well, if we’re going to thrive, let alone survive, the power of A.I. can’t end up in the hands of the few.

It’s obvious: We need ongoing regulation and government intervention. Even an A.I.-reincarnated economist can see what’s on the line: Our livelihood. Our sanity. Our future.
