SUMMARY

The New York Times is a thriving company in a thriving industry. It asked: “What if The New York Times goes out of business — like, this May?” But against these long odds, The Times is still standing.

ARTICLE

So You Want to Publish a Newspaper
How on earth did The New York Times, a seemingly ossified institution in a dying industry, survive the most destabilizing period in its history — and emerge stronger?
By A.G. Sulzberger
Published 2026-09-30 09:02 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/opinion/new-york-times-family-ownership-stewardship.html

This essay was originally delivered as a speech at the Wharton Center for Performing Arts at Michigan State University on Tuesday.

Let me start in the year 2004. The New York Times is a thriving company in a thriving industry. It boasts a best-in-class product, an esteemed brand and a uniquely influential readership. Many call it the greatest newspaper in the world. But it has grown to be much more than that: a diversified media conglomerate with over 12,000 employees and $3 billion in revenue. It’s an auspicious time to break ground on the construction of a grand new headquarters designed by one of the world’s most acclaimed architects.

What could possibly go wrong?

Well, at the same time, this disruptive force called the World Wide Web was gaining steam, ready to plow through any tradition-bound incumbent standing in its path. In the next decade, The New York Times Company lost about three-quarters of its work force. Revenues dropped by over half. The stock price fell from $48 to $4. That fancy new headquarters? Desperate for cash, the company sold it, just two years after it opened. We were reduced to renting back space in the building bearing our name.

Remarkably, the situation looked likely to get even worse. Modest gains in digital revenue were not close to offsetting the continued decimation of the print newspaper business. A new crop of internet-native start-ups like BuzzFeed and The Huffington Post were attracting far more readers. And creative and forward-thinking colleagues — the very people The Times needed to help find a way out of this mess — were quitting because the company culture was stifling innovation.

Xerox. Kodak. Blockbuster. The New York Times looked to be another once-great company that became too comfortable, too complacent, too slow to change. One of yesterday’s firms — a cautionary tale to be taught in lecture halls like this one. The conventional wisdom that the paper was destined to fail was best captured in a 2009 story in The Atlantic titled “End Times.” It asked: “What if The New York Times goes out of business — like, this May?”

But against these long odds, The Times is still standing. Indeed, not just standing but thriving — heralded as a case study in how to transform a legacy company for a new era. In a period when most news organizations watched their audience and revenue collapse, our company has grown from about one million paying subscribers to more than 13 million. Revenue and profit are also growing steadily, enabling an unprecedented expansion of our newsroom. The stock price — now higher than it was at our pre-internet peak — suggests that investors believe that this old newspaper’s best years are still to come. And, yes, we own our headquarters again.

Which raises the question: How on earth did The New York Times, a seemingly ossified institution in a dying industry, survive the most destabilizing period in its history — and emerge stronger?

On Sept. 18, 1851, the first edition of The New-York Daily Times rolled off the press. In a crowded field of sensationalist newspapers, The Times stood out immediately for prioritizing serious journalism on serious issues. It earned a reputation for quality, sobriety and fairness.

The New York City of the day lacked a single building taller than a church spire. America consisted of just 31 states and 24 million people. Indoor electricity wouldn’t be widely available for decades — let alone wonders like radio, telephones, cars, television, airplanes and computers. The rise of all these new technologies would be chronicled in the pages of The Times as they upended culture, politics and, of course, the world of business.

With each disruption, legacy companies that long dominated their industries faltered and failed, much as The Times nearly did following the arrival of the internet. Those that survived found the sweet spot between continuity and change — grounded in institutional history yet propelled forward by the fresh energy of innovation.

On the occasion of our 175th anniversary, I want to talk about the secret recipe behind the endurance of The New York Times. At the heart of our success — as a journalistic enterprise, as a business, as an enduring American institution — is to approach our work as stewards guided by two foundational, ironclad commitments: to value and to values.

Value is about the product you make. In our case, journalism. To prioritize value is to obsess over quality, to focus relentlessly on delivering the most useful and rewarding experience possible. It means never trying to game your way to success by chasing the latest fad or riding buzzy marketing. Value requires knowing your craft and caring, in a deep and authentic way, about your customers.

Values are less tangible. They’re easier to write off as impractical idealism. In today’s business environment, with its short-term focus and frenetic, Slack-driven pace, too many people see values as liabilities rather than assets. Our experience has taught us the opposite. At The Times, values like independence, integrity and public service are central to our work. And we have found that staying true to them is not just the right thing to do but also central to our business success over the long term.

Value and values alone are not enough to sustain a thriving company. You also need talented people, a strong business strategy, effective operations and an adaptable culture. But our focus on making a product that the public needs — and doing so with values that elevate principle above profit and put the public interest before self-interest — has been central to our business success.

That brings me to stewardship. Stewardship is a model of leadership that puts the long-term health of an enterprise first. A steward must have the humility to recognize that a great institution is bigger than any single person, that one’s own tenure is just a chapter in a longer story. But stewards must also understand the ways in which their chapter is distinct — the unique challenges they must overcome, the unique changes they must embrace. Great leaders can be measured in many ways. They can drive revenue growth, increase share price or achieve market domination. Great stewards must do something singular: hand their enterprise to capable successors, stronger and more resilient than it was handed to them.

My family, the Ochs-Sulzbergers, has stewarded The Times for 130 years. How that looks behind the scenes is much less interesting, thankfully, than anything you might have seen on “Succession.” That is not just because we’re boring, though being boring helps. It’s because our family’s ethos is far too idealistic to survive a TV writers’ room. Our mission is not to seek great fame or fortune. It’s not to dominate politics or culture. It’s to protect and strengthen an essential American institution. Each generation teaches the next — maybe indoctrinates is a better word — that The Times doesn’t serve the family; the family serves The Times. And, as my great-grandmother Iphigene often reminded us, “No big heads allowed.”

For this reason, my family has preferred to stay out of the spotlight and let the work of our journalists take center stage. But The Times’s big anniversary arrives amid an epidemic of distrust in America’s institutions — as well as increasingly direct attacks on the rights and legitimacy of news organizations. So I thought I’d use the occasion to share more about how The Times works as an institution and how the family works to support the paper’s mission “to seek the truth and help people understand the world.”

To be clear, my predecessors and I have made mistakes of all types, including some big ones. Some areas of coverage have aged poorly; as a business, we’ve pursued any number of dead ends. But you don’t get to be this old without getting some big things right. Each of the five generations of family leaders has had to transform The Times while also ensuring that it endured with its soul intact. Through two World Wars, economic booms and busts and the arrival of the internet, we’ve stuck to our central formula — a stewardship mind-set guided by value and values — because long experience tells us it works.

Adolph Ochs, my great-great-grandfather, was the last member of my family who could fairly claim to have pulled himself up by his bootstraps. A high school dropout and the son of immigrants, he had worked his way up from manning the printing presses at newspapers in his home state of Tennessee to owning The Chattanooga Times. Then he wanted to take on the nation’s biggest and most competitive market. The New York Times may have seemed like a surprising candidate for such a conquest. It had a circulation of just 9,000 and was teetering on the edge of bankruptcy. But Ochs was drawn to its reputation for quality journalism. In 1896, he pulled together money and loans to purchase The Times for $75,000, the equivalent of about $3 million today.

As part of the deal, Ochs had to hit several challenging financial targets before he could secure his ownership. That was no sure thing, given the paper was hemorrhaging money. To stem those losses, he cut business and administrative positions.

But he also did something counterintuitive. He expanded his spending on journalism, including new features, like a book review and a magazine. Then he dropped the price of The Times from three cents to one cent. While the added journalistic costs combined with the price drop would hurt profits in the short term, Ochs was confident that these moves would encourage more people to try The Times and recognize it as a superior product, propelling the business in the long term.

Thus was born my family’s formula for doubling down on value in periods of economic pressure.

Ochs was equally radical in the emphasis he placed on the paper’s values, particularly journalistic independence. In his first day as publisher, he promised readers that, unlike the partisan press of the day, The Times newsroom would “give the news impartially, without fear or favor.” The editorial pages, rather than just parroting one point of view, would provide a forum for “intelligent discussion from all shades of opinion.” That commitment to ensuring the independence of news coverage — the insistence of putting values like fairness and accuracy above personal views, political affiliation and financial interests — changed the direction not just of The Times but also of American journalism.

This commitment would be tested almost immediately, when Ochs received a written demand from a prominent banker who was also one of his most important shareholders. The banker believed that The Times’s finance reporter was too focused on corporate wrongdoing, and he told Ochs to fire him. Ochs’s response was direct. “I am very sorry that you believe you can write such a letter to me,” he wrote. “I do not understand that you have any control whatsoever of the editorial conduct of The New York Times.” The Times was willing to say no to anyone who attempted to influence its coverage, no matter how powerful he was or how much he mattered to its bottom line.

None of that is to say Ochs wasn’t a canny businessman. He was a relentless innovator who embraced new technologies like photography and radio. He was a brilliant marketer who rebranded his neighborhood as Times Square and created the New Year’s Eve ball drop to draw attention to the newspaper. During his tenure, he grew daily circulation 50-fold. But he was first and foremost a steward. Under Ochs’s ownership, nearly all of the newspaper’s profits were reinvested to improve and expand its journalism. The strength and resilience of the business today owes much to that farsighted approach.

Ochs was succeeded as publisher by his son-in-law, Arthur Hays Sulzberger. Arthur Hays used the financial success of The Times to continue investing in journalism and to add new features, like a food column and a daily crossword puzzle. But the true test of his commitment to value came, as such tests usually do, under pressure. In World War II, the government began rationing the paper that newspapers were printed on. Publishers faced a quandary: fewer articles or fewer ads? Journalists were taking great risks to bring wartime news home to readers; several Times reporters were killed or taken prisoner while covering the conflict. So Arthur Hays turned away advertising to offer the public more news instead. By the end of the war, readership was soaring.

A generation later, Arthur Hays was succeeded first by his son-in-law who died just two years later and then by his son, Arthur Ochs Sulzberger, better known as Punch. Facing the brutal 1970s economy and the consumer shift to television, newspapers struggled for revenue and relevance. Punch met this pressure by embarking on a historic expansion of the paper’s offerings, doubling the number of daily sections, with new ones focused on science, sports and lifestyle. When others are thinning the broth, he believed, it is best to put more tomatoes in the soup. As a result of those investments, The Times became more valuable to subscribers and advertisers alike, driving a period of historic business growth.

That brings us to my father, also named Arthur. And I do apologize for our lack of creativity with our names — Sulzbergers are nothing if not consistent. My father became publisher at the dawn of the internet. He recognized that this was not just another technological shift — it was the end of our 150-year model of making money by printing and distributing newspapers. To position The Times for this new world, my father made two brave bets: putting the entire newspaper online before there was a proven business model and, 15 years later, charging for digital subscriptions while industry experts still insisted that “information wants to be free.”

But his bravest bet came amid the collapse of our longstanding business model. My father oversaw the sale of more than 40 properties owned by the Times Company — newspapers, magazines, television stations, websites, even a chunk of the Boston Red Sox — effectively every asset that wasn’t The Times itself. The company also laid off a huge percentage of its business staffers at the paper. Between the divestment and the layoffs, our work force shrank by nearly three-quarters to 3,500 employees.

Yet — and this is the brave bet — he held the head count in the Times newsroom flat, even as revenue and profits continued to fall. This steady investment hid a major shift, with investigative reporters and foreign correspondents suddenly joined by a new breed of video, audio and multimedia journalists. Media pundits scoffed at this strategy of continuing to pour money into an apparently failing business. But my father believed that the key to a successful news business in the digital age, as it had been in the print age, would be offering something worth paying for. Thanks to that stubborn commitment to value, The Times now has more paying digital subscribers than any news organization in the world.

One reading of this history is that the three Arthur Sulzbergers who preceded me were maverick business geniuses who zigged when others zagged. In truth, they simply did what good stewards do. They didn’t just focus on short-term profit. They also stubbornly insisted, even under great pressure, that good journalism has value — to its readers and to society at large. They were confident that if The Times continued to invest in creating this value, the company would benefit over the long term.

Making hard choices to uphold the values of The Times shows a similar through line across generations. The most fundamental of these is journalistic independence, the commitment to following the facts wherever they lead. Independence requires a stubborn insistence on telling the whole story, even the parts some people don’t want to hear. It demands that we be willing to upset the powers that be by asking questions they may not want to answer or publishing facts they may not want the public to know. And more often than you might imagine, it necessitates that we be willing to pay a clear financial price to ensure the integrity of our journalism.

The Times regularly publishes stories we know may lead readers to cancel subscriptions and businesses to pull ads, that may lead activists to protest outside our headquarters and powerful people to take us to court. We even insist on investigating our own mistakes, believing we owe readers a full airing of where we went wrong, no matter how uncomfortable those revelations might be for us. Our editors and executives — and, yes, publishers — have all received unflattering coverage in our own pages.

Over the years, politicians, business leaders and others have tried unsuccessfully to stop such coverage by attempting to buy our silence or threaten us into submission. In the 1870s, New York’s most powerful politician, known as Boss Tweed, offered a bribe that today would be worth well over $100 million in a failed attempt to stop The Times from exposing his corruption, which would soon land him in jail. Nearly a century later, Alabama segregationists weaponized the local courts, filing a wave of dubious lawsuits intended to halt The Times’s civil rights coverage or, even better, bankrupt the paper altogether.

Our interactions with American presidents tell a similar story. President John F. Kennedy once invited my grandfather to the White House to suggest that he reassign a reporter whose Vietnam War coverage was a bit too honest for the administration’s taste. Punch refused. He proceeded to stand up to even greater pressure from President Richard Nixon after The Times obtained the government’s classified history of the Vietnam War, which documented how politicians and military leaders had misled Americans about the conflict. Despite the risk of imprisonment, Punch decided to publish what became known as the Pentagon Papers.

Decades later, President George W. Bush, sitting in the Oval Office, asked my father not to publish a story disclosing that his administration was secretly wiretapping Americans’ phone calls, in apparent defiance of the law. If The Times wrote about the antiterrorism program and another attack occurred, the president warned, he would regard the paper as responsible for the deaths of Americans. After long and careful consideration, the story was published, enabling an important debate about how to balance national security and civil liberties.

I have sat across from President Trump — who has sued us three times, used multiple government agencies to target our business, expelled journalists from the Pentagon and now the White House and insulted us more times than anyone can count. I told him that a free press is an essential part of our national fabric and that our journalists will not be deterred by his attacks. And they have not been. Just this year, our investigative reporting exposing how Mr. Trump has used his power to enrich himself and his family was awarded a Pulitzer Prize.

The independence of our journalism extends to our own commercial interests. Harvey Weinstein’s status as a major advertiser, for instance, did not insulate him from our reporters exposing allegations of extensive sexual misconduct against him. Similarly, in 2012, after we had just spent millions to start a Chinese-language website, one of our reporters discovered that the family of the Chinese premier had secretly enriched itself during his tenure. Despite explicit threats of retaliation from the Chinese government, The Times still published the story. The government immediately shut down all access to our website and, eventually, our apps. Years later, both remain walled off there.

From time to time, I’ll meet with a billionaire who has just purchased a news organization. These are generally people who have had far more business success than I ever will. But I offer them one bit of advice: Running a news organization is unlike running any other company. It requires an unabashed love of and respect for journalism. There are far easier ways to make money and friends. News requires an almost counter-evolutionary willingness — insistence, even — to do things that may appear to be damaging to the company and its interests. To publish articles that will upset readers, enrage advertisers and be weaponized by your fiercest critics. Each hard choice in favor of value and values is a deposit that strengthens the bond of reader trust and is the lifeblood of a news organization that succeeds over the long term.

Which brings me back to stewardship. Although my family is often said to own The Times, the reality is more complicated. Roughly 100 members of my extended family are actually the controlling shareholders of the company through a family trust. This isn’t your typical family trust — the sort that’s mainly worried about how to pass on a fortune. Our trust’s primary obligation was first laid out in the will of Adolph Ochs. It called on his descendants to maintain the editorial independence and integrity of The New York Times and to continue it “as an independent newspaper, entirely fearless, free of ulterior influence and unselfishly devoted to the public welfare.”

That mandate, which explicitly puts the best interests of The Times and its readers first, still guides us.

One of my aunts frequently says that if losing her leg would help The Times, she would saw it off herself. And that’s actually an apt metaphor for what she and her generation did financially to ensure The Times would continue to benefit from its special governance structure. Having watched other newspaper families splinter amid arguments about wealth, Ochs’s great-grandchildren decided to lock up the controlling shares in a family trust for another century. And they adopted creative provisions to further strip any temptation their descendants might have to cash out. Perhaps the most remarkable move was combining four trusts held by different — and differently sized — branches of the family into a single trust. That act meant that some gave up nearly half of their holdings to establish the truly shared control they hoped would foster family unity.

The result of these moves is that the family effectively eliminated any potential windfall for generations. Instead, the family’s central reward is the knowledge that its stewardship model — its commitment to the paper’s value and values — continues to be of service to an important institution, the journalists who work there and the public that depends on their reporting.

Having spoken about the family at length, I should also say that the family leadership gets more credit than it deserves. One of the most important decisions any good steward can make is to surround oneself with smarter and more talented leaders. Our brilliant chief executive, Meredith Kopit Levien, is the most impressive business leader I’ve ever seen. Our steel-spined executive editor, Joe Kahn, is similarly the best in journalism. Our board of directors is majority independent, ensuring the company benefits from the expertise of a wide range of accomplished leaders from other fields. And below these top executives are countless other best-in-class editors and business leaders. Though family leaders like me are deeply involved in strategy and operations, our most important contribution is as a permission structure: encouraging leaders at all levels to place big bets, to stay strong under pressure, to do the right thing, to take the long view.

A 175th birthday certainly offers some evidence that our model continues to work. And that our work continues to matter. But we take no false comfort from our longevity. Simply having been around a long time is not a guarantee of a bright future. The Hudson’s Bay Company made it twice as long — 355 years — before closing last year.

Tradition, legacy, even consistent excellence can be powerful forces to discourage change. But good stewardship requires recognizing the ways an institution must evolve to keep pace with changing times, technologies and consumer preferences.

That’s why I often tell colleagues that the main thing we’ve won over our last decade of transformation and growth is the right to compete for the next decade. We must remain oriented toward the future, awake to both its opportunities and its risks. We must remember that though we may be a success story in our industry, the industry is systematically failing. We are a fraction of the size of the tech giants that dominate the flow of information and attention. Google makes more profit every day than The Times does in an entire year. Not only do Netflix, Amazon and Spotify have hundreds of millions more subscribers, The Times also lags streaming platforms like Starz and Crunchyroll.

My generation is about a decade into our chapter of stewardship. My job — in partnership with my cousins Sam Dolnick and David Perpich, both driving forces in the transformation of The Times — is to shepherd the paper through the next round of challenges and opportunities this era presents, from standing up to attacks on press freedom to navigating the emergence of artificial intelligence. Our formula will be the same one that has served the place for five generations.

First, we’re adding value. We’ve nearly doubled the newsroom’s head count in the last decade. This includes significantly expanding our national and international coverage and more than tripling the ranks of investigative reporters. It also includes embracing new formats. “The Daily” and The Morning are now the largest news podcast and the largest newsletter in the country, each reaching far more people than the print newspaper ever did. Our video operation has more than doubled in the last two years. We’re using A.I. in ambitious ways, from helping our reporters comb through large data sets to creating an audio version of every story we publish.

At the same time, we’ve transformed how we support audience interests and passions. Once constrained to publishing a few recipes a week in the newspaper, our NYT Cooking app now serves as a comprehensive, interactive guide through 25,000 handcrafted recipes. The Athletic boasts the largest roster of sports reporters in the world, while Wirecutter offers the most rigorously tested product reviews. Our NYT Games app has expanded from the Crossword to a broad suite of beloved offerings like Connections, Spelling Bee and Wordle.

To accomplish all this, we’ve had to transform large parts of our culture. The Times is far more creative, collaborative, diverse and innovative than it was two decades ago. But we’ve held tight to the company’s guiding values, making clear that any change that requires The Times to compromise on independence or integrity isn’t a change worth making.

In a media ecosystem increasingly overrun by pundits and influencers, The Times is investing more in original reporting than ever. As others chase what’s trending on social platforms, we still focus first and foremost on the issues that really matter. As polarized groups protest journalism that challenges their preferred narratives, we maintain our stubborn belief in the importance of providing different perspectives, even — perhaps especially — those you may disagree with. And as the rights and freedoms of journalists face growing pressure, no news organization has proved more willing to stand strong — and, when necessary, to fight the government in court — to ensure that the press is able to continue to ask important questions on behalf of the American public.

As The Times celebrates its 175th birthday, the United States is celebrating its 250th. It’s no overstatement to say the story of our great nation and its paper of record are bound up together. America’s commitment to free expression and free inquiry enshrined in the First Amendment has enabled The Times’s model of journalism “without fear or favor.” In turn, our journalism has provided the public a reliable source of news and information that has strengthened our country — its economy, its security, its civic bonds — in countless ways.

A disproportionate amount of what the public knows about this moment — and the 175 years that preceded it — they know because our journalists went to places, talked to people, asked tough questions and shared what they learned with the public as fully and fairly as possible. We have spent many billions of dollars and taken great risks to build the definitive archive of America’s history, one that is cited everywhere from college essays to Supreme Court rulings.

Along the way, our work has helped expose miscarriages of justice, save taxpayer dollars and lead to lifesaving reforms. But our main purpose has always been to help people of all stripes better understand what’s happening and why it matters, to help them engage more deeply with their world. Every president, regardless of his party or his complaints, reads our work. So do millions of others, from the leaders of Wall Street and Silicon Valley to the teachers, librarians and professors nurturing the next generation of minds. Which is a reminder that success takes many forms.

I can’t pretend all this has been easy. And it’s a safe bet that even larger challenges loom. But if I can complete my tour of service by handing off a stronger company to a capable successor, then I’ll have done my job. And it will be up to the next generation to push the place to new heights. That is what it means to be a good steward.

So let me ask all of you, particularly those of you preparing to embark upon a career, to borrow from the recipe that has served The New York Times — and our nation — so well.

When you build, build something of value. When you face hard choices, face them with considered values. And when you lead, lead in the spirit of stewardship.

Your investments may take a while to pay off. But when they do, your reward will be that highest of professional achievements: being part of something worthy and enduring.

SUMMARY

Chief Justice John Roberts has accomplished so much of his agenda that it’s not easy, as he begins his 22nd Supreme Court term, to think of what unfinished business might remain. The plaintiffs’ basic argument was that under the analysis the Supreme Court applied in the secondary school tuition case from Maine, Colorado’s refusal to grant the exemption violated the First Amendment’s guarantee of the free exercise of religion. “This case is different,” the appeals court said.

ARTICLE

Religion Is the Roberts Court’s Unfinished Business
This case has flown under the radar, but it won’t stay there.
By Linda Greenhouse
Published 2026-09-30 09:01 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/opinion/supreme-court-john-roberts-religion.html

Chief Justice John Roberts has accomplished so much of his agenda that it’s not easy, as he begins his 22nd Supreme Court term, to think of what unfinished business might remain.

Affirmative action is dead. Roe v. Wade is a fading memory. The Voting Rights Act of 1965 is in shreds, rendered incapable of serving its original mission of preventing states from undermining the political power of minority citizens. The executive branch agencies known collectively as the administrative state have lost their independence, with the president now able to fire nearly all agency heads for any reason or no reason at all. Federal judges are no longer to defer to an agency’s interpretation of its own authority, instead being told to decide for themselves the validity of agency regulations. Historical claims that fly under the banner of “originalism” have frozen the government’s ability to regulate the ownership of lethal weapons.

While it’s a daunting list, some readers might notice that I have omitted one major focus of the Roberts court. Doesn’t religion belong in any inventory of completed projects?

Not yet.

That may seem a startling conclusion, given how significantly the court over the past decade has reoriented the relationship between church and state — a recent law review article by three constitutional law scholars calls the shift “a systematic dismantling of the previous legal regime.” A series of decisions, most of which bear the chief justice’s name, has established the principle, without precedent in constitutional history, that whatever public benefit secular institutions get, religious institutions are entitled to as well. The first of these, in 2017, required Missouri to include a church’s school in a state program to resurface school playgrounds, despite a “no aid” provision in its Constitution that barred the state from giving money to churches. Exclusion of the church from the program, Chief Justice Roberts wrote, was “odious to our Constitution.”

In 2022, the court declared unconstitutional Maine’s exclusion of religious schools from a program that subsidizes private school tuition for families in districts without a public secondary school. If the leap from preschool playgrounds to secondary school tuition seemed head-spinning, it was a leap the chief justice did not acknowledge in his opinion, Carson v. Makin. The principles of the first decision “suffice to resolve this case,” he wrote.

That is a huge amount of ground for the Supreme Court to have traversed in a short time. More is on the way. In its new term that begins next week, the court will decide whether the equality principle these cases have established is enough, or whether religion is entitled not just to equality, but to preference, in this instance a carve out from the rules that constrain secular institutions. The case is from Colorado, where a state “universal preschool” program operating since 2023 offers free prekindergarten to all 4-year-olds. Families can choose any participating preschool, secular or religious, that meets the quality standards established at the direction of the legislature. One of the standards is a nondiscrimination requirement: In admitting students whose families apply, the school may not discriminate on the basis of “race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level or disability.” Some 2,000 public and private schools, including dozens of religious schools, take part in the program.

For the Archdiocese of Denver, the sexual orientation and gender identity portions of the nondiscrimination provision posed a conflict. The archdiocese requires that parents who send their children to its schools accept the Roman Catholic Church’s teachings on marriage and family, asking them before enrollment to sign a statement of “community beliefs.” Same-sex and transgender parents need not apply. The archdiocese told its parishes not to participate in the program and requested an exemption from the two provisions. The state’s Department of Early Childhood replied that there was no option in state law for an exemption; every aspect of the nondiscrimination policy applied to all.

Two parishes, St. Mary, in Littleton, and St. Bernadette, in Lakewood, sued the state, along with a husband and wife from Littleton who wanted a state-funded Catholic education for their children. (The archdiocese joined the lawsuit but was dismissed for lack of standing.) The plaintiffs’ basic argument was that under the analysis the Supreme Court applied in the secondary school tuition case from Maine, Colorado’s refusal to grant the exemption violated the First Amendment’s guarantee of the free exercise of religion. The Federal District Court in Denver, in a decision affirmed by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit, disagreed.

“This case is different,” the appeals court said. It explained that while the Maine case and the cases that preceded it concerned a public program’s actual exclusion of religious schools, Colorado has “welcomed and actively solicited their participation.” The court added: “The only relevant limitation on any preschool’s participation is the nondiscrimination requirement which applies to all preschools regardless of whether they are religious or secular.” It noted that the state was neither targeting religion nor “attempting to prohibit funds from being used for religious purposes.”

The anodyne sound of that observation — that of course the state wasn’t preventing the direct use of public money for religious education — shouldn’t obscure the full dimension of the change the court has wrought in the constitutional law on religion. The notion that the First Amendment’s other religion clause, the prohibition against the “establishment” of religion, might have anything to say about this arrangement sounds now like the vestige of a distant past, so thorough has been the establishment clause’s erasure from constitutional notice.

This case, St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, puts to the justices the question of whether they are satisfied with what they have accomplished so far. Is equality enough? And if discrimination is an issue in the case, wherein does the discrimination lie?

For the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, the powerhouse religious law firm that brought this case to the Supreme Court, the question is clear. The news release it issued in April, when the court granted its petition, offered this account: “The Supreme Court today agreed to decide whether Colorado can continue excluding Catholic families and preschools from the state’s ‘universal’ preschool program because of their faith.” A tendentious framing, but well tailored to reach the ears of those justices primed to take an apocalyptic view of any seeming incursion on the interests of religious believers.

A friend of the court brief filed on the state’s side by Marci Hamilton, a religion scholar known for opposition to the court’s current course, proposes this counter framing: “This court should not undermine Colorado’s commitment to equality by transforming religious freedom into a doctrine that mandates taxpayer-subsidized discrimination.”

This case has flown under the radar in the months since the court granted the Becket Fund’s petition, but it won’t remain there as the Nov. 3 argument date approaches. Equality or preference? The choice is stark — and Chief Justice Roberts’s project, for now, remains unfinished.

Linda Greenhouse, the recipient of a 1998 Pulitzer Prize, reported on the Supreme Court for The Times from 1978 to 2008.

trump-vance-fraud-congress.html
Source: PreloadedData  Paragraphs: 15  Words: 988/1043
================================================================================

SUMMARY

Since March, Vice President JD Vance has been tasked with rooting out any fraud perpetrated against the federal government. The White House says that since then it has “uncovered” hundreds of billions of dollars in fraud and “stopped” tens of billions in ongoing fraud. If it’s done just before the end of the fiscal year, the White House can effectively cancel the appropriation, since the funds will have expired by the time Congress votes on the rescission request.

ARTICLE

Trump Wants to Get His Hands on the Power of the Purse
The search for fraud in the federal government must always end in the same place.
By Jamelle Bouie
Published 2026-09-30 09:09 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/opinion/trump-vance-fraud-congress.html

Since March, Vice President JD Vance has been tasked with rooting out any fraud perpetrated against the federal government. “This is a very big thing that we’re doing,” President Trump said when he announced the task force. “If we found half of the fraud that’s taking place in this country — and I think you have a chance of doing that — we would have much more than a balanced budget.”

The White House says that since then it has “uncovered” hundreds of billions of dollars in fraud and “stopped” tens of billions in ongoing fraud. But, as my newsroom colleague Linda Qiu notes in a recent report, “It is difficult to verify those figures because there is no publicly available breakdown of the total.” And while fraud is real, there has been no independent verification of the administration’s claims. They’re asking us, in short, to take their word for it.

Last week, in a news conference with Mehmet Oz, administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, the vice president announced a new quarry in his hunt: an alleged 750,000 people fraudulently enrolled in health insurance through the Affordable Care Act. “We had a system in this country that rewarded brokers, that made people rich for enrolling fake people in programs that are meant to ensure that our fellow citizens have health care,” Vance said. “This was a scandal.”

Again, the White House has given us very little to verify that this was actual fraud. We are supposed to trust that this administration is earnestly looking for fraud in public programs even as it seeks to undermine the programs themselves.

But the biggest reason to be skeptical of the administration’s narrative is the fact that it comes as the White House itself, starting from the very top, actively works to defraud the American people.

It does not receive as much attention as Trump’s assault on American cities or his draconian program of deportations and removals, but the president and his administration have been waging an all-out war on Congress’s once-sacrosanct power of the purse.

In an effort spearheaded by Russell Vought, director of the Office of Management and Budget and a key architect of the Heritage Foundation’s Project 2025, the White House has unilaterally canceled billions of dollars of spending approved by Congress. It has withheld funds for both Head Start and the Federal Emergency Management Agency; for grants issued by the National Institutes of Health and for funds allocated under the Inflation Reduction Act. According to the Government Accountability Office, a watchdog agency within the legislative branch, the administration is engaged in serial violations of the Impoundment Control Act, a Watergate-era law meant to block presidential attempts to rewrite or otherwise ignore congressional appropriations.

In an April hearing before the Senate Budget Committee, Vought denied accusations from Democrats that the White House had broken the law. “We have not impounded anything,” Vought said. But what he has done is try to run out the fiscal clock on spending funds through the end of the government’s fiscal year, which closes Sept. 30. To do this, he is using a presidential request to Congress to not spend the appropriation, called a rescission, as a means of delay.

When the president requests a rescission, the money is put on hold for 45 days. If it’s done just before the end of the fiscal year, the White House can effectively cancel the appropriation, since the funds will have expired by the time Congress votes on the rescission request. This is known as a “pocket rescission,” and it is a way to game the process so that the president can pick and choose what he wants to spend.

Trump’s attempt last week to slash roughly $800 million in spending on refugee resettlement, grants to migrant students and funds for minority businesses was a pocket rescission — an attempt to get around Congress’s spending authority.

It is difficult to overstate the way this subverts the basic structure of the American system. The power of the purse is paramount — it gives Congress ultimate authority over the entire operation of government. A president who wields this power is a president who can effectively cancel any law or nullify any agency he dislikes by refusing to spend the money appropriated for it.

The framers placed the power of the purse in the legislature, and specifically in the House of Representatives, because they believed it was important to tie it as closely as possible to the direct interests of the people. In so doing, they were informed by the experience of 17th-century England and Parliament’s clash with monarchical power during and after the English Civil War. To place the power to spend — and tax — in the hands of the people, however defined, was to safeguard liberty from the grasping hands of a tyrannical king or corrupt executive.

Trump’s attempt to seize spending power from Congress is not just about his preferred policies; it is also about his effort to etch himself into the nation’s built landscape with new structures and monuments. Hundreds of millions, if not billions, of dollars in taxpayer funds are flowing to the president’s ballroom and triumphal arch, among other supposed beautification projects. This is true despite the fact that Congress has yet to make a specific appropriation for Trump’s gaudy revamp of the nation’s capital.

But much of the trouble involves the president treating the public treasury as his own to use as he sees fit. Trump rejects any distinction between himself and the office he holds. The presidency belongs to him, as does the nation itself. (This helps explain why he felt he could remove journalists from the White House. In his mind, they are in his house, accountable only to him.)

And if it all belongs to him, then who is to say that he can’t decide what he wants to spend? Who has the right to tell him anything at all?

SUMMARY

The OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna, have pulled out of a $25 million donation that they had planned to give to a leading artificial intelligence advocacy group, a sign of how sensitive the company has become to the growing backlash to A.I. The group, a super PAC called Leading the Future, said last summer and repeated in later comments that the Brockmans planned to donate a total of $50 million, with the first $25 million in 2025 and a second $25 million this year. Mr. Brockman’s support for Leading the Future has been divisive inside OpenAI, The New York Times reported in June, with top policy executives trying to distance themselves from the super PAC.

ARTICLE

OpenAI Executive Backs Out of Second $25 Million Donation to A.I. Super PAC
Greg Brockman, OpenAI’s president and co-founder, said internally that the super PAC, Leading the Future, had become a “distraction” for the A.I. company.
By Theodore Schleifer and Mike Isaac
Published 2026-09-30 21:11 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/technology/openai-brockman-super-pac-leading-the-future.html

The OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna, have pulled out of a $25 million donation that they had planned to give to a leading artificial intelligence advocacy group, a sign of how sensitive the company has become to the growing backlash to A.I.

The group, a super PAC called Leading the Future, said last summer and repeated in later comments that the Brockmans planned to donate a total of $50 million, with the first $25 million in 2025 and a second $25 million this year. That second commitment has since wilted away.

Mr. Brockman’s retrenchment was never announced publicly. But inside OpenAI, the 38-year-old executive shared in June that he had no plans to make additional donations beyond the first $25 million.

“I also want to say that I feel terrible about the fact that LTF keeps reflecting on the company and become so much of a distraction for people here,” Mr. Brockman wrote that month in a Slack message obtained by The New York Times. “I’ve been thinking hard about how to turn the ship on it. We’ve donated $25m so far, and have no plans to donate more at this time.”

OpenAI has drawn fire for a host of safety concerns and the A.I. industry’s lobbying effort has attracted scrutiny in recent months. Some in the industry view Leading the Future as too dismissive of calls for A.I. safety, just as OpenAI tries to stake out a middle ground of sorts. Several ideological allies of the super PAC have also had issues with the group’s at-times aggressive tactics against opponents, including a high-profile effort against a New York congressional candidate.

In June, 10 days before Mr. Brockman’s internal message, OpenAI published an unusual blog post distancing itself from the super PAC.

“OpenAI does not direct the activities of LTF, or have visibility into their operations,” the San Francisco company wrote, adding in bold: “We want to be explicit: No outside political group speaks for OpenAI or represents our company’s views.”

Mr. Brockman, who increasingly oversees day-to-day management at OpenAI, has aligned himself tightly with the Trump administration, and appeared on Tuesday at an A.I. policy meeting hosted by President Trump. He has said his donations to Leading the Future, along with another $25 million he and his wife gave last year to Mr. Trump’s super PAC, are in pursuit of backing “team humanity.”

“There’s a small number of politicians who I think — despite realizing it’s not the most popular thing — are really putting themselves out there to say, actually, we think [A.I.] is important for the country,” Mr. Brockman told Wired earlier this year. “Anything I can do to support this technology benefiting everyone is a thing that I will do. In this sense, maybe supporting the team is bigger than the people that I happen to be employed with. It’s really team humanity.”

Mr. Brockman’s support for Leading the Future has been divisive inside OpenAI, The New York Times reported in June, with top policy executives trying to distance themselves from the super PAC.

The super PAC told The Times in February that the Brockmans’s second $25 million donation would come in the first quarter of 2026. It did not, nor did it come in the second quarter. The third quarter ends Wednesday.

A representative for Mr. and Ms. Brockman declined to comment. Leading the Future declined to comment.

Leading the Future is not hurting for cash. It accepted $50 million from the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, which has invested in A.I. companies, and Leading the Future’s groups had about $43 million on hand as of June 30. After spending tens of millions of dollars on the primary season, the super PAC network has not done much spending ahead of the general election. The group’s allied nonprofit is focusing its spending on promoting data centers in a few key states.

(The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

Cade Metz and Sri Muppidi contributed reporting.

SUMMARY

An Ohio woman filed a lawsuit accusing a hospital and her doctors of amputating the wrong leg during an operation last year. The woman, Sharon Jacks, of Meigs County, Ohio, said her original surgery was intended for her right leg. Instead, her left leg was amputated at Selby General Hospital in September 2025, according to the lawsuit, which was filed this month in Washington County Court in Marietta, Ohio, where the hospital is based.

ARTICLE

Ohio Woman Sues Hospital After Wrong Leg Is Amputated
Sharon Jacks, 74, said she went into surgery for the amputation of her lower right leg last year, but her left leg was removed instead. She has accused Selby General Hospital of negligence.
By Johnny Diaz
Published 2026-09-29 21:32 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/29/us/amputee-wrong-leg-lawsuit-ohio.html

An Ohio woman filed a lawsuit accusing a hospital and her doctors of amputating the wrong leg during an operation last year. The 74-year-old woman is now a double amputee after the correct surgery was later performed at another facility.

The woman, Sharon Jacks, of Meigs County, Ohio, said her original surgery was intended for her right leg. Instead, her left leg was amputated at Selby General Hospital in September 2025, according to the lawsuit, which was filed this month in Washington County Court in Marietta, Ohio, where the hospital is based.

Ms. Jacks filed the lawsuit with her husband, Dannie. It accuses nine defendants, including the hospital and Ms. Jacks’s medical and surgical teams, of gross negligence, battery and reckless conduct.

She underwent the correct operation on her right leg four months later at another hospital in Ohio, her lawyer, Brad Layne, said in a statement on Tuesday.

Ms. Jacks has “suffered physical injury, permanent disability, pain and suffering, emotional distress, humiliation, loss of enjoyment of life, medical expenses and other damages,” according to the 32-page complaint.

“The conduct of defendants demonstrated a conscious disregard of fundamental safety principles universally recognized within the medical profession,” it added.

On Sept. 19, 2025, Ms. Jacks agreed to have her lower right leg amputated after her doctor recommended the procedure as part of a treatment plan for a diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma, a type of skin cancer, Mr. Layne said.

Ms. Jacks “consented only to surgery involving her right lower extremity,” the lawsuit said, noting she “never consented to amputation of her left lower extremity.”

Mr. Layne said that standard operating procedure requires a surgical team to take “surgical time outs” to verify that they are performing the right procedure in the right place on the right patient “before proceeding with surgery.”

Though medical records stated that “two time outs” had taken place, “the surgical team still amputated the wrong leg,” Mr. Layne added.

“The performance of surgery upon the wrong extremity constituted a complete failure of basic safety procedures,” the lawsuit says.

Selby General Hospital, part of the Memorial Health System in Ohio and West Virginia, did not respond to requests for comment on Tuesday. In a statement to WBNS-TV of Columbus, the hospital acknowledged mistakes and said “our expected operating room procedures were not followed.”

The statement added the medical workers who were involved in the surgery are “no longer in their positions.”

“We are saddened by what occurred, and our team continues to keep this patient and their family in our prayers,” the hospital’s statement said.

Ms. Jacks is requesting unspecified punitive and compensatory damages, her lawyer said.

Alain Delaquérière contributed research.

california-governor-race-debate-becerra-hilton.html

SUMMARY

The two candidates running for California governor will meet Wednesday for a nationally televised debate that is likely to be their only face-off before the Nov. 3 election. It’s been two decades since California voters elected a Republican to statewide office, so many Democratic candidates in the state have come to wage fiercer fights in the primary against party rivals and then kept a lower profile in less competitive general elections. Mr. Becerra has run a low-profile campaign, Ms. Nalder said, and many voters may be unfamiliar with Mr. Hilton unless they watch Fox News.

ARTICLE

California Governor Candidates to Face Off in Televised Debate
Xavier Becerra, a Democrat who served in the Biden administration, will debate Steve Hilton, a Republican former talk show host, in what’s likely to be their only face-off before the election.
By Laurel Rosenhall
Published 2026-09-30 12:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/california-governor-race-debate-becerra-hilton.html

The two candidates running for California governor will meet Wednesday for a nationally televised debate that is likely to be their only face-off before the Nov. 3 election.

After a wild primary campaign this year, the governor’s race has settled into a low-key affair. Xavier Becerra, a Democrat who served as health and human services secretary under President Joseph R. Biden Jr., is a heavy favorite in a state dominated by his party. He is facing Steve Hilton, a Republican who was once a Fox News television host and an aide to David Cameron, the former British prime minister.

CNN will host the debate at 6 p.m. local time, just days before ballots begin landing in voters’ mailboxes.

Univision, the Spanish-language network, told The New York Times that both candidates have also agreed to participate in a town-hall-style forum on Oct. 20. But the candidates will not appear at the same time at that event.

Mr. Hilton, 57, who has lagged in polls and fund-raising, stands to gain more than Mr. Becerra from the national exposure that Wednesday’s debate will provide. He has been traveling the state to hold campaign events and sit for media interviews, trying to catch voters’ attention however he can.

By comparison, Mr. Becerra, 68, has made limited public appearances since the June primary. It’s been two decades since California voters elected a Republican to statewide office, so many Democratic candidates in the state have come to wage fiercer fights in the primary against party rivals and then kept a lower profile in less competitive general elections.

The two men are vying to lead a state during a moment of economic pessimism, recent polling shows. Price increases and high housing costs are straining many households, and reducing the cost of living is a top priority for a plurality of likely voters.

Gov. Gavin Newsom, who must leave office in January because of term limits, made sparring with President Trump a core part of his strategy as governor. The candidates running to replace him are taking cues, as Mr. Trump remains deeply unpopular in California.

Mr. Becerra has attacked Mr. Trump’s moves to restrict voting access while serving as an adviser on a lawsuit against a Republican sheriff who seized ballots and while campaigning against a California ballot measure to require voter identification. Mr. Becerra was California’s attorney general before he worked for the Biden administration.

“It’s really a threat to our democracy, and he’s working hard to protect people’s right to vote,” said Jonathan Underland, a spokesman for Mr. Becerra.

Mr. Hilton got Mr. Trump’s endorsement, which may have benefited him in the primary but now requires a difficult balancing act. He is trying to appeal to California voters who dislike the president while still keeping MAGA voters in his camp.

“Can you be anti-Trump but still vote for me?” Mr. Hilton asked in a full-page newspaper ad this summer that outlined the reasons he believed voters who oppose the president should still support him.

He said he’s met many voters on the campaign trail who tell him, “One-party rule just isn’t working, and we need a bit of balance.”

“I hear that often,” Mr. Hilton said in an interview.

For the Univision town halls in October, the candidates will appear separately and take questions from the audience. Mr. Becerra will address voters in Spanish, which he grew up speaking in California with his parents, who immigrated from Mexico. An interpreter will translate the responses given by Mr. Hilton, who grew up in England with parents who emigrated there from Hungary.

Most voters view debates as a partisan “team sport,” said Kim Nalder, a political science professor who leads the Project for an Informed Electorate at California State University, Sacramento. But she said that the debate may help some voters decide whom to support given that many are still learning about the candidates.

Mr. Becerra has run a low-profile campaign, Ms. Nalder said, and many voters may be unfamiliar with Mr. Hilton unless they watch Fox News.

“In this particular case, I think it is possible that some persuasion might happen because the impressions are not already formed,” Ms. Nalder said.

In general, she said, televised political debates have had less impact in recent years as media habits have changed and candidates have focused more on turning out their supporters rather than persuading undecided voters to choose them.

This summer, Mr. Hilton called for at least six debates. But front-runners like Mr. Becerra who enjoy a lopsided partisan advantage often decide that they have more to lose than gain from debating.

Mr. Newsom was even more elusive than Mr. Becerra in 2018, the last time California had an open race for governor. The two candidates met for just one debate ahead of the general election — and very few people saw it.

Mr. Newsom, a Democrat who was lieutenant governor, debated John Cox, a Republican businessman, on the radio. No television cameras were allowed to broadcast the event. And it took place in the middle of a Monday morning.

SUMMARY

A federal court on Wednesday ordered a pause on the execution of Christa Pike, convicted of the murder of a classmate in 1995, just hours before she was set to die by lethal injection in Nashville. Ms. Pike, 50, would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. The lone woman on Tennessee’s death row, Ms. Pike has expressed remorse for her crime.

ARTICLE

Court Pauses Execution of Tennessee’s Lone Woman on Death Row
Christa Pike tortured and murdered a classmate in 1995. She had been set to die on Wednesday, the first woman executed in the state in 200 years.
By Emily Cochrane
Published 2026-09-30 14:14 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/christa-pike-stay-execution-tennessee.html

A federal court on Wednesday ordered a pause on the execution of Christa Pike, convicted of the murder of a classmate in 1995, just hours before she was set to die by lethal injection in Nashville.

Ms. Pike, 50, would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. But her lawyers mounted a fierce last-ditch campaign to stop the execution, arguing that her defense at her initial trial had failed to consider her history of child sexual abuse and neglect.

The ruling came after the Supreme Court on Tuesday had declined to intervene in the execution. Gov. Bill Lee, a Republican, also denied a request to allow Ms. Pike to serve out the remainder of her life in prison.

The office of Jonathan Skrmetti, Tennessee’s attorney general, quickly appealed directly to the U.S. Supreme Court after Wednesday’s ruling, calling it a “technical issue” and vowing to “advocate for the lawfully-imposed sentence.”

Tennessee’s “strong interest in finality and the surviving victims’ right to closure require rejection,” the state wrote in its filing.

The execution had been scheduled for 10 a.m. in Nashville.

Reporters and witnesses had gathered Wednesday at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville. There were white and purple mums on display outside, near large posters of Colleen Slemmer, the 19-year-old student Ms. Pike and two others tortured and killed in 1995. Ms. Slemmer’s family, steadfast in their support of the execution over three decades, had cobbled together the money needed to drive from their Florida home.

But on Wednesday, a divided panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit said the pause was necessary to consider the new arguments from Ms. Pike’s legal team and the state’s response.

“The interests of justice and the finality of Pike’s impending execution compel the entry of a short stay of execution in order to properly analyze the parties’ fully briefed arguments,” Judge Jane B. Stranch wrote, joined by Judge Karen Moore.

The court’s order amounted to at least a brief reprieve for Ms. Pike while litigation continues.

It was the latest twist in a decades-long legal battle over the case. The lone woman on Tennessee’s death row, Ms. Pike has expressed remorse for her crime. She was diagnosed and treated while in prison for bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, which her lawyers said had contributed to her violence. Women who were incarcerated alongside Ms. Pike said she was a supportive and kind presence.

But May Martinez, Ms. Slemmer’s mother, remained adamant that Ms. Pike could not atone for the death of her daughter and should be executed.

“Christa Pike’s case has galvanized public opinion like few cases we have seen in recent years,” said Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center. She added that the last-minute stay “is a kind of high-wire balancing act, when the risks and stakes are at their most extreme.”

In the grassy fields outside the prison, where protesters gathered both in favor and against the death penalty, there was confusion and disbelief over the last-minute intervention. Some people walked away, frustrated that another legal hurdle had temporarily delayed the execution.

“I’m really sort of torn,” said Michelle van Allen, 48, who drove in from Kentucky and stood on the side marked off for supporters of Ms. Pike’s execution and the death penalty. The last-minute stay, she said, was “messing with people’s emotions.”

Across the fence separating the two sides, Veronica Stokes, 42, wiped away tears, emotional as she spoke about Ms. Pike and her opposition to the execution.

The pause, she said, “gives us more time to pray.”

Ann E. Marimow contributed reporting. Seamus Hughes contributed research.

ARTICLE

California Governor Candidates to Face Off in Televised Debate
Xavier Becerra, a Democrat who served in the Biden administration, will debate Steve Hilton, a Republican former talk show host, in what’s likely to be their only face-off before the election.
By Laurel Rosenhall
Published 2026-09-30 12:00 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/california-governor-race-debate-becerra-hilton.html

The two candidates running for California governor will meet Wednesday for a nationally televised debate that is likely to be their only face-off before the Nov. 3 election.

After a wild primary campaign this year, the governor’s race has settled into a low-key affair. Xavier Becerra, a Democrat who served as health and human services secretary under President Joseph R. Biden Jr., is a heavy favorite in a state dominated by his party. He is facing Steve Hilton, a Republican who was once a Fox News television host and an aide to David Cameron, the former British prime minister.

CNN will host the debate at 6 p.m. local time, just days before ballots begin landing in voters’ mailboxes.

Univision, the Spanish-language network, told The New York Times that both candidates have also agreed to participate in a town-hall-style forum on Oct. 20. But the candidates will not appear at the same time at that event.

Mr. Hilton, 57, who has lagged in polls and fund-raising, stands to gain more than Mr. Becerra from the national exposure that Wednesday’s debate will provide. He has been traveling the state to hold campaign events and sit for media interviews, trying to catch voters’ attention however he can.

By comparison, Mr. Becerra, 68, has made limited public appearances since the June primary. It’s been two decades since California voters elected a Republican to statewide office, so many Democratic candidates in the state have come to wage fiercer fights in the primary against party rivals and then kept a lower profile in less competitive general elections.

The two men are vying to lead a state during a moment of economic pessimism, recent polling shows. Price increases and high housing costs are straining many households, and reducing the cost of living is a top priority for a plurality of likely voters.

Gov. Gavin Newsom, who must leave office in January because of term limits, made sparring with President Trump a core part of his strategy as governor. The candidates running to replace him are taking cues, as Mr. Trump remains deeply unpopular in California.

Mr. Becerra has attacked Mr. Trump’s moves to restrict voting access while serving as an adviser on a lawsuit against a Republican sheriff who seized ballots and while campaigning against a California ballot measure to require voter identification. Mr. Becerra was California’s attorney general before he worked for the Biden administration.

“It’s really a threat to our democracy, and he’s working hard to protect people’s right to vote,” said Jonathan Underland, a spokesman for Mr. Becerra.

Mr. Hilton got Mr. Trump’s endorsement, which may have benefited him in the primary but now requires a difficult balancing act. He is trying to appeal to California voters who dislike the president while still keeping MAGA voters in his camp.

“Can you be anti-Trump but still vote for me?” Mr. Hilton asked in a full-page newspaper ad this summer that outlined the reasons he believed voters who oppose the president should still support him.

He said he’s met many voters on the campaign trail who tell him, “One-party rule just isn’t working, and we need a bit of balance.”

“I hear that often,” Mr. Hilton said in an interview.

For the Univision town halls in October, the candidates will appear separately and take questions from the audience. Mr. Becerra will address voters in Spanish, which he grew up speaking in California with his parents, who immigrated from Mexico. An interpreter will translate the responses given by Mr. Hilton, who grew up in England with parents who emigrated there from Hungary.

Most voters view debates as a partisan “team sport,” said Kim Nalder, a political science professor who leads the Project for an Informed Electorate at California State University, Sacramento. But she said that the debate may help some voters decide whom to support given that many are still learning about the candidates.

Mr. Becerra has run a low-profile campaign, Ms. Nalder said, and many voters may be unfamiliar with Mr. Hilton unless they watch Fox News.

“In this particular case, I think it is possible that some persuasion might happen because the impressions are not already formed,” Ms. Nalder said.

In general, she said, televised political debates have had less impact in recent years as media habits have changed and candidates have focused more on turning out their supporters rather than persuading undecided voters to choose them.

This summer, Mr. Hilton called for at least six debates. But front-runners like Mr. Becerra who enjoy a lopsided partisan advantage often decide that they have more to lose than gain from debating.

Mr. Newsom was even more elusive than Mr. Becerra in 2018, the last time California had an open race for governor. The two candidates met for just one debate ahead of the general election — and very few people saw it.

Mr. Newsom, a Democrat who was lieutenant governor, debated John Cox, a Republican businessman, on the radio. No television cameras were allowed to broadcast the event. And it took place in the middle of a Monday morning.

SUMMARY

ARTICLE

Congress Set to Leave Washington for the Midterms With No A.I. Progress
Senate Democrats blocked a measure that would encourage, but not require, states to protect consumers from power rate hikes tied to data center growth, and had no limits on A.I. use or deployment.
By Michael Gold and Cecilia Kang
Published 2026-09-30 16:55 UTC
https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/30/us/politics/congress-ai-safety.html

Facing a growing backlash over the boom in data center construction and widespread concern over the safety of artificial intelligence, Congress is set to depart Washington this week ahead of the midterm elections having accomplished nothing to address either issue.

Eager to show they hear the public alarm over A.I. as they fight to keep their majority, Republicans in the Senate on Wednesday attempted to bring up a bill intended to insulate Americans from rising electricity costs tied to data centers. But Democrats blocked it, noting that the legislation was not enforceable and arguing it would do little to significantly curb energy prices.

The bill, sponsored by Senator Jon Husted of Ohio, a Republican in a difficult re-election battle, also would not impose any regulation on the use or deployment of artificial intelligence in the wake of several revelations that A.I. agents evaded safeguards meant to constrain them.

With widespread disagreement over the best path forward but lawmakers eager to show voters progress on the issue before facing them in November, members of both parties have in recent days released a barrage of legislation, letters and statements of concern about A.I. and held a Senate hearing on “Rogue A.I.” on Wednesday afternoon as they rushed for the exits.

“I remain an A.I. optimist. I am not an A.I. doomer,” Senator Mark Warner, a Virginia Democrat who is also up for re-election, said. “But we are at a moment in time, particularly over the last few weeks, where I think the whole world has recognized we’ve got to do something.”

It comes as President Trump has played down A.I. safety risks and lawmakers in both parties remain uncertain about how to proceed on the issue as major players in the industry are spending heavily to influence the midterms. Though Mr. Trump convened top technology executives at the White House on Tuesday, the group agreed only to voluntary safety agreements and to follow the president’s preference in rebranding A.I. as “super intelligence.”

Some Republican senators have argued there is a need for stronger oversight. Senator Josh Hawley, Republican of Missouri, who has sponsored several pieces of legislation that would limit A.I., convened Wednesday’s hearing and said that companies should be subject to consequences when their technology is misused.

“It’s time to talk about what we’re going to do to hold the companies, the product makers accountable, rather than all of this talk about the end of the world,” Mr. Hawley said. None of the executives who joined the White House meeting attended; Mr. Hawley said that Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, had declined his invitation to participate.

Still, Republicans also are facing blowback for having included tax breaks in their major tax and spending cut legislation last year that benefited data center developers. Mr. Hawley has introduced legislation that would bar data centers from taking advantage of the incentives.

It is unclear whether Congress’s lack of action on the issue will have political consequences in November. A poll conducted this month by The New York Times and Siena University found that neither party had a clear advantage with voters on A.I., even as voters broadly opposed the construction of data centers.

Still, Democrats have sought to make data centers a central issue in competitive races across the country, including Mr. Husted’s in Ohio.

Before he was appointed to the Senate last year, Mr. Husted, the state’s lieutenant governor, backed tax incentives for data centers. Democrats have spent millions on television advertisements labeling him as the “face of data centers.” In August, Senate Republicans’ campaign arm distributed a memo warning that the issue was threatening Mr. Husted’s re-election bid.

Wednesday’s vote was seen as a potential boon for his campaign.

The legislation, which passed the House overwhelmingly earlier this month, would order state utility regulators to consider adopting rules requiring the centers to cover higher costs associated with their power use. But it would not force state regulators to follow federal standards when they are setting electricity rates, and it would give them two years to weigh changes.

Mr. Husted argued that the bill was the best mechanism available for Congress to quickly address energy prices. He pointed to its bipartisan support in the House and said it was the only legislation ready to make it to the president’s desk.

“This is the only game in town,” Mr. Husted said. “This bill passing is the only way to get a chance to prove to the American people before the midterm elections whose side you’re on.”

Democrats have argued that Mr. Husted’s bill is little more than a symbolic gesture that will have little effect on electricity costs. Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, pronounced it “toothless” and called for more meaningful regulations.

“An optional guardrail isn’t a guardrail at all,” Mr. Schumer said. “At a time when Americans are calling out for real guardrails on A.I., Senate Republicans are trying to secure an ineffectual participation trophy before they skip town.”

Though four Democrats joined Republicans, they still fell short of the 60-vote threshold required to proceed.

Republicans accused Democrats of putting politics first while seeking to flip Mr. Husted’s seat. But Senator John Kennedy, Republican of Louisiana, said he was frustrated that lawmakers had waited until the last minute to try to do something about data centers.

“That’s the sort of thing that I wish we’d started talking about a month or a month and a half ago and tried to work something out with the Democrats,” Mr. Kennedy said of Mr. Husted’s bill. Instead, he said, “we’re doing it at the last minute.”

Lawmakers from both parties have introduced a flurry of proposals hoping to slow the pace of A.I. development, impose guardrails and address the national security risks that could be posed by rogue A.I. agents. But their bills have largely gone nowhere in the face of deep disagreements both within the parties and between them.

Even lawmakers who are calling for swift regulation are being careful to say they do not want to stop A.I. development outright.

On Tuesday, three Democratic senators, including Mr. Warner, asked their colleagues to quickly take up and pass a bill that would establish a federal panel to oversee safety standards for A.I. models and to evaluate models before they were deployed.

But Mr. Warner framed the effort in part as a chance to stem the rising A.I. backlash.

“We should not miss the moment to put a safety protocol in place now,” Mr. Warner, whose state has benefited from data center growth, said. “If Congress goes out, God forbid we have an incident, A.I. is already suspect by most Americans. We could see the stop of innovation if an A.I. tool took over a hospital or water system.”

Senator Ted Cruz, Republican of Texas, objected and blocked the legislation, saying that he feared giving the government too much authority over A.I.

He also accused his colleagues of moving too quickly.

“Congress must not legislate on the issue of artificial intelligence hastily or in a closed manner,” he said.

SUMMARY
